text:
For several days this spring, trapped inside a Texas immigration detention center, Luis made frantic phone calls, one after the other, to everyone he could think of.

Could anyone help him find his 11-year-old son?

He’d last seen Andrés, a sensitive boy who likes to draw and paint, at an ICE holding facility near Camp East Montana, the sprawling detention center on a military base in El Paso where Luis now found himself.

Luis and Andrés had come to the United States from Venezuela in 2023. They were taken into custody together this past April after Luis, a construction worker, was arrested by federal agents outside his home. For hours, he and Andrés sat alone in a cell that felt to them like a dungeon. Around midnight, ICE officers showed up and ordered the boy to come with them.

No, Luis had pleaded. Andrés was just a kid—he needed his dad. But the officers seemed unmoved, he said, slipping on gloves and tugging on the boy’s arms as father and son clung to one another. Luis recalled that the officers promised Andrés would be in touch with him, so he let go and watched them take him away.

Three days had since gone by without a word, and Luis was in a state of panic. Neither he nor his family on the outside—Andrés’ mother and stepmom—could get any information on the child’s whereabouts. Worse, there was no sign of Andrés in ICE’s online detainee locator. Where had they taken him?

“Since he was little he’s been with me,” Luis told us later from detention, his voice filled with anguish. (Luis and Andrés are pseudonyms, and other family members’ names were changed to protect their privacy. Some attorneys who spoke with us also requested anonymity, in order to describe cases without exposing their clients.)

Finally, after about five days, Luis learned that ICE had transferred Andrés to the Office of Refugee Resettlement (ORR), an agency within the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) that cares for “unaccompanied” migrant children. Federal law defines unaccompanied minors as kids younger than 18 with no lawful immigration status and no parent or guardian in the United States available to care for them.

In the past, most unaccompanied minors in ORR custody were children who had recently crossed the US-Mexico border by themselves—not kids who arrived with a parent and had been living in the country for years. Andrés was never unaccompanied, but ICE confusingly labeled him that way. As a result, Luis learned, ORR would place him in temporary foster care with another Texas family.

Andrés felt betrayed, as a lawyer who later took his case recalled to us. “He was saying, ‘The government lied to me. I asked them to be with my dad, and they took us to a place, and we were separated.’”

Luis, stuck in detention, could not believe it. “You tricked me!” he thought angrily of ICE.

“You kidnapped my son.”

If this sounds familiar, it’s because something similar happened during the first Trump administration. In 2018, under the so-called zero tolerance policy, immigration agents tore families apart as they crossed the US-Mexico border, detaining parents and transferring their children to ORR custody. One of ORR’s responsibilities is to place unaccompanied kids in shelters, group homes, or foster care until they can be released to sponsors, who are often relatives. Historically, these arrangements were never intended for children who arrived with parents, but Trump’s advisers wagered that separating families would deter new migrants from making the trip. The zero-tolerance policy made national headlines and was denounced on both sides of the political aisle as inhumane, and a federal court eventually ruled it illegal.

Yet now, eight years later, the Trump administration is again separating families, except this time it’s doing so more quietly, and away from the border: Federal agents have picked up hundreds of immigrant children in the interior of the country and sent them to ORR, a vast departure from prior administrations, when interior referrals to the agency were rare. Anywhere from 500 to more than 700 of these kids, according to sources familiar with the cases, had previously crossed the border alone and spent time in ORR custody, but were living with their sponsors when ICE returned them to the agency. These “re-referrals” are the subject of lawsuits and investigations.

But there’s another group of kids that has received less attention—kids like Andrés who were sent to ORR even though they were never unaccompanied. It’s unclear how many children fall into this category, because ORR doesn’t systematically track them, and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) ignored our questions about them. But a source with knowledge of federal immigration data told us they now make up a “huge chunk” of ORR’s caseload.

We spoke with more than a dozen attorneys for this story who confirmed this trend, and were alarmed by it. “It’s confusing why those kids are being deemed unaccompanied,” says Diane de Gramont, also with the National Center for Youth Law, who recently raised this concern in court.

“We’re talking about kids who have a mom, a dad, and siblings who want them to be living with them,” says Jessica Richardson, an attorney who works with The Door, a New York nonprofit that helps detained minors. “They don’t want them to be in the shelter, and there’s absolutely no reason why they can’t go home to their families.”

It’s “family separation,” says Becky Wolozin, another attorney from the National Center for Youth Law, who notes that some of the children are as young as 8.

The administration is, in effect, creating unaccompanied minors. “They’re kidnapping people’s kids and keeping them in government custody,” says Jen Smyers, who served as ORR’s deputy director during the Biden administration. And why? It’s part of a “longer-term vision,” she suspects, “to make sure no one ever sends their kids to the US again.” And, other attorneys add, to deport those already here.

Andrés had been separated from his dad for days and was trying to be brave when an ORR social worker handed him the phone. It was his stepmom, Mariana.

She’d been searching for the 11-year-old all week, worried sick, when the agency finally let her know his whereabouts. “How are you?” she asked Andrés in the recorded call, which we translated from Spanish. “How are they treating you? Have you eaten?”

“It’s a particularly heartbreaking conversation,” says Michelle Brané, a renowned immigration expert who tried to help the family locate Andrés, “more for what he doesn’t say than for what he does.”

Andrés didn’t tell Mariana he was scared, for example. And he didn’t ask the kinds of questions one might expect, like “Where’s Dad?” or “What’s going on?” He didn’t talk much at all beyond reassuring her, that yes, he was behaving, and yes, they gave him food, and he had showered. When she asked if he had been crying, he said no.

“You’ll be with us soon,” she told him.

“He’s in survival mode,” says Brané, “a sweet little 11-year-old’s voice saying he’s strong and he’ll do what they tell him.”

Mariana wondered why Andrés hadn’t called sooner, and he said he wanted to, but they wouldn’t per let him. “They told you that?” she asked. He confirmed it, without specifying whom he was referring to. He did have one question: Could he see his baby brother? Mariana switched to a video call and pointed the camera toward the baby. “He doesn’t recognize me,” Andrés said quietly.

Andrés had met Mariana after he and his dad came to the United States and settled in El Paso. She was a recent immigrant from Colombia and had started dating Luis, who’d fled Venezuela, she said, because he supported the political opposition and faced threats. Luis was one of more than 600,000 Venezuelans with Temporary Protected Status, a humanitarian designation for people whose countries the government deems too dangerous to return to. (Andrés’ mom lives in Colombia.) Luis found a construction job, and he and Mariana had a baby in 2025. But that fall, the Supreme Court let President Trump revoke TPS for Venezuelans.

Luis and Andrés were at home the afternoon they were arrested. The boy was playing outside with friends, and Luis was just heading out to give an estimate on a construction job when SUVs blocked him in the driveway. Mariana walked out to see what was happening and saw masked ICE agents with guns.

She demanded a warrant, but the officers would not show her one. Luis had missed an immigration court hearing, they claimed, an allegation the family denies. Then, she recalls, an officer looked at Andrés and the baby in her arms, and asked whether Luis was their dad. When she said yes, the officers said they couldn’t take an infant born in the United States. But they loaded Andrés into a vehicle with his father as Luis cried for help.

And then they drove away.

Andrés and Luis were arrested together, but Trump’s ICE agents often deem children unaccompanied after encountering them alone in the community. In one case in Texas, a 15-year-old boy with an intellectual disability wandered away from his mom’s fruit stand to find a bathroom. When he didn’t return, she searched for him all over before reporting him missing. Authorities found him the next day but didn’t realize he was the same boy andfailed to locate a legal guardian. They contacted ICE, which sent him to ORR. He stayed in the agency’s care for 48 days, even as his mother pleaded for his release, and even after he developed appendicitis and was rushed to the hospital for emergency surgery.

Some kids are sent to ORR simply because they were in the wrong place at the wrong time. That was true for a 13-year-old girl in Pennsylvania who, after law enforcement encountered her at the scene of someone else’s arrest, was placed in ORR custody in New York and Texas for more than a year, even though she’d been living with her family when she was detained, according to an attorney who worked on the case.

Many others have been sent back to ORR after being accused of a minor crime like shoplifting, smoking, or fishing without a license. “If the child were a US citizen,” says Jennifer Vanegas, an attorney at the Young Center for Immigrant Children’s Rights, “the police would call the kid’s parents and send them home.”

DHS lists these petty infractions as reasons to re-refer children to ORR, but the justification is often pretextual, according to another source with knowledge of the cases. Charges are usually dismissed once the child is transferred to a shelter. “You could see a pattern: They were trying to find literally any basis to force an encounter with the child, seemingly fabricate or exaggerate the encounter, use that as the basis to take them into DHS custody, refer them to ORR, and then dismiss that charge,” the source noted. (DHS directed all questions involving ORR to Health and Human Services.)

As in Andrés’ case, parents aren’t always notified promptly that their child was transferred to ORR. An Ecuadorian father in Minneapolis “was horribly distraught” after his teenager didn’t come home in January, according to his attorney, Claire Glenn. The teen had called to tell his dad he was being arrested by ICE, but the agency claimed it didn’t know where he was. “I did not know whether ICE was lying or mistaken, or whether I had a very different case on my hand of a child that had been abducted by people who were impersonating ICE and perhaps were trafficking children,” Glenn says. She asked an investigator to locate the kid. It turned out he’d been sent to an ORR shelter in Michigan, even though he, like Andrés, came to the United States with his dad and was never unaccompanied.

In another case, a teen told ICE officers he lived with his dad down the block, but that his dad was deaf. They didn’t try to contact the father before sending his kid to ORR, according to an advocate. “There is a parent down the road, waiting for their child to come home,” says Kara Finck, a law professor at the University of Pennsylvania who was speaking about such cases in general. “To think that simply because your child is an immigrant, they can be declared unaccompanied and not returned to your care is a real assault on the very basic principles and tenets of family autonomy.”

Kids will say, “‘I told them my dad was at work a mile away or my mom was at home,” but the officers “don’t care,” former ORR deputy director Smyers told us.

When authorities do reach out, it can come with a risk. Last year, Mileidy Yamaly Contreras Flores got a call from the police department in Chelsea, Massachusetts. It was her 15-year-old son, who had immigrated with her from Honduras in 2019. He’d been in a fight and gotten arrested, and he needed an adult to pick him up at the station. Her husband went—and was detained by ICE after he arrived, according to a subsequent lawsuit. The teen was then sent to ORR in another state. By the time the suit was filed, he had been separated from his family for nearly seven months.

ICE initially sent Andrés out of state, too; he stayed in several hotel rooms in Arizona, according to a legal filing, before officers brought him back to Texas. It was determined he would live with a foster family but spend his days at an ORR shelter and attend school there.

Mariana could not understand why the government labeled her stepson unaccompanied. “The child was never alone,” she said.

DHS wouldn’t answer questions about how it makes such determinations or decides to separate immigrant parents and children instead of keeping them together in family detention. Asked about claims that the administration is “kidnapping” immigrant children, a spokesperson insisted: “ICE does not separate families.”

ORR said Andrés would remain in its care while officials carried out “the family reunification process,” but that process dragged on. In May, Andrés’ lawyer Kristin Etter asked a federal court to order his release, arguing that he was unlawfully detained. “[He] should not have been designated as an unaccompanied child because he was encountered together with his father and his stepmother,” she wrote in the petition. Family separation was unnecessary, Etter argued.

The boy and his family waited for the court to weigh in.

There are fewer unaccompanied minors in federal custody now than in the past. That’s largely because not as many kids have been entering the United States by themselves. ORR received just 3,500 referrals from July 2025 through May 2026, according to a source familiar with the data. But a record number of these children are being referred by ICE, an agency that in the past hasn’t sent many kids to ORR, at least compared with US Customs and Border Protection. As a result, the share of referrals from the nation’s interior, rather than the border—kids like Andrés who are already settled into American life—has increased dramatically.

Jonathan White, who managed ORR’s unaccompanied children program in 2017, says interior referrals represented between 3 and 5 percent of total referrals to the agency during the Obama administration and the first Trump administration. They were also “very rare” under Biden, Smyers says. But from July 2025 through May 2026, interior referrals were about 20 percent of the total, according to the source familiar with the data. Many of the attorneys we interviewed believe the shift from border to interior referrals has only grown more pronounced since then, and that interior referrals now make up about half of all new ORR cases.

This change matters enormously, advocates say, because the government’s shelter system wasn’t designed for children who are already settled in the United States. ORR staffers, too, are concerned, according to a source with knowledge of the situation: “I think most people agree that it’s only hurting kids and hurting families and not at all part of ORR’s central mission.”

Although federal law requires that minors be placed in the “least restrictive setting possible,” ORR’s shelters often have a carceral feel. The kids have to wear approved clothing, any valuables they have are confiscated, and they are allowed to eat and shower only at designated times. “I feel imprisoned and very closed in here,” a 16-year-old girl being held in a Texas ORR shelter said in a sworn legal declaration. “We cannot touch each other, we cannot hug, we cannot share food.”

“We’re putting them in prisons, essentially,” says attorney Richardson.

A young person who just crossed the border alone benefits from a bed and the chance to see a doctor, Smyers told us, but the “Americanized” immigrant kids experience a kind of culture shock when they’re detained. Instead of studying algebra or world history, as they would at their regular school, they might have to sit through ORR lessons on how to tell time, or how to name fruits and vegetables in English.

Children are also being held in custody longer. The average stay in ORR has increased from about one month under President Biden to roughly six months under Trump, according to the agency’s own data, and some kids are locked up for more than a year. ORR shelters are not equipped for long-term care, Smyers says, and children are struggling with their mental health. Suicidal ideation and behavioral problems are increasingly common, according to Smyers, attorneys who represent kids in ORR care, and other sources familiar with the agency’s work.

It is “the same routine every day,” says Alexa Sendukas, a Texas attorney who represents unaccompanied children. It’s “incredibly stressful and confusing, especially for the little ones. They don’t understand why they can’t get out.”

Attorneys blame Trump’s policy changes for the longer stays. Relatives can apply to sponsor the kids and bring them home, but the administration has made the application process more arduous, narrowing the types of accepted identification and proof-of-address documents, and requiring potential sponsors to attend in-person appointments. When children are re-referred, ORR requires their old sponsors—who were previously vetted and approved—to jump through these hoops too.

In a statement, ORR said the changes are intended to ensure that children are not placed with criminals. The Biden administration, “prioritized speed over safety,” a spokesperson said, resulting in “children being released to sponsors who abused, assaulted, or trafficked them.” DHS sent us a list of unnamed sponsors who it claimed had been arrested for domestic violence and other crimes. ORR is being “careful, not slow, because children’s lives are at stake,” the spokesperson added.

While some cases do raise legitimate welfare concerns, parents and guardians say the administration is depriving other children of homes that are perfectly safe.

Lawyers representing four children in shelters in Texas and New York who’d been re-referred to ORR sued the administration in February—the kids had been languishing in the agency’s care while their families tried, without success, to get them out. “These children have been forced to spend extremely long periods of time away from their family, friends, school, and community without justification,” their complaint reads.

It can be dangerous for guardians to try to get their children back. ORR shares information with ICE, which has arrested people who show up to complete fingerprinting and other sponsorship requirements. “They are using the children as bait,” Sendukas says. Fear can deter relatives from stepping up. The Acacia Center for Justice reported last year that releases from ORR to sponsors were “as low as they could possibly be.”

The new restrictions have “basically brought the entire [unaccompanied children] program to a halt,” says a source familiar with the situation. “Because sponsors can’t come forward, kids have nowhere else to go.” ORR, the source added, has become a “de-facto arm of DHS to facilitate their enforcement and detention mission.”

There’s a reason Congress placed ORR within HHS and not DHS. Namely, lawmakers didn’t think the agency overseeing the care of immigrant children should be the same one that handles enforcement and deportations. But those lines are now blurred.

Today, the administration offers teens it deems unaccompanied a payment of $2,500 or more if they’ll agree to leave the United States. Children also are given a handout that threatens lengthy detention and criminal prosecution of noncitizen parents should they take their case to court, as they are legally entitled to do. “You will be detained,” the memo promises, “for a prolonged period of time.”

The administration, Smyers says, is “scaring kids as a way to circumvent the law.”

“They are putting in place all of these different pressure points to force kids out of this country without due process and without any protections,” concurs Melissa Adamson, a senior attorney at the National Center for Youth Law.

All this appears to be part of a broader crackdown on immigrant children. Last year, the government tried to fly dozens of Guatemalan children from ORR shelters out of the country in the middle of the night, but a court intervened. ProPublica reported that unaccompanied minors have been detained and removed from the United States at three times the rate they were during Trump’s first term.

Making matters worse, immigrant children are contending with an acute shortage in legal representation. The administration recently ended a long-standing contract with an experienced nonprofit network that represented unaccompanied minors in court, handing the job instead to an organization founded by a former ICE agent. Increasingly, young children have been appearing before immigration judges without a lawyer.

“Donald Trump and his accomplices have directed every element of the federal government towards meeting their deportation quota, even if that means tearing families apart and traumatizing children,” Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.), the top Democrat on the committee with jurisdiction over ORR, whose office is preparing a report about children in the agency’s care, told us in a statement. “Just like Trump’s first term, the cruelty is the point. The individuals responsible for flouting federal laws and harming children in the process will be held to account.”

In court last month, a Justice Department attorney said ORR has a responsibility to accept referrals from other federal agencies that have deemed a child unaccompanied. That determination, by definition, “means that the child has no parent available to provide care or custody in the United States,” the attorney said.

But ORR officials don’t always agree with those assessments. Angie Salazar, the agency’s acting director, who came to ORR from ICE, has on occasion objected to classifying minors with a parent in the community as unaccompanied, according to a source familiar with internal deliberations. In a few cases, she has intervened personally, the source claimed, and demanded the child be released to their parent. But, Smyers points out, when there’s a disagreement, “unfortunately DHS normally wins.” (ORR and Salazar didn’t respond to a request for comment on this.)

Andrés’ father was released from detention on bond a few months after his arrest. He would soon have to return to Venezuela. But Andrés remained stuck in foster care and was struggling. At one point, ORR caseworkers told the family he was unable to sleep, and screaming for his parents at night; a doctor suggested medication to help him rest, but Luis and Mariana didn’t want to approve pharmaceuticals because of his young age.

The caseworkers also told Mariana that Andrés had been acting out. Another boy who lived with the foster family complained that he wanted to be left alone, but that Andrés, lonely and looking for a friend, kept trying to hug him. “My son is suffering,” Luis told us. “He’s small. He needs his father.”

While Luis was still in detention, Andrés had called and “started crying, saying that he didn’t want to be there anymore, that he wanted to be with us already,” Mariana said. She’d tried to become his sponsor but couldn’t meet ORR’s new requirements because she lacked a taxpayer ID number, so she withdrew her application.

Eventually, Andrés took what seemed like the only route left: He asked an immigration judge to let him go back to Venezuela and be reunited with his biological mom, who said she could meet him at the airport. The judge granted him voluntary departure in July.

This didn’t mean he was free to leave ORR care right away. There had been earthquakes in Venezuela. It might take weeks or months to arrange his travel, and who would watch him in the meantime? A federal judge found that even if he wasn’t unaccompanied when ICE separated him from his dad and stepmom, he was unaccompanied now. He “does not have a parent or legal guardian in the United States who ‘is available to provide care and physical custody,’” the judge wrote in an order dismissing Andrés’ petition to leave foster care. “[W]ithout a sponsor, he cannot be released.”

And so, Andrés waited, counting the days until he could board a flight to Venezuela and be with a parent again. Finally, in August, more than three months after his apprehension, he was allowed to travel.

But when the plane landed in Barcelona, Venezuela, Andrés’ mother was nowhere to be found. The US government hadn’t told the family what time, or even what day, he would arrive. “We just had to give her our best guess,” says Etter, Andrés’ attorney.

After all the fanfare around vetting sponsors, supposedly for the safety of the children, no one in the administration had bothered to make sure an adult would be present to receive Andrés on the other end. He ended up waiting on the side of the road outside the airport until later that night, when Etter was able to help his mom locate him.

“They literally were gonna fly an 11-year-old boy by himself and just dump him in Venezuela,” she says. “They don’t really care who the kids are going home to, or what they’re going home to, just as long as they’re going home.”

text:
​Nearly $70 million in funding for international education and foreign language programs is at stake under the Trump administration’s latest rescissions package, submitted to Congress just days before the end of the fiscal year.

The timing left lawmakers little opportunity to act on the request before the funding expired, a tactic known as a “pocket rescission.” In a Sept. 30 letter to congressional leaders, ACE and five other higher education associations called on Congress to reverse the rescission and take steps to prevent similar efforts in the future.

The $810 million fiscal year 2026 rescissions package continues a pattern of efforts to “change, terminate, and restructure programs that have been authorized and appropriated by Congress,” the groups wrote.

The package includes $70 million for International Education and Foreign Language Studies (IEFLS) Domestic Programs at the Department of Education. Congress had appropriated $70.4 million for the programs, which provide grants to colleges and universities to strengthen foreign language and international studies and increase the number of Americans with expertise in those areas.

“These programs serve a critical role in ensuring that America has sufficient expertise in areas vital to our national security and ability to compete globally,” the associations wrote.

The rescission request came after the Department of Education had already renamed its international education programs, entered into an interagency agreement with the Department of State, and held a grant competition in June.

Inside Higher Ed reported that approximately $69.6 million of the $70.4 million Congress provided for the domestic international education programs was set to expire at the end of the fiscal year. The programs have historically supported instruction in less commonly taught languages and helped develop expertise important to diplomacy, national security, international business, and other fields.

The latest action also follows funding disruptions for international education programs in fiscal year 2025, when previously appropriated funds were redirected to other grant programs, according to Inside Higher Ed.

The Government Accountability Office concluded Sept. 29 that the administration could not use the rescission request to withhold the appropriated funds through the end of the fiscal year. Under the Impoundment Control Act, funding proposed for rescission must be made available for obligation unless Congress acts to rescind it, GAO said.

ACE and the other associations said the broader concern is the growing uncertainty created when an administration terminates, redirects, or withholds money that Congress has already approved. They called on lawmakers to work to reverse the rescission and establish greater stability in the federal funding process.

title: ICE arrest in Baltimore backyard raises question: what can homeowners do? | WYPR
description:
When she looked outside, she saw ICE agents wrestling a man to the ground.
Attorneys who spoke with WYPR said homeowners’ rights in these situations are ultimately determined by the Supreme Court.
The Fourth Amendment protects people from “unreasonable searches and seizures,” including on private property.
“If police are tailing somebody, trying to make an arrest, and that person who is being chased goes from public property to private property as they try to escape police, then legally speaking, that may give police the right to enter private property to actually make the arrest,” Parsons said.
You shouldn't be able to just, like, track people onto private property.
text:
When Sydnee Logan bought her first home in Baltimore’s Patterson Park neighborhood two and a half years ago, she was drawn to the things that make city living feel like a community: the walkability, the nearby park and neighbors who know one another.

“I didn't expect to be able to get a house like this,” Logan said. “And I do really love my house. I love living near the park. There's always fun stuff happening. And for living in the city, parking on my side of the street is not terrible.”

She never imagined Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents would one day be part of that picture.

Last Monday morning, Logan was making a snack when she noticed the gate to her backyard was open. When she looked outside, she saw ICE agents wrestling a man to the ground.

Logan said she has no connection to the man who was arrested. She stayed inside and began recording. In the video, the man can be heard pleading as agents take him into custody.

Immigrations and Customs Enforcement has not responded to a request for comment.

The unexpected encounter left Logan with a question that is becoming relevant as immigration enforcement becomes increasingly visible across Maryland: What rights do homeowners have when ICE takes place on their property?

There is extensive guidance available for immigrants who encounter ICE. But the answers are less clear for homeowners caught in the middle.

Attorneys who spoke with WYPR said homeowners’ rights in these situations are ultimately determined by the Supreme Court. But there are a few laws on the books that generally explain what a homeowner can do.

The Fourth Amendment protects people from “unreasonable searches and seizures,” including on private property. But that protection is not absolute.

Matt Parsons, a community lawyer with the Baltimore Action Legal Team, said there are exceptions in which law enforcement can enter private property without a judicial warrant.

One is known as the “hot pursuit” exigency.

“If police are tailing somebody, trying to make an arrest, and that person who is being chased goes from public property to private property as they try to escape police, then legally speaking, that may give police the right to enter private property to actually make the arrest,” Parsons said.

Fatmata Barrie, an immigration attorney who has practiced law for more than 20 years, said homeowners can still assert their rights when ICE agents come onto private property.

That can include asking agents through a window to show a judicial warrant, declining to consent to entry and, depending on the circumstances, asking the person being arrested to step outside rather than allowing agents into the home.

Barrie said the details matter, including the jurisdiction and the circumstances surrounding the agents’ presence.

“Weigh and asses your own risk, especially if you’re Black and Brown,” she warned. “The biggest thing I always tell people is don’t physically interfere with the arrest.”

A new way to sue?

Maryland law also recently changed the options available to people who believe their constitutional rights have been violated by federal officials.

On Oct. 1, the No Kings Act, SB0346, took effect. It allows individuals and the Maryland attorney general to bring civil lawsuits in state court against federal officials who violate constitutional rights “under color of law.”

Lawsuits must be filed within five years.

If federal agents cause significant property damage, Parsons said homeowners may also have a potential avenue for seeking compensation under the Federal Tort Claims Act.

In Logan’s case, only a down spout was displaced.

Who Can you call?

Logan said she called Baltimore police, but they weren’t any help.

Parsons said people who witness ICE activity on private property should document the encounter.

Homeowners and witnesses can also report incidents to CASA’s hotline (1-888-214-6016) or contact their elected representatives.

Democratic Congressman Kweisi Mfume is a Ranking Member of the House Oversight Subcommittee on Government Operations.

A spokesperson didn’t say whether they are keeping track of such incidents, but sent the following statement:

"Under the Trump administration, ICE agents are recklessly running across our nation, repeatedly showing a blatant disregard for civil rights, human rights and, too often, human life," said Congressman Kweisi Mfume. “Any additional funding for ICE should be accompanied by enforceable safeguards, including appropriate training, body-worn cameras, meaningful reporting requirements and independent oversight. Federal agents must enforce the law while respecting the Constitution and the civil rights of every person.”

Home feels different

Logan is still processing what happened.

The backyard where Logan once grilled, barbecued and hosted gatherings is now the place where she watched an immigration arrest unfold.

“I really don't want to make this about me,” she said. “There should absolutely be ways for homeowners to hold ICE accountable. You shouldn't be able to just, like, track people onto private property. You shouldn't be able to attack people in schools. It's those things are unsafe.”

What Logan wants most is for homeowners and witnesses to know what they can do if something similar happens to them, and how they can safely support someone who has been detained.

At their home in Queensbury, Aurilio sees reminders of Carrion everywhere — his phone, his car, the everyday responsibilities he once helped shoulder. Even the couple’s cat, she said, seems to know he’s gone.

For Carrion, the separation has taken a different toll. He had once been optimistic about how his asylum case would play out, but that hope has faded. Upon being detained, he was promised a bond hearing within two weeks, and a habeas corpus petition was swiftly filed to halt his removal. But the court has yet to schedule a time for Carrion to appear before a judge.

More:ICE detentions at Malta office leave families waiting, legal challenges mounting

Aurilio, who is an American citizen, said her husband “can’t stand” being in Batavia anymore. As a result, the couple, married for three years, has chosen to have Carrion withdraw his asylum claim and voluntarily return to his home country of Peru.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Their decision reflects an experience becoming increasingly common across the Capital Region and the nation as immigration enforcement under President Donald J. Trump reshapes the options available to people pursuing legal pathways to citizenship. ICE detentions reached record highs over the summer; in the 33 days after Carrion’s detention alone, the agency arrested nearly 2,200 people across New York in a targeted operation.

Voluntary departure is a form of legal relief issued by an immigration judge and differs from self-deportation done through the U.S. Customs and Border Protection Home App, which the Trump administration has pushed and incentivized through thousand-dollar payments. During the second Trump administration, voluntary departures have increased sharply. The independent research organization Vera Institute reported in May that more than 10 times as many cases ended in voluntary departure as at the end of the previous administration’s term.

Feeling as if their options were limited, Aurilio said it was important to make the decision about Carrion’s future themselves. By leaving the country voluntarily, Carrion can keep pathways open for a future in the U.S., as opposed to having a judge issue a formal removal order that triggers a 10-year ban from reentering. And as third-country deportations remain in effect, they wanted to ensure Carrion would end up somewhere safe and familiar.

“It feels like you’re not really given a choice,” Aurilio said. “You either choose to leave or stay in detention until they decide to send you out of the country.”

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Right now, the road ahead remains uncertain. Carrion will not be given the chance to return to his home before leaving the U.S., and since the order for voluntary departure remains to be issued by a judge in a court with significant backlogs, Aurilio is not sure how much longer her husband will be in detention.

In Peru, Carrion will be able to connect with his adult children. But until then, Aurilio is worried about her husband’s physical health and mental fortitude. Several blood tests have shown Carrion experiencing dangerously high blood glucose levels, she said. He has no history of diabetes, which would offer a typical explanation for this condition, and has not been able to see a doctor regarding the condition, even as the ICE Health Service Corps reports “exceptional” care at the Batavia facility.

Aurilio has had her own health concerns — preexisting conditions that have worsened with her husband’s absence, making it harder for her to drive four hours to Buffalo to see him before he returns to Peru.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Her uncertainty over whether — or when — she will see Carrion again is a particular source of pain. It echoes the uncertainty that has come to shape her life over the past two months. To her, it feels as though her own life, too, has been suspended by decisions made far beyond her reach.

title: 'Do Something Democrat' Don Leonard hopes to flip the script in Ohio's 15th Congressional District
description:
Democrat Don Leonard is challenging Republican Congressman Mike Carey this November in Ohio's 15th Congressional District.
Don Leonard: What I believe is that the Democratic Party has got to fundamentally reinvent itself for the 21st Century.
Don Leonard on money in politics George Shillcock: So get into the idea of money in politics that you just talked about.
Don Leonard: I think it's a growing trend because the American people realize that you cannot serve two masters.
Don Leonard: You know, earlier you were asking me about what it means to be a "do-something Democrat."
text:
Democrat Don Leonard is challenging Republican Congressman Mike Carey this November in Ohio's 15th Congressional District.

Some election forecasters, such as the Cook Political Report, have the usually Republican- leaning district on its radar as "Likely Republican" in a midterm election where the Democratic Party expects to make large gains. Leonard, a former Ohio State University professor and west Columbus resident, believes he can unseat Carey, a German Village resident and former coal lobbyist.

WOSU has reached out to Carey several times for an interview, but have not received a response.

WOSU's George Shillcock spoke with Leonard about the race and whether he can buck the odds.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

George Shillcock: Don, thanks for joining us. During the campaign, I've noticed that you're framing yourself as a "do-something Democrat." I wanted to ask you, why that label?

Don Leonard: Yeah, we've got big problems right now, and we need big politics to solve those problems. What we see in America right now is an economy that no longer works for the people that create wealth. It works for people who sit at home refreshing the stock portfolios on their trust funds. What we need to do is create a politics where we actually create solutions that are as large as the problems that are facing my constituents here in central Ohio. And that means we got to get there and get stuff done.

George Shillcock: How are voters reacting when you tell them that you're a "do-something Democrat"? Is that something that they're pretty open to? I'm sure some Democrats feel a certain way about it. But what about other voters like Independents, maybe some Republicans who may even consider you?

Don Leonard: Yeah, I think we're in a moment as a country right now where folks realize that both parties have establishment practices that aren't serving the common person. So, they are looking for outside solutions. When you go back to 2016 and the fight inside the Democratic Party between Bernie Sanders and the "establishment pick," (and) Donald Trump staging a hostile takeover of the Republican Party. People are really frustrated with business as usual. What I think our opportunity is in the final days of MAGA is to show the American people that they're right to be angry, they're right to be frustrated, they're right to be looking for different alternatives, but let's ground those alternatives in things that we know to work. The kind of things that got us out of the Great Depression and saved the farmers in the Dust Bowl and helped the GIs when they came back from World War II buy homes and start families. Those are the kind of things that we know how to do. We just gotta learn from our parents and grandparents and then refresh those ideas for the 21st Century.

George Shillcock: Going to what you kind of talked about, I think people can see that both political parties are kind of having an imaging problem right now. Neither is really popular, but especially the Democrats in Congress are having a popularity problem. The label "do-something-Democrat" kind of implies the existence of "do-nothing-Democrats." I wanted to ask if you can kind of give a couple of examples? Who are people that don't really have this attitude that you're bringing to this campaign?

Don Leonard: You know, it's an astute observation. I was really inspired by Gov. [J.B.] Pritzker up in Illinois when he gave his speech in New Hampshire back in the spring of last year where he just lambasted "do-nothing Democrats." What I like to think is that we should put the focus on where we wanna go. So I'm less interested in pointing fingers at individuals and attacking the structure that undergirds why the Democratic Party... it's not just an image problem. It's a reputation problem. We do not have the reputation of getting things done in Washington. What we need to do is pass a 28th amendment in the year 2028 to get the corporate money and the foreign lobby money out of our politics. It's not the people going to Washington corrupt, it's the corrupting influence of money in our politics that's breaking our democracy. So unless we fix the underlying structure, it's absolutely impossible to escape from the place we're at.

George Shillcock: I did want to follow up real quick and check. There is some talk that there needs to be leadership change if the Democrats do take power in the Senate, in the House. Are you looking at that too? Like in the U.S. House, would you support U.S. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries taking the speaker's gavel or would you want to see a kind of different approach?

Don Leonard: What I believe is that the Democratic Party has got to fundamentally reinvent itself for the 21st Century. And if Speaker Jeffries is unable to do that, he will not have my vote.

Don Leonard on money in politics

George Shillcock: So get into the idea of money in politics that you just talked about. Obviously this traces back to Citizens United, the U.S. Supreme Court case. I wanted to ask you about this stance that you're taking. I believe you don't want corporate political action committee money, right, you're not taking corporate PAC (money). That's correct?

Don Leonard: Zero dollars (from) corporate PAC.

George Shillcock: Why take this stance? I've seen a lot of Democrats taking this stance. Why do you think this is a growing trend right now?

Don Leonard: I think it's a growing trend because the American people realize that you cannot serve two masters. And when you have the ability of corporations to give exorbitant amounts of money on what they call the "hard side" of the campaign, directly into the candidates' coffers, as well as into the "soft side" of the campaign, taking positions in these super PAC attack ads for or against you, what it does is it creates channels of dependency (on) corporations and billionaires. Unholy access to the politicians that are there not to serve corporations and billionaires, but to serve the people back home in their districts. So, it's simply an observation and it's fundamentally an experiment that we're running. Can a candidate that takes no money from corporations; can a candidate who takes no money from the Israeli or any other foreign lobby; can that candidate like that win in a seat like this here in central Ohio? That's the experiment we're running. We won our primary in a hotly-contested race with that (kind of) people power underpinning it. We're gonna take that to Nov. 3 and find out if we can scale this thing and show the nation what the people power can do if you take bold, credible stands against the corrupting influence of corporate PAC money.

George Shillcock: Another thing that's being floated in Congress, I believe there may have been a small bill passed regarding stock trading, right? Do you believe that congressmembers should be able to own stock? Or should that be restricted in some way? Or is that okay?

Don Leonard: Look, since my wife and I got to Ohio 10 years ago, we put all of our retirement savings in a S&P 500 index fund, and we just let it ride. I think a diversified portfolio of stock that you come into Congress with probably makes sense. What we can't have is day trading or moving your portfolio around based on information you have. About how government action is going to adversely or positively impact one community or another. So I am a staunch opponent to congressional stock trading and I believe that anyone who's willing to take time away from their jobs to go serve the public has a responsibility to eliminate any potential for conflicts of interest.

George Shillcock: You touched on this a minute ago, but ideological PACs. AIPAC is an example of one, the American Israeli Public Affairs Committee. How do you explain to voters the difference between those? One's coming from a business, one's coming a foreign lobby or even an ideological lobby. What's sort of the line you draw especially for that? Is it just foreign lobbying groups?

Don Leonard: I think it's about making sure we're representing the interests of our constituents. So I am a proud endorsee of the Planned Parenthood Action Fund, which is their political arm and their PAC. I stand for women's reproductive rights and I am happy to take money from an organization that collects donations from individuals to help them provide a future for people like my daughter that will give them the bodily autonomy that they so deserve under this nation of freedom.

George Shillcock: You're running against Congressman Mike Carey, who made his career and his money as a coal lobbyist. Obviously, the energy sector is probably a big donor throughout politics. Democrats get some, Republicans get some. Does that influence your take on this issue?

Don Leonard: I think it's a perfect example of what's so broken with our politics. There's nothing unique about Mike Carey. Mike Carey is a symptom of a deeper disease that is the unfettered corruption of our democracy by corporate interests working their way into the voting booth on Election Day. You can't be a registered lobbyist for 20 years, go to Congress, and remain the number one recipient of coal money, despite the fact that there's no coal mines in my district. There are no coal power plants in my district, and yet somehow Mike Carey is magically the number one recipient of coal industry money. If that doesn't tell you everything you need to know about who Mike Carey is and who he's fighting for, I don't know what does.

Don Leonard on data centers and education

George Shillcock: I wanted to touch on your background a little bit. You're a former OSU professor.

Don Leonard: That's right.

George Shillcock: Education right now, that may not be the top of people's minds, but the Trump administration has sought to dismantle the U.S. Department of Education, and I believe they're actively doing so, moving things like student loans to other places, and just generally less of a focus on the federal level for education. If you get to Congress, President Trump will still be the president at that time. What do you think Congress can do under a Republican president to try and change this trajectory that they've been taking?

Don Leonard: You know, earlier you were asking me about what it means to be a "do-something Democrat." I think another feature of that is that sometimes you fight the fights that you can win, but I think sometimes you just have to fight the fights that are worth fighting. And I think that's also what it means to be a "do-something Democrat." If Donald Trump wants to continue cutting after-school programs that protect our youth and keep them out of trouble as they're going into those critical, you know, hormonal years, how dare he, and make him veto my legislation, when we vote to restore funding to our K-12 institutions, when we go to restore funding for school districts accommodating kids with special needs that are right now laying off staff and struggling so hard to keep the little ones taken care of. How dare he be thinking about... I just learned yesterday, they're trying to pull student loans from folks who are going to college to do social work. Is cruelty really the point? Is that what they're try to do? To strip our society of the best and the brightest of us who are willing to make the least amount of money to try to help one another. I mean, if there's not an opportunity for us to stand up and say no more, I can't think what that would be in the moment we're in right now.

George Shillcock: One issue kind of roiling Ohio politics, but also national politics right now, is artificial intelligence and data centers. I wanted to ask you if you can explain any proposals you have regarding AI and data centers? Do you think there should be more of them? Do you think we should kind of rein this in and add some regulations?

Don Leonard: Look, I'm a huge fan of technology. I sometimes joke, if you were to come over to my house and look at how much electronics I own, you could probably open a Best Buy. I'm just a huge of fan of gadgetry. That being said, I am not against all data centers, but I am against dumb data centers. And what has happened in Ohio over the last 10 years is the force feeding of our region with these data centers that do nothing for our local tax base. They do nothing for our local employment, in terms of the creation of jobs. These things run on skeleton crews, and they take up our valuable farmland, they encroach themselves up against our residential communities, and they jack up our electricity prices, threaten to contaminate our water systems. It's just a lose, lose, lose, lose situation when these people of central Ohio are being asked to become a dumping ground for our nation's addiction to AI.

George Shillcock: I think some labor unions, especially, have spoken up and pushed back on anti-data center stances. They're okay with regulations and adding safeguards and making sure pollutants aren't bad and stuff like that, but they would push back and say "Hey, these are good for us. These do create temporary construction jobs that could lead to even more jobs for people in the trades." What would be your message to people like them?

Don Leonard: Look, I have so much empathy for those folks who are paying their mortgages and feeding their families with good paying union construction jobs. And that's why I am not against all data centers. What I am against and what I caution them against is allowing us to go through this boom and bust phase. You know, it's so rife in American history where there's some new technology, there's new opportunity. Folks come rushing into town, they go to exploit it. They exploit the local population and then they walk away and in five, 10 years, this stuff is obsolete. What I would rather have is these data centers being built as gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton has proposed on existing brownfield sites, former industrial sites that aren't taking up our valuable farmland, they're not encroaching against our residential communities and they're creating real opportunities in places that could surely use them. At the end of the day, what we need is a bill of rights as a nation for these data centers. That means specifying how far they have to be from our communities. That means making sure that they're not jacking up our electricity prices or putting us in a downward spiral of carbon emissions and climate crisis with the amount of power that they consume. And most of all, making sure that they actually give communities the opportunity to decide for themselves. Whether or not this is the right opportunity for them.

Leonard criticizes Trump administration's immigration actions and the Iran War

George Shillcock: One major issue that has happened since President Trump took his second term is immigration. We've seen a large crackdown on this and the administration revoked Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for Haitian immigrants. Elsewhere in the country, we saw ICE agents kill people, as well as arrest immigrants in the U.S. and here in Ohio. What has been your reaction as you've seen this immigration enforcement? And what do you think Congress can do to kind of curtail this?

Don Leonard: I think there's two things happening right now. First, we've got Donald Trump has a bone to pick with a congresswoman named Ilhan Omar up in Minnesota. So he sends federal agents in masks, walking around with high-powered weaponry to harass and repress the folks of Minneapolis, killing American citizens and terrorizing a community, all because he's got a bone to pick with a congresswoman. Secondly, when it comes to TPS, and the folks that are here fleeing violence and famine around the world. You mentioned Haiti. It's a place I know very well. I've been there a handful of times. It was a subject of my dissertation research. The folks of Haiti are facing a level of violence and hunger that is almost unprecedented in the Western hemisphere. And they were brought here as guests of the American people and taken to a community that was asking for workers. And the people of Springfield...have told me just how wonderful the contributions of Haitian Americans have been to that community. And for us to take these guests, for us take an incredible young man like Pierre Damas Bel and ask him to report to a detention center, a federal detention center and put on an ankle bracelet, this guy was a scholar. He was a national honor scholar. He was an athlete. He was ready to go to college on a soccer scholarship. He couldn't play soccer with that ankle bracelet. He had too much dignity to allow Donald Trump to treat him like a criminal, so he stepped in front of traffic and took his own life. In the wealthiest country in the world, this is not how we should treat our guests, especially the ones who are in most danger of being returned to places where they cannot protect themselves or their families.

George Shillcock: On that note, some Democrats want to restrict the budget for the Department of Homeland Security. Some Democrats are even saying we should abolish ICE and just get rid of it as an organization. And where do you stand on the range of maybe consequences that ICE should be facing?

Don Leonard: Look, we are a nation of laws. We've got to enforce our laws. We've gotta secure the southern border. It's the basis of beginning comprehensive immigration reform and providing dignity and compassion to those who are allowed by our government to come here without documents and contribute to our society and pay taxes into programs that they would never be able to draw from, right? We have got to maintain the rule of law. That being said, there is nothing about the modern iteration of ICE that we see today that has anything to do with our constitution, our nation of laws and our system of due process. They have turned a federal enforcement agency into the president's secret police, deploying in cities to harass populations at his whim. And we have got to replace ICE completely with the kind of humane law enforcement that treats nonviolent offenders of our immigration laws with the kinds of nonviolent responses that that requires. You know, it's not too far back in our country's recent history that immigration officers used to walk around with polo shirts and clipboards, not flack jackets and sidearms, right? They're walking around as if they're busting MS-13 or some criminal gang. And by all means, we have got to get those gangs and their drugs out of our country. But the folks that they are harassing and intimidating and shooting are unarmed, innocent people who are here without legal documents. That is not a criminal offense. That is a civil offense, and our immigration laws for those individuals should be enforced by civil means.

George Shillcock: I wanted to touch on foreign policy. We're seeing a growing number of Republicans call for an end to the Iran war as we're seeing gas and diesel prices spike. With the Iran War, it may wrap up before Democrats take office in January if there is a blue wave. What's going on with the Iran War in your mind? What do you think needs to happen if this is still ongoing come January, if you take office?

Don Leonard: Well, I'm glad the Republicans are finally coming around to the idea that the Iran War should be shut down. I wish it wasn't because gas prices were just too darn high and their constituents were, you know, PO'd about it. The fact of the matter is this. It is the responsibility of Congress, not the President, to make or declare war. It is a responsibility of the Congress, and not the president, to set our nation's tariff rates. And I think for decades now, we have allowed this steady creep of executive authority consuming more and more of the responsibilities of Congress. And as part of this new politics, we have got to send politicians to Washington on both sides that are willing to stand up to the president. And unfortunately, now we have to stand up to this Supreme Court as well, who's been packed by these justices groomed by the Federalist Society. If you don't know, Google it. This is a moment of constitutional crisis that I think has no precedent since at least the Civil War. We have got to send people to Washington who demand that Congress exercise its responsibilities, its powers and its checks and balances on executive and now judicial authority.

Leonard responds to attacks by Carey, national Republicans

George Shillcock: There is a full-page mailer that attacks you for being arrested before the primary in Grove City during the No Kings protest. I've never seen a full-paged mailer like that before. That's got to cost a lot of money, right. Going back to that incident, that is probably how a lot people were first introduced to you. Do you stand by your actions that day?

Don Leonard: One hundred percent. Let's review what happened. On a Saturday at 2 p.m. on March 28, I got up on the tailgate of a pickup truck with a bullhorn and was about 45 seconds into a two-minute speech when a police cruiser came sweeping up, asked me to step down, took my bullhorn, I complied. (Police) walked me over towards the sidewalk out of the lane of traffic, I complied (and) informed me that I'd violated a noise ordinance. I nodded in agreement and I said, "okay." Of course, I had given that same, you know, a speech at that same corner back in October at No Kings 2.0, but upon being informed that I had violated a noise ordinance, I told him to write me up. He went to his cruiser with my ID, came back, moved his cruisers down the road and asked me to walk away from the public and allow myself to become detained out of sight of the public. And I refused. At that moment, I realized that I was under guard with two officers behind me, a third officer trying to motion me away from the public. And in that moment I realized that this had nothing to do with a noise ordinance. If you don't know, it's basically like a parking ticket. You don't really don't get detained for violating a parking ordinance, right? At that movement, I realize that this had nothing do with enforcing a noise ordnance. This had to do with me exercising my First Amendment rights. So when he ordered me to step away from the observers, the witnesses and towards the cruiser, I refused. He ordered me a second time and I acknowledged his order and let him know I was refusing it. He arrested me, they booked me, they fingerprinted me, they took my mug shot and then two weeks later they dropped the charges.

The Grove City Police Chief went in front of City Council and apologized to me and to the people of Grove City for his failure to give clear, better instructions to his officers. You know, what I said to the people of Grove City is that their officers did treat me with respect. You know they didn't cinch up the cuffs too bad. They weren't wearing masks. They didn't jerk me around. But at the end of the day, these are the facts. A candidate for public office was standing on the back of a pickup truck holding a bullhorn at 2 p.m. on a Saturday during a protest and we're being told the people across the street couldn't even hear the bullhorn, because the traffic and the honking of people going by was too loud. And I think at the end of the day, it was just a really bad look for the Grove City Police Department. I think they know that. I think that they've apologized for that. I've apologized for violating their noise ordinance, which I was not aware of. And we made up and we go on. And anybody who wants to try to make anything else out of that? Well, I think we know what that's about.

George Shillcock: Your opponent has attacked you for something you said on a podcast. You said that you are not a Democratic Socialist, but even if you were, you'd lie to the people in the district in order to get their votes. Is that a correct quote? Is that what you actually said? Why say something like that?

Don Leonard: Unfortunately, it is absolutely a correct quote. I was on a podcast. It was about 50 minutes into an hour-long podcast. I was getting ready to talk about this exact issue of how we need a politics as big as the problems we face. And this Bernie Sanders quote came into my mind and I thought, you know what, I'm gonna quote him. And I thought "You know, what, if I quote Bernie Sanders, everybody's gonna think I'm some kind of Democratic Socialist." So I made a tongue in cheek joke. If you listen to the unaltered version of it. You can hear me kind of snickering and just sort of reflecting on how everybody calls somebody a socialist if they give Bernie Sanders any credit for anything, right? At the end of the day, I made a joke on a podcast. They're putting it out there as if it was some kind of hot mic, you know, secret backroom cocktail party kind of deal. And if anybody ought to be able to take a joke, it's the Republicans right now. They ought to take look at their own policies.

George Shillcock: I do need to ask are you lying? And if not, how can people trust you?

Don Leonard: Well first of all, I'd invite you to go to the podcast, it was called The Hilliard Beacon, and tune in, I think it was maybe around one minute, 50 seconds. Please listen to it in context. Second of all, unlike my opponent, I am showing up everywhere, and I allow everyone to film me at every event. We post, over the summer, we did a 15-stop listening tour where we invited folks from Piqua to Hillsboro to Washington Court House and everywhere in between to come out here, Republican, Independent, Democrat, film me, ask me questions, let's have a conversation. I am the most unscripted, unfiltered, un-firewalled candidate you will ever see. So I would invite you to come find me at some future event and ask me the question of your choice. At the end of the day, I am a person whose, you know, scholarly writings are still up on the internet from the time where I was a professor for the last 10 years. I'm a person who has a blog that's still up on the internet. If you're one of my Facebook friends, I haven't deleted any of my posts. If you like Reddit, you can probably figure out who I am on there. Folks, I'm just a common person bringing together a set of issues that I think we all care about, and I think if you take a look at me and then you take look at my opponent and where he gets his money from, well, I'll let you make up your own mind as who you think is the most trustworthy person in this race.

Can Ohio's 15th Congressional District be won? Leonard thinks so.

George Shillcock: Last topic, the 15th Congressional District, both in its current iteration and past iterations, hasn't really been friendly to Democrats, even in 2018, which was a previous blue wave. Is this district really winnable for Democrats? And if so, how do you get there in a year like this, where election forecasters are expecting pretty large Democratic gains?

Don Leonard: You know, we're gonna win our election this year if the voters have the opportunity to hear our message and what we're fighting for, and if they have a chance to get to know who their current congressman is and who he's been fighting for for the last five years in Washington. What concerns me the most is, how do we hold this district two years from now or four years from when the pendulum of politics swings away from the Democrats and towards the other guys? And I think the only answer to that is by rebuilding trust. Trust is not given, trust is earned. Trust is being able to pick up the phone, call a member of your congressperson's office, and get solutions to the problems facing everyday Americans. That's the trust we're gonna start building the day after we win on Nov. 3, and that's the trust that we're going to keep growing and demanding across the Democratic Party nationally so that we can truly know, so that the American people can truly know that there's only one party out there that's fighting for us, the working families of America.

George Shillcock: You're a first-time candidate. Not a lot of first-time candidates have success on the first try and they try and try again. Do you wanna keep running if this isn't your year?

Don Leonard: I am running right now despite all of my better instincts. My family lives paycheck to paycheck. We put our groceries on credit card if we have a problem with our car or something in the house breaks. I loved my day job working at Ohio State for the last 10 years and preparing the next generation of city planners. And as of January of last year, I'm the father to a beautiful baby girl. This job has a lot of downsides to it, but I am so determined to give my daughter a better future that this race in this moment means the world to me. What I can tell you is this, in the year and change that I've been on the trail, I've learned just how important it is that we recruit the right kind of people to run for office and that we embrace competitive primaries. So win or lose, I can promise you this, I'm gonna be out there finding the next school board members, the next city council members, the next state reps to help the country and the state of Ohio realize that we have an alternative to the last 20-25 years of Republican domination. They've been giving away the farm to corporate interests. We pay the highest property taxes as residents and small businesses and the lowest property taxes for corporations in this state. We have got to turn this ship around and by recruiting the right candidates, we can do that. Win or lose, I want to be part of the growing of the Ohio Democratic Party to make sure that the people of Ohio know that they have a better choice when they step into that ballot box.

George Shillcock: All right, that's all I wanted to ask. Don, thank you again so much for coming on. I really appreciate it.

title: Supreme Court's new term kicks off with blockbuster climate change case - OPB
description:
A new Supreme Court term begins Monday with arguments in a blockbuster case about the reach of state power.
In 2018, Boulder County slapped the giant energy companies Suncor Energy and Exxon Mobil with a lawsuit.
But the energy companies are asking the U.S. Supreme Court to throw out the case now.
The conservative supermajority on the Supreme Court may be uncomfortable letting state juries decide some of these pressing issues.
But legal experts say they’re not sure quite how the justices might shape a decision in the Boulder case.
text:
A new Supreme Court term begins Monday with arguments in a blockbuster case about the reach of state power.

Boulder, Colo., is suing two big energy companies, arguing they deceived people about the harms of fossil fuels and contributed to disasters that cost Boulder a lot of time and money.

The dispute could have ramifications far beyond the climate, to other areas where states are trying to hold companies accountable for their alleged harms to local communities.

In 2018, Boulder County slapped the giant energy companies Suncor Energy and Exxon Mobil with a lawsuit. Boulder argued the companies and a trade group knew decades ago that fossil fuels would hurt the environment, raising the risk of floods, extreme heat and wildfires.

Three years later, in late December 2021, the Marshall Fire swept across the county.

Daryl McCool left her home southeast of Boulder so fast she couldn’t remember whether she locked the front door.

As it turned out, that didn’t matter.

“There’s basically nothing left,” McCool said. “A 2,000-degree fire burns everything, like coins were melted, bicycles melted.”

The historic 1901 house where she raised her son had turned to ash. McCool spent years helping her neighbors file insurance papers and apply for grants to rebuild their homes. Now, she tries to educate people about the human costs of climate change.

Who has power to grapple with climate change

Corey Riday-White is legal director at the Center for Climate Integrity. It supports communities trying to hold oil companies responsible for environmental harms.

“This case represents whether or not we believe as a society that corporations should be held to the same standards that all of us are, right?” Riday-White said. “If you know you are going to cause harm, and you don’t tell someone, then you should help clean up that harm.”

Boulder’s lawsuit has not gone to trial; it’s still in the early stages in the Colorado court system. But the energy companies are asking the U.S. Supreme Court to throw out the case now. The companies say only the federal government has the power and expertise to grapple with something as big as climate change. To let Boulder’s case proceed, they say, would have huge implications.

Todd Zywicki is a professor at the Antonin Scalia Law School at George Mason University.

“This is about whether a bunch of rich hippies in Boulder County are allowed to dictate environment and energy policy to the entire rest of the world,” Zywicki said in a recent webinar about the case.

Exxon referred NPR to the company’s court filings. Suncor didn’t respond to an email requesting comment.

The Trump administration is siding with the energy companies, arguing global warming is a global issue.

“Essentially Boulder claims that Colorado can reach around the United States, the entirety of the United States, and to my mind, regulate production everywhere by attaching liability to it,” said Sai Prakash, a law professor at the University of Virginia who filed a friend of the court brief backing Suncor and Exxon.

“It Boulder can attach liability to these two companies … I think it can attach liability to thousands of others as well,” Prakash said.

Seeking to recover past and future costs

Boulder argues it’s not suing to regulate greenhouse gas emissions. Rather, it says, it wants to recover past and future costs of repairs, emergency services, and property damage.

Dozens of similar cases where states and municipalities are suing energy giants have been moving through the courts at early stages. Any Supreme Court ruling could have repercussions for many of them.

Jonathan Adler, a law professor at the College of William and Mary, points out in court papers that Congress has the authority to override state laws here, but federal lawmakers haven’t done anything.

Corey Riday-White, of the Center for Climate Integrity, said for the justices interested in ruling based on the text of the Constitution or federal statutes, there is not much to support Suncor and Exxon.

“They want the court to say, you can’t bring any of these cases in court because this is the purview of the federal government,” Riday-White said. “The problem is the big oil companies can’t point to any legal doctrine, any statute, any part of the Constitution that backs up that finding.”

How the court decides to draw the lines on state power could influence a lot more than climate litigation, according to Deepak Gupta, who regularly argues before the high court.

“Pollution by forever chemicals, nuisance suits over AI data centers, opioids litigation, all of these are about the local effects of conduct that runs across borders,” Gupta said at a recent briefing sponsored by Georgetown’s Supreme Court Institute.

The conservative supermajority on the Supreme Court may be uncomfortable letting state juries decide some of these pressing issues. But legal experts say they’re not sure quite how the justices might shape a decision in the Boulder case.

Louie Delaware, who lost his Boulder-area home in the Marshall fire, said he plans to be at the Supreme Court Monday as it hears arguments in the case. Delaware said he tried to fight off the fire with a garden hose, but he lacked the appropriate protective gear, so he realized that he needed to drive away quickly.

“You know it’s our responsibility to leave things better for the next generation,” Delaware said. “And the way we’re going right now is counter to what that’s been in the past.”

Last-minute Alito recusal

In a surprise move, the court notified lawyers in the case just one week before argument that Justice Samuel Alito had decided not to participate. The court clerk provided no explanation in his letter. But environmental organizations and watchdog groups had been calling for Alito’s recusal because of his investments in Phillips 66 and ConocoPhillips.

Justin Kloczko of the group Consumer Watchdog said the decision is “the right decision, and one he should have made from the start.”

“The public should not have to wonder whether a justice’s personal investments could benefit from a ruling that shields the fossil-fuel industry from liability,” Kloczko said in a written statement.

Alito’s decision to step aside means eight justices will hear the case. In the matter of a 4-4 tie, that means the decision of the Colorado Supreme Court—allowing Boulder’s lawsuit to proceed—will prevail.

But the high court may have left itself another option: among the questions the justices said they’ll consider is whether they have jurisdiction to hear the Suncor case now, because it’s still at an early stage in Colorado state courts.
