title: The Biggest Cases Coming in the Next Supreme Court Term | The New Republic
authors: Matt Ford, Cruel & Unusual Matt Ford, Blowing Smoke Aaron Regunberg, Babble On, On Matt Ford, Hafiz Rashid, Edith Olmsted, Ellie Quinlan Houghtaling
description:
Next week the Supreme Court will return from its summer recess to hear a new term of cases.
The Supreme Court has not heard a Second Amendment challenge to laws banning a specific type of firearm this century.
The Supreme Court has not elucidated the scope of the excessive fines clause or what counts as “excessive” in this context.
The Supreme Court will also tackle what we can call the “known unknowns.” These are cases that the court is likely to hear but hasn’t yet intervened in.
The Supreme Court rejected Trump’s legal bids to overturn the 2020 election six years ago.
text:
Next week the Supreme Court will return from its summer recess to hear a new term of cases. While the court is already slated to make rulings with far-reaching consequences, the most important decisions looming this term may not even be on its radar yet.

Earlier this week, the justices announced that they would take up what may be the most important case of the term. The Trump administration had asked the court to hear Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha to review lower court rulings against its mandatory-detention policy for undocumented immigrants. How the Supreme Court decides the case could have vast implications for the Trump administration’s ability to carry out mass deportations.

At issue in Rhoney is whether the federal government can indefinitely hold undocumented immigrants in custody while their deportation proceedings take place. Since at least the 1980s, immigration courts have routinely allowed them to post bond while they await the outcome of their cases. The Trump administration changed tack in July 2025, arguing that it could instead hold undocumented immigrants without bond.

To support this position, the administration cited a 1996 law known as the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act. Everyone calls it IIRIRA instead. Under IIRIRA, the Justice Department has claimed that one provision in the law requires federal officials to detain undocumented immigrants who illegally crossed the U.S. border. That provision says that “an alien who is an applicant for admission” into the United States “shall be detained” if “the examining immigration officer determines that an alien seeking admission is not clearly and beyond a doubt entitled to be admitted.”

To that end, the Justice Department has invoked the IIRIRA provision to justify holding any undocumented immigrant in custody without bond hearings until their deportation hearings are concluded—or, importantly, until they “voluntarily” agree to leave the country. Since the Trump administration has detained tens of thousands of immigrants in squalid conditions over the past 18 months, an unknown number of those held have agreed to forgo deportation hearings to leave the country.

Holding people indefinitely without due process has been illegal in the Anglo-American legal tradition since Magna Carta in 1215. More to the point, the administration’s policy appears to be based on a misreading of federal law. While the provision they cite does require mandatory detention in a narrow set of circumstances, it only applies to people who are an “applicant for admission”—meaning that they presented themselves at the U.S. border for entry.

Ricardo Barbosa da Cunha, the plaintiff in this case, did no such thing. He crossed the U.S. border in 2004 after traveling from his native Brazil through Mexico. He and his family have lived in Massachusetts for the last two decades, where he owns a small construction business. Barbosa da Cunha has had a legal work authorization since 2016 and has no criminal record. Federal immigration agents arrested him on the way to work last year and have kept him in custody since then.

In April, the Second Circuit Court of Appeals sided with him and rejected the administration’s interpretation of IIRIRA. The section it cited does not apply to undocumented immigrants “who were not apprehended while entering the country or shortly thereafter,” Judge Joseph Bianco wrote for the court. Instead, immigrants like Barbosa da Cunha fall under a different section of IIRIRA that does allow for bond hearings before an immigration judge.

Lower courts are often divided and splintered about how to read certain federal statutes. This case is not one of them. The New York Times reported earlier this week that more than 500 federal district-court judges have rejected the Trump administration’s mandatory-detention policy as unlawful, as have nine of the 11 federal circuit courts of appeal. The Trump administration is hoping that it can garner at least five votes from the justices to outweigh them.

The Supreme Court will also hear another major immigration case later this term on the Trump administration’s aggressive approach to third-country removals. Most deported immigrants have typically been returned to their home countries, aside from recent arrivals at the U.S. border in Mexico who are returned there. In their zeal to remove as many immigrants as possible from the United States, Trump administration officials have shipped thousands of them to countries in Africa that agree to take them in exchange for favorable diplomatic and financial treatment.

Multiple lower courts have held that immigrants must be able to challenge third-country removals, which the Trump administration has vociferously rejected. Some deportation flights have stranded immigrants in countries where they do not speak the language or—as in the case of South Sudan—where they are at risk for torture and abuse by local officials. The Supreme Court declined to forbid the Trump administration from carrying out these types of deportations while it considers the case—a grim sign for the immigrants’ hopes that the justices will ultimately side with them.

The first case of the term next week will also be one of the term’s most important decisions: Suncor Energy v. County Commissioners of Boulder County. At issue is whether local communities that are harmed by climate change and its effects can seek damages in state courts from oil and gas companies that contributed to higher carbon emissions. The town of Boulder, Colorado, argued that its claims fit well within traditional causes of action for harms caused by companies.

Fossil fuel companies have urged the Supreme Court to reject these claims, arguing that federal law preempts the town’s lawsuit and that state courts cannot hear them at all. The high court may also decide to punt the case on procedural grounds for now. Though the court is hardly averse to ruling in favor of the fossil fuel industry, Boulder received some good news on Monday when Justice Samuel Alito announced that he would recuse himself from the case after resisting past suggestions to do so.

In Viramontes v. Cook County, the justices will examine whether state assault-weapons bans can survive under the court’s new Second Amendment precedents. The plaintiffs in the case are challenging bans on AR-15s and similar rifles in both Illinois’s most populous county and the state of Connecticut. (The justices consolidated them on appeal.) Almost a dozen states have similar laws on the books. The Supreme Court has not heard a Second Amendment challenge to laws banning a specific type of firearm this century.

More than a few plaintiffs asked it to do so after proclaiming an individual right to bear arms in 2008, but the court long declined to hear such cases. In 2022, the court’s conservative majority made it substantially easier for gun owners to challenge gun laws when it laid out a new, stricter Second Amendment test that requires states to find a “historical analogue” for laws to survive judicial scrutiny. How that test comports with earlier Supreme Court decisions that allow states to restrict “dangerous” and “unusual” firearms will be the central question for the court.

On the constitutional front, one of the most curious upcoming cases this term is Jouppi v. Arizona. The case centers on an Alaska pilot who flew into a dry town with a passenger who had a six pack of beer in their possession. In response, state officials charged the pilot with violating state liquor laws—which are aimed at reducing alcoholism and domestic violence in the state’s isolated interior—and seized his airplane, which is valued at more than $77,000.

Jouppi, the pilot, argued that confiscating his Cessna violated the Eighth Amendment, which forbids levying excessive fines as punishment for a crime. He argued that seizing an airplane for carrying a few cans of beer met that threshold. The Supreme Court has not elucidated the scope of the excessive fines clause or what counts as “excessive” in this context. How the court decides the case could affect criminal forfeiture laws across the country.

The Supreme Court will also tackle what we can call the “known unknowns.” These are cases that the court is likely to hear but hasn’t yet intervened in. One area where the court may feel compelled to weigh in is on legal challenges to prediction markets and sports betting. A Supreme Court ruling in 2018 struck down a federal ban on sports betting, allowing dozens of states to pass laws to legalize and regulate sportsbooks within their borders. Last year, prediction-market companies like Kalshi and Polymarket also began allowing users to place wagers on the outcomes of professional and amateur sports at all levels in all 50 states, even those that have not legalized sports betting.

The prediction-market industry argued that it wasn’t really offering “bets.” Instead, it claims to be offering “swaps,” where customers could buy contracts on its exchanges that would pay out depending on the outcome of an event. (As courts have noted, its advertising often said otherwise.) The industry also argued that it was regulated by federal law through the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, preempting state enforcement with an extremely favorable regulatory regime from the Trump administration.

State regulators in Nevada and state attorneys general in California, New York, and other states sued Kalshi and Polymarket nonetheless for operating illegal sports-betting websites in their states. The states won a major victory over the summer when the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that prediction-market swaps on sports are bets and that federal law on derivatives exchanges hadn’t displace the states’ traditional authority to regulate gambling. At least one other circuit reached the opposite conclusion, making it likely that the justices will need to resolve the split in the coming term.

Another obvious area where the court will likely feel compelled to involve itself is on President Donald Trump’s extraordinary claims of executive power. During the summer recess, for example, the Supreme Court forbade a lower court from blocking construction of an illegal ballroom on the ruins of the White House’s East Wing, over the dissents of Chief Justice John Roberts and the court’s three liberal justices. Litigation over the fate of the Kennedy Center, which Trump has demanded to be illegally renamed in his honor or face financial ruin, or a heavily armed 250-foot arch outside Arlington National Cemetery, could also reach the court this term.

Since it is an election year, among the most important cases will be election-related ones. The court routinely hears a small number of cases involving ongoing elections on the shadow docket every two years, usually involving last-minute changes or new restrictions. Since last year, the justices have already considered a spate of cases involving the partisan-gerrymandering wars, which it largely let play out without further intervention. Some of those gerrymanders came about after the court effectively legalized racial gerrymandering last term.

This time, the concern is about what Trump could do after the election if he and Republicans suffer major defeats and lose control of Congress, as polls suggest they likely will. The Justice Department’s seizure of ballots in Georgia earlier this year stoked fears among voting rights groups that the administration will interfere in the certification of state results under the false guise of investigating voter fraud. The Supreme Court rejected Trump’s legal bids to overturn the 2020 election six years ago. How they respond to any illegal and extralegal attempts to corrupt the 2026 midterms could be the most important test that the justices face this term.

“Since the start of the second Trump Administration, the federal government has often refused to provide local law enforcement with critical evidence in shootings and other use-of-force incidents involving ICE and CBP officers.
Several months later, ICE agents killed Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Texas and have also refused to work with state and local law enforcement.

text:
Washington, DC – Recently, Congresswoman Delia C. Ramirez (IL-03), Ranking Member of a Committee on Homeland Security Subcommittee, and Congresswoman Andrea Salinas (OR-06) introducedH.R.10698(link is external), the ICE Shootings Transparency Act, to provide local and state law enforcement agencies unfettered access to evidence in Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection (CBP) officer-involved shootings and other use of force incidents.

“DHS lies to avoid accountability. DHS agents use reckless and unlawful force, and then DHS issues public statements justifying the use of force that are repeatedly proven false or highly misleading,” said Congresswoman Ramirez. “That’s why I’m joining Rep. Salinas to require DHS and the Attorney General to share evidence related to shootings by ICE and CBP officers with local law enforcement agencies to carry out investigations. We will not stop until we have justice for every person who was killed or harmed at the hands of DHS agents. We will reimagine true safety, abolish ICE, dismantle DHS, and hold all perpetrators accountable.”

“When an ICE or CBP agent kills or injures someone in our community, transparency needs to be the bare minimum,” said Rep. Salinas. “Since the start of the second Trump Administration, the federal government has often refused to provide local law enforcement with critical evidence in shootings and other use-of-force incidents involving ICE and CBP officers. My bill would ensure that when these incidents occur, state and local law enforcement agencies would have unrestricted access to this evidence to deliver full justice to victims and their families.”

In January 2026, when ICE killed Renee Good, Minnesota’s Bureau of Criminal Apprehension was tapped to conduct a joint investigation with the FBI. However, shortly after the announcement, the state agency said that they had been kicked out of the investigation, leaving the investigation in the hands of the Trump Administration. Several months later, ICE agents killed Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Texas and have also refused to work with state and local law enforcement. The administration’s actions have included blocking local and state law enforcement officials from accessing investigatory materials, such as Salgado Araujo’s work van and the scene of the incident.

The members introduced the ICE Shootings Transparency Act to address issues that some local agencies and prosecutors have encountered with ICE and CBP officers-involved shootings that result in the injury or death of a civilian. Their bill would require the U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and the Attorney General to share evidence on an ongoing basis with appropriate local law enforcement agencies related to shootings by ICE and CBP officers that injure or kill someone.

Additionally, this bill would require DHS and the Attorney General to provide access to the location of the incident to state and local law enforcement agencies with jurisdiction over the area to carry out regular investigative functions.

The ICE Shootings Transparency Act is cosponsored by Reps. Eleanor Holmes Norton (DC-At Large), Jim Costa (CA-21), Mike Quigley (IL-05), Steven Horsford (NV-04), Suzanne Bonamici (OR-01), and Sylvia Garcia (TX-29).

The legislation is endorsed by the National Immigration Law Center (NILC).

Congresswoman Ramirez has led the calls for accountability of DHS and its leadership. As the Trump administration’s deportation campaign continues, the nation’s elected leaders have a moral obligation to ensure there’s rigorous oversight when someone is killed or injured by a federal immigration agent.

Congress has not entirely ignored that responsibility. Republican-led committees held oversight hearings in February following the deaths of Renee Good and Alex Pretti. But roughly eight months after the two Minnesotans were killed, fundamental questions about the investigations, use of force and accountability remain unanswered.

That makes what happened at a Sept. 22 congressional “shadow hearing” deeply disturbing.

At the event in Washington, D.C., those who have lost a loved one or watched as immigration agents gunned someone down pleaded for answers. Among those who spoke were Good’s mother and brother, Donna and Brent Ganger. Good is the Minneapolis mom fatally shot in her SUV during Operation Metro Surge in January.

Also there was Stella Carlson, who filmed the death of Alex Pretti, a Veterans Affairs health system nurse shot by federal agents in Minneapolis later that same month.

They’d carved time out of their lives to travel to the nation’s capital and speak at the invitation of Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., ranking member of the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, and Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., ranking member of the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee.

Blumenthal had hoped the gathering would be bipartisan. But no Republican members of Congress showed up.

“Just Democrats were present … from both the House and Senate. We’ve tried to engage with our Republican colleagues over the course of this Congress about working together on conducting oversight of the Trump administration but we haven’t received any interest, which is why we had to convene this forum and it wasn’t a formal Committee hearing called by the majority,” Blumenthal’s office told me Sept. 24.

That’s why the event wasn’t an official hearing, but instead what’s sometimes called a “congressional forum” or “shadow hearing” on Capitol Hill. This diminished status, and an audience from just one political party, is unacceptable.

The Gangers deserved better than being relegated to the shadows. So did Rachel Reyes, whose son, Ruben Ray Martinez, was killed in March 2025 by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent in Texas.

The same is true for the family of Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, the 25-year-old Colombian father killed in July 2026 by an U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent in Maine, whose attorney came to Washington to represent them. And for Ronaldo and Lorenzo Salgado, whose father, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, who was also fatally shot this past July by immigration agents in Houston.

It’s an outrage that not one Republican member of Congress could be bothered to come listen to them. Minnesota Democrats Sens. Amy Klobuchar and Tina Smith and Rep. Ilhan Omar participated in the forum. The absence of Minnesota Republicans was both conspicuous and disappointing, especially when Minnesota’s Rep. Tom Emmer is in a powerful GOP leadership post.

Good’s and Pretti’s deaths stunned Minnesota and the nation and were a harbinger of more violence ahead. While Republicans responded with congressional oversight hearings in February, the responsibility is ongoing, especially when people continue to be seriously hurt or lose their lives.

Questions also remain unanswered about whether there have been any consequences for the agents who pulled the trigger on Good, Pretti and others who have died. Minnesota law enforcement officials have had to sue to gain access to federal evidence in the investigations of both Good’s and Pretti’s deaths.

“We still have so many questions. What are the names of the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents who killed our dad? It’s been two and a half months, and we still don’t have my dad’s belongings back,” Lorenzo Salgado testified at the Blumenthal-Garcia forum.

Even if you support stronger immigration enforcement, public trust in government and law enforcement rests on the foundation that safeguards are in place to ensure that force is used appropriately. Without this accountability, the danger is that deadly encounters continue and even become the norm.

I fear that line has already been crossed. On Sunday, Sept. 20, came news of another shooting, this time involving a 28-year-old Venezuelan man in Austin, Texas.

Wilber Rafael Garces Perez was making a DoorDash food delivery when an U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer shot him during a traffic stop, according to the Austin American-Statesman.

Reyes, the mom who testified at the forum and whose son died in 2025, understandably sees these shootings not as isolated episodes but as a pattern.

“Though the circumstances surrounding his death and these other victims are distinctly different, the pattern is the same,” Reyes testified. She pointed to “no warnings; no attempt to de-escalate; excessive force followed by deflection, and a lack of accountability after the fact.”

She added: “What happened to my son is personal, but it should be a concern for us all.”

That point was underscored by Good’s mother, Donna Ganger. She told lawmakers that she is a registered Republican who voted for President Donald Trump and believed federal agents were there to protect Americans.

The lesson from her family’s tragedy: No one should assume they and their loves ones are safe when there are few checks and dubious accountability for federal agents.

“We need this never ever to happen again and destroy another family or a community,” Ganger said.

Jill Burcum is a Minnesota Star Tribune columnist.

Although the change in the Government’s proposals recognises that the backlog facing the Criminal Courts cannot be resolved by removing or seeking to manipulate fundamental protections, we are opposed to those which remain – increasing magistrates’ sentencing powers and removing the right of defendants to elect to be tried in a Crown Court.
We look forward to the Government continuing to work with the Bar and the wider legal profession to address the real causes of the backlog and to tackle the injustices they create.

title: Inside the 'shadow surge' driving ICE arrests to new heights - KNSI
authors: Doug Livingston for The Marshall Project
description:

text:
Arrests began climbing gradually in March and by July had risen sharply. In nearly every state, arrests exceeded the number from the same period the year before. A Marshall Project analysis of Immigration and Customs Enforcement data published by the Deportation Data Project at UC Berkeley and UCLA found that in many places the surge in enforcement has been dramatic. Even without a focus on high-profile operations, immigration arrests more than doubled in 15 states and Washington, D.C.

Republican-led states and communities across the country offered up their own law enforcement agencies to help, from the Texas and Florida highway patrols to sheriff’s departments in Ohio and local police in Missouri.

A Department of Homeland Security press release reported ICE made nearly 51,000 arrests in August, higher than any month on record.

“We call it the ‘shadow surge,’” said Jill Garvey, director of States at the Core, a nonprofit that supports grassroots organizations confronting authoritarian threats. “It’s this much quieter, but no less violent or deadly, enforcement.”

Public outrage exploded in January when federal agents killed Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis during an enforcement mission called Operation Metro Surge. Their deaths marked a turning point in the Trump administration’s campaign to round up and deport immigrants without authorization to be in the United States.

After months of flashy, made-for-media enforcement — agents piling out of a rented Penske truck at a Los Angeles Home Depot, rounding up hundreds of Korean autoworkers at a plant in Georgia, arresting a five-year-old boy in a bunny hat in Minneapolis — Trump fired Border Patrol commander-at-large Greg Bovino and Department of Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem.

Trump’s new pick to run the department, Markwayne Mullin, promised to pursue the president’s goals with more cooperation from local law enforcement and less public backlash. Congress had already approved tens of billions of dollars to fund that mission.

The enforcement that has followed has been widespread, diffuse and harder for the national media to track. It’s also been measurably more effective.

ICE’s stepped-up enforcement looks different across the country. Federal authorities have cracked down on commercial truck drivers and arrested people at airports who had overstayed their visas. ICE has continued arrests of immigrants in neighborhoods and public places like hardware store parking lots. These operations can still be chaotic, like a raid of a Memphis bar that began as a state investigation into gambling and drugs and ended with immigration arrests, or immigration agents striking protestors with batons and dragging them from the porch of a home in Frederick, Maryland. In some states, immigrants are still most frequently brought into ICE custody through a transfer from a prison or jail, but increases in other kinds of arrests have led to a summer surge.

Roughly 2,000 state and local law enforcement agencies have signed agreements with the federal government to conduct immigration stops or hand over immigrants who are in local jails. Since ICE reset its tactics, arrests from these programs have grown considerably.

Texas and Florida, each led by Republican governors with possible national aspirations, have emerged as Trump’s top enforcers.

Texas accounted for a quarter of all immigration arrests in July. In Florida, ICE logged more than 7,000 immigration arrests, more than triple the number in that month the year before. Both states have directed their state troopers to conduct immigration stops. In Florida, the arrests often begin when people are stopped for traffic violations or driving without a license, said Palm Beach immigration attorney Jackie Delgado.

“They are not being taken to a jail and being booked in and seeing a judge,” she said. “They’re skirting the justice system and heading directly to ICE.”

Other states, including Missouri and Ohio, are blips on the nationwide scale of immigration enforcement. But each has seen arrests climb as local police lean into the cooperation agreements with ICE.

In 2024, neither state had a single local police agency enforcing immigration laws for ICE through what are colloquially called 287(g) agreements — a reference to the federal regulation that created the program. Today, 130 law enforcement agencies in Missouri and 20 in Ohio have signed up.

“The signing of these 287(g) agreements has really turned all of our local law enforcement into these ‘show me your papers’ forces,” said Gabby Eissner, advocacy strategist at the St. Louis-based MICA Project, which provides low-cost and pro bono legal services to immigrants. “People are getting picked up at traffic stops, and those traffic stops are happening because of the color of their skin.”

Since June, ICE has set new monthly records for signing up local law enforcement partners, according to a Marshall Project analysis of agreements listed on the agency’s website. With greater swaths of the country patrolled by ICE’s local partners, advocates say it’s getting harder to distinguish routine traffic stops from targeted immigration arrests.

“The 287(g) agreements and the cooperation with local law enforcement are making it challenging for people to document what’s happening in their communities,” said Garvey, who leads the authoritarian watchdog organization.

In Southwest Ohio, the quietly expanding immigration machinery is on full display in Hamilton, the seat of conservative Butler County. There, Sheriff Richard Jones has had an “Illegal Aliens Here” sign outside the jail for two decades. He quickly inked 287(g) agreements after Trump returned to office last year.

Jones told The Marshall Project that 44 of his deputies, or about a quarter of his law enforcement personnel, are ICE-trained to identify undocumented immigrants. They initiate most of the hundreds of stops that have led to ICE arrests in the county, but police officers working for other local departments also call his deputies, widening the net.

So far in 2026, ICE recorded more immigration arrests in Hamilton — a city of fewer than 65,000 residents — than anywhere else in Ohio. Arrests there have more than quadrupled this year compared to the same time period last year, and nearly all of those arrests are tied to 287(g) agreements.

Jones said he expects to bring in $20 million in revenue this year from the agreement with the federal government. That money outweighs the daily protests outside the county jail. He estimates that 4,700 immigrant detainees have come through the jail in the past 18 months.

“A few of them get released from here and don’t get deported,” he said. “But it’s not many.”

Even with broader collaboration between federal immigration agencies and state and local law enforcement, ICE’s data shows that in July, half of arrests were of people with no prior contact with the criminal justice system. This percentage has grown along with the increase in arrests.

ICE and Customs and Border Protection have more funding than ever to conduct immigration enforcement, with more than $200 billion allocated since Trump took office last year. Congress approved about $70 billion of that funding in June. That cash infusion is greater than the fiscal 2026 budgets for the FBI, Drug Enforcement Administration and U.S. Marshals Service combined, according to the Brennan Center for Justice at New York University School of Law.

ICE has so far used the money, which can be spent through fiscal 2029, to more than double its personnel, hire more charter flights for faster deportations and expand its technology to include “shock gloves” and robot dogs.

Cities are still targets for immigration enforcement, with less fanfare. Immigrant advocates in Chicago and St. Louis say calls to hotlines for legal services and to report ICE arrests increased dramatically in July.

The St. Louis Rapid Response Hotline has fielded nearly 9,000 calls for help dealing with immigration arrests over the past year, according to the Ashrei Foundation, which runs the hotline. Data collected during those calls shows more than half of immigration arrests in St. Louis and eastern Missouri were made by police during a traffic stop. The same pattern is evident in Chicago.

“They are quieter arrests,” said Alycia Jameson, a Chicago-based immigration attorney. “It’s a lot of suburbs. It’s a lot of traffic stops. It’s not the Midway Blitz Operations [in Chicago] — it’s not that. But the numbers are really up.”

text:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has been ordered to temporarily stop conducting vehicle stops in the wake of two deadly shootings in Texas and Maine, sources told ABC News.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin gave the directive, a law enforcement source told ABC News, after he spoke with Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, who said she urged Mullin to "cease all non-urgent vehicle stops."

In most cases, ICE officers will stop a target on the street once they leave their house or office, but ICE will still use vehicle stops in cases involving the most dangerous targets, according to a source.

Multiple sources said the pause is temporary and that ICE officers will receive new training on vehicle stops.

On Monday, 26-year-old Joan Sebastian Guerrero was fatally shot by an ICE agent in Biddeford, Maine, after agents tried to stop the car he was driving, according to Sen. Angus King, I-Maine.

Guerrero, a Colombian national, was not the target of the operation and ICE agents had been given a final order for another man they were targeting to be removed from the U.S., King told ABC News.

An ICE spokesperson said that the agency was "conducting targeted surveillance on the last known address of an illegal alien with a final order of removal," and when an "illegal alien departed the residence in a vehicle," ICE agents "attempted to conduct a vehicle stop."

"The vehicle attempted to flee the scene and fearing for public safety an officer discharged his weapon," ICE said.

The Maine Attorney General's Office said "the suspect attempted to flee in the vehicle in the direction of the officer and was fatally shot."

Witness Daniel Boucher told ABC News that he watched agents pull the shooting victim from his car and put him on the ground.

"I heard the young man say, 'I tried to stop.' I clearly heard him say that," said Boucher, adding that he overheard one of the ICE agents allegedly say the driver tried to run him over.

In response to growing community concerns regarding U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE)-related interactions, the Westchester County Human Rights Commission is offering a comprehensive set of general resources and best practices for individuals to familiarize themselves with and utilize should they encounter ICE in a variety of situations.

Westchester County Human Rights Commission Executive Director Tejash Sanchala said: “Anti-immigrant discrimination is not tolerated in our County. name: Human Rights
title: How the U.S. Can Lead on Human Rights Post-Trump
authors: Suzanne Nossel, David Miliband, Samuel Moyn, Cullen Hendrix, Stephen M. Walt, Jeremi Suri, Maria Kuznetsova, Dan Storyev, Nicholas Bequelin, Yaqiu Wang
description:
For 80 years, the United States styled itself as a defender of human rights and freedom on the global stage.
Already, when surveyed, people under 35 in traditional U.S. allied countries are especially likely to say U.S. democracy has never been a model worth following.
There will be no return to the era when the United States could plausibly cast itself as a standard-bearer for democracy and human rights.
By turning pluralism into a practical foreign-policy agenda, Washington can reestablish the standing it needs to lead again on democracy and human rights.
The promotion of pluralism as enshrined in this framework could avoid some of the obvious pitfalls of any U.S. human rights agenda in the post-Trump era, when international partners will be wary of U.S. overreach.
text:
For 80 years, the United States styled itself as a defender of human rights and freedom on the global stage. While its record was never pure, the language of values cut across Republican and Democratic administrations, lending credibility and distinctiveness to Washington’s global leadership. Even routine charges of hypocrisy underscored that there were certain principles that Washington purported to stand for, though they might too often be honored in the breach.

Of the many pillars of U.S. foreign policy that President Donald Trump’s administration has sent tumbling down, values-based leadership may be among the toughest to erect anew. That’s because it is premised on firm ideals and commitments. While U.S. partners have come to expect a certain amount of wavering, fundamental betrayals are hard to overcome. By the end of Trump’s second term—12 years after he first came to power—younger generations will have little lived memory of values-based U.S. leadership. Already, when surveyed, people under 35 in traditional U.S. allied countries are especially likely to say U.S. democracy has never been a model worth following. After Trump, observers will be primed to view U.S. values as empty.

Future U.S. administrations will have to build on this cracked foundation. There will be no return to the era when the United States could plausibly cast itself as a standard-bearer for democracy and human rights. But Washington can still painstakingly earn back credibility by demonstrating sincerity, engaging partners, and delivering on commitments. Perhaps the best place to start is by rededicating the country to what it has long been known for: civic pluralism, including respect for ethnic and religious differences. By turning pluralism into a practical foreign-policy agenda, Washington can reestablish the standing it needs to lead again on democracy and human rights.

The notion that values should guide U.S. foreign policy goes back at least as far as Woodrow Wilson’s presidency. It ran through Franklin D. Roosevelt’s and Harry Truman’s efforts in establishing the United Nations to Jimmy Carter’s elevation of human rights as a bureaucratic and policy cornerstone to Ronald Reagan’s invocation of freedom as a Cold War rallying cry. Over the decades, Washington built an expansive global democracy and rights infrastructure, encompassing the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) and myriad State Department offices and emissaries focused on religious freedom, LGBTQ+ rights, international justice, and more.

By the early years of the 21st century, the so-called war on terrorism compromised Washington’s already checkered record on rights. As geopolitical competition intensified, values increasingly took a back seat in relations with China, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, and other countries. That trend accelerated when Trump returned for his second term in 2024.

Since reentering office, Trump has torched much of the U.S. infrastructure on rights and democracy. He demolished USAID and retracted billions of dollars in U.S. funding and commitments for global rights and democracy protections, undermining decades of policy and programs worldwide that had depended on Washington’s support. Trump’s flouting of human rights norms—including through lawless strikes on alleged Caribbean drug boats, extrajudicial immigration detention and deportation, and attacks on the International Criminal Court—has evinced contempt toward a global system that the United States established less than a century before.

Now what? In many areas—democracy, international justice, anti-corruption, and digital rights, among others—it will be hard for the United States to assert strong global influence, at least for a while. Some of these issues touch domestic tripwires in the U.S. Congress, potentially sapping political capital and funding prospects. If the United States continues to face a sharply divided government, for instance, congressional support for LGBTQ+ advocacy and global reproductive rights may lag. Yet it will be vital for a new U.S. administration to assert some measure of leadership on values that contrast with Trump’s “America First” transactionalism.

Pluralism has the potential to revive values-centric U.S. leadership. The essence of civic pluralism is the idea that people with different religions, origins, convictions, cultures, and ways of life can belong equally to a shared community, respect one another’s differences, and be governed under common rules. A step beyond mere “tolerance,” pluralism demands institutions and protections that prevent any single religious, ethnic, ideological, or cultural group from using the state to subordinate others. It embodies the U.S. motto “e pluribus unum,” or “out of many, one.”

The philosophy of pluralism is more relevant than ever as the world grapples with mass migration, rapid demographic and social change, and escalating episodes of religious harassment. Countries urgently need models for societies that are hospitable to varied cultural, national, racial, and religious backgrounds as they seek to restore faith in the ability of politics to reconcile the dueling pressures of difference and homogenization, building societies that encompass both rather than being engulfed by either.

Washington is uniquely well positioned to catalyze progress in this area. Faith in pluralism is fundamental to the United States, a nation of immigrants that was founded on freedom of religion and conscience. And compared with Washington’s main global rivals, pluralism is a distinctively U.S. ethic. Both Russia and China crack down on religious and ethnic minorities, pushing conformity and a single dominant culture that buttress autocratic control.

The United States can elevate pluralism by promoting it at home and abroad. On the domestic front, this can take many forms. As alarm has risen over worsening polarization, efforts have intensified to build healthy civic culture and foster dialogue across different communities. Philanthropies, universities, and local and state governments are currently leading interventions to bring together diverse groups, and research shows that at least some of these have helped redress social divisions.

International examples include government-sponsored “Harmony Circles” in Singapore and the Council of Europe’s push to cultivate multiculturalism at the city level. In recent years, Canada has significantly expanded its use of law and public policy to protect vulnerable communities, including by creating a new security program for religious and cultural institutions at risk of hate-motivated violence. In 2026, Canada also enacted stronger hate-crime and anti-intimidation protections. Sharing such strategies across borders can reinforce these efforts.

In pursuing this agenda on the global stage, Washington can draw on past U.S. lessons dating back to the first Obama administration. In the mid-2000s, U.N. member states were sharply divided over a debate on the “defamation of religion.” Led by the Organization of the Islamic Conference (OIC), now known as the Organization of Islamic Cooperation, a majority of nations supported adopting international instruments that would ban insults to religion. The agenda was spurred by the Danish newspaper Jyllands-Posten’s publication in 2005 of a series of cartoons lampooning the Prophet Muhammad. The United States and its allies in Europe and elsewhere opposed the prohibitions on the grounds that they would infringe on free expression, legitimizing censorship and blasphemy laws. These bitter disagreements continued for years.

In 2010, the United States changed its approach. U.S. diplomats approached Pakistan, then the lead OIC member on the defamation resolution, and suggested collaboration on a global agenda to reduce religious intolerance, offering a tangible substitute for the proposed defamation ban. Their solution sought to prioritize the protection of members of religious communities rather than religions themselves. It spelled out eight concrete measures to cultivate pluralism, which included training officials in outreach to religious communities, fostering intergroup dialogue, and tracking and prosecuting hate crimes.

After months of negotiation, the Human Rights Council adopted the proposal in March 2011. The resolution launched a regular cadence of high-level meetings, initially chaired by U.S. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton and the OIC chair.

In the ensuing 15 years, the compromise has held, reinforced by national reports on the resolution’s implementation and global meetings to review progress, convened under an umbrella designated the “Istanbul Process.” This process has helped turn the resolution from a diplomatic compromise into a lasting forum for practical cooperation, leading to international models for, among other measures, specialized police training to recognize religiously motivated hate crimes and partnerships between law enforcement and community organizations that make victims more willing to report abuse. Even a fraught debate after a series of Quran burning incidents in Europe in 2023 did not derail the consensus.

Despite its success, the Istanbul Process is ripe for invigoration, as its meetings and reports have become less frequent in recent years. Yet the groundwork of an accepted global mandate, an established U.S.-OIC partnership, and a catalogue of national practices would all give a new U.S. administration a lot to work with. In the future, Washington could collaborate with its fellow conveners—Pakistan, Turkey, and the United Kingdom—to reinstate the high-level review gathering as an annual event, support countries on implementation, and find new ways to reinforce pluralism in the digital era.

The promotion of pluralism as enshrined in this framework could avoid some of the obvious pitfalls of any U.S. human rights agenda in the post-Trump era, when international partners will be wary of U.S. overreach. The agenda dovetails with universal human rights principles without being too prescriptive. It does not involve, for example, promoting electoral rules, constitutional structures, or cultural norms in other countries.

Still, any future administration must design a civic pluralism agenda carefully. Respect for racial and religious differences does not mean a free-for-all. The Istanbul framework is centered on protecting rights for people both as members of religious groups vis-à-vis the state and as individuals within their own communities. This does not allow for child marriage, the subordination of women, the persecution of LGBTQ+ individuals, and other forms of bigotry.

The elevation of civic pluralism would bring a series of other benefits to the United States. It would vest Washington in a broadly supported multilateral effort, turning back toward the U.N. system that Trump has often spurned. It would help it fortify frayed relationships with Muslim nations and the global south and provide a way to address the scourges of both Islamophobia and antisemitism as forms of bigotry rather than geopolitical side effects. It would also reinforce the United States’ dedication to its own identity as a pluralistic society, rebutting domestic political appeals to an ethnonationalism that is hostile to minorities and dissenters.

The Trump administration will cast a long shadow over the United States’ reputation, one that will be overcome only gradually and deliberately through steps that demonstrate that the country is determined to stand for something. U.S. values-based leadership should begin again by championing the contested principle that increasingly diverse societies must find ways for people who disagree profoundly to remain equal members of a shared political community. Civic pluralism offers an entry point to repair relationships, restore credibility, and demonstrate Washington’s readiness to help the world tackle common challenges, paving the way for the broader promotion of human rights and democracy across the globe.

name: Human Rights
title: The Trump DOJ's Backwards Model of Federal Civil Rights Enforcement - Just Security
authors: Regan Rush, Megan Marks, Jeremy Chin, Margaret Lin, Just Security, Tim Wood, Daniel Forti, Mariea Sekijima, Michael Mattler
description:
For decades, Department of Justice (DOJ) career attorneys like us developed federal civil rights cases from evidence.
That process left room for DOJ’s political leadership to set enforcement priorities in broad strokes, but it also emphasized accuracy and principled decision-making, and it helped keep federal civil rights enforcement independent of improper partisan influence.
DOJ’s Civil Rights Division increasingly draws conclusions first and looks for facts later, if at all.
Those concessions weaken protections for the communities federal civil rights laws were designed to serve.
Anything less is not civil rights enforcement—it’s political retribution that threatens the rule of law itself.
text:
“Presumptively illegal.”

That was the warning the Justice Department’s top civil rights official, Harmeet Dhillon, attached to her promise to investigate a water safety and lifeguard program in Eugene, Oregon—a verdict reached before any investigation had begun and without reference to a single person alleging discrimination. It came 12 hours after Libs of TikTok, a far-right social media account, posted a photo of a flyer for the program and tagged Dhillon. A post, a tag, and a foregone conclusion.

For decades, Department of Justice (DOJ) career attorneys like us developed federal civil rights cases from evidence. We gathered facts, analyzed the law, weighed risks, documented conclusions, and moved recommendations up the chain. That process left room for DOJ’s political leadership to set enforcement priorities in broad strokes, but it also emphasized accuracy and principled decision-making, and it helped keep federal civil rights enforcement independent of improper partisan influence. Even when a potential case lead, a tip, or a news story came to the attention of DOJ’s political leaders, they typically forwarded it to career staff with instructions to handle it “in the normal course.”

The current Trump administration has inverted that sequence. DOJ’s Civil Rights Division increasingly draws conclusions first and looks for facts later, if at all.

We trace how today’s conclusion-first enforcement works in practice, how the groundwork for this model was laid during the first Trump administration in 2020, and who ultimately bears the cost.

A Preview From the First Trump Administration

In the run-up to the 2020 election, DOJ’s politically appointed leadership directed a public announcement of inquiries into four states led by Democrats: New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, and Michigan. The allegation was grave. DOJ said in a press release that state policies governing nursing facility admissions during the early months of the COVID-19 pandemic “may have resulted in the deaths of thousands of elderly nursing home residents.”

In response, New York Gov. Andrew Cuomo and Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer pointed out that the relevant state policies were modeled on federal guidance, and that multiple Republican-led states had similar policies but faced no DOJ inquiries. DOJ Civil Rights Division alumni criticized the inquiries as “nakedly corrupt.”

Years later, the DOJ Office of the Inspector General assembled a record showing that these inquiries were pretextual, that the targets were chosen for political effect, and that the evidence did not drive the decision.

The press release announcing the nursing facility inquiries, according to a veteran DOJ public affairs officer, read as if the Civil Rights Division had been “working backwards” from a conclusion it had already reached. It was. DOJ political leadership had tasked career attorneys with justifying allegations made by two Republican members of Congress and amplified by the New York Post. When those career attorneys produced data supporting probes into two Republican-led states, Texas and Indiana, political leadership set the findings aside. DOJ barreled ahead with the public announcement, and, as the Office of the Inspector General’s report explained, did so “without knowing whether the ‘offending’ state orders were still in effect (they were not, having been rescinded or revised months earlier), whether such orders were consistent with federal guidance at the time (they were largely consistent with federal guidance), or whether other states had issued similar orders (they had).” One senior DOJ official involved in the 2020 effort revealed the political motive in writing, stating that a news leak related to additional inquiries in New York and New Jersey was “our last play on [the two Democratic governors] before [the] election but it’s a big one.”

This episode departed from DOJ’s longstanding policies and norms and illustrated the risk of misusing the Department’s significant authority for political ends. It also proved to be an early indicator of an approach that the second Trump administration would revisit and expand upon.

The New Approach: Conclusions in Search of Evidence

Under the current Trump administration, DOJ has accelerated and expanded this playbook. It now routinely announces investigations or even conclusions, sometimes within days or hours of a social media flare-up or public controversy, with little to no evidence of fact-finding.

Assistant Attorney General Dhillon makes no secret of the method. She reports scouring social media accounts for investigation ideas, calling the practice “fun and creative” and boasting that sometimes a single post “immediately puts a stop to” a civil rights “violation.”

The Eugene, Oregon, swimming program that Libs of TikTok flagged was a “BIPOC Water Safety and Lifeguard Cohort” that met twice a week. The program was started to address barriers to building water safety skills. As the federal government has documented and as the city has recognized, there are longstanding racial disparities in drowning rates. In response to Dhillon’s post declaring the program “presumptively illegal,” the city explained that no one is turned away or screened based on race and that the cohort supplements, rather than replaces, Eugene’s other water safety programming. Acknowledging racial disparities and inviting BIPOC youth to join a program does not, on its own, make that program discriminatory against white people.

In another example, a week after a Libs of TikTok post drew attention to an Illinois community college’s resources for undocumented immigrant students, Dhillon publicly warned that the college “will face the consequences at this @CivilRights Division!” She posted a letter concluding, without an investigation, that the college’s support for undocumented students, “on its face, appears to discriminate against . . . students based on their ‘national origin.’” But the Supreme Court has recognized that national origin discrimination is not interchangeable with discrimination based on citizenship or immigration status. Dhillon’s letter ignores that distinction.

The pattern repeated after a leaked memo describing a Minnesota hiring policy addressing underrepresentation of women and people of color in state employment was posted on social media. Dhillon responded the same day with a two-word verdict: “Not legal,” along with her signature threat, “FAFO” (shorthand for a profane version of “mess around and find out”). DOJ’s later lawsuit, United States v. Minnesota, shows almost no sign of an investigation behind it, relying instead on the policy’s text alone, without identified victims or evidence that the policy caused anyone harm.

Now-former DOJ attorneys assigned to high-priority matters during this administration have publicly disclosed that conclusions preceded investigation. “We were told what the outcome will be: ‘You have one month to find evidence to justify a lawsuit and draft a complaint,’” one attorney told ProPublica about a 2025 investigation into the University of California system. More recently, a whistleblower disclosure by a DOJ attorney assigned to work on Department of Health and Human Services civil rights investigations in 2025 related to Brown, Harvard, and Columbia described the outcomes of the investigations as “predetermined, without regard to the evidence” and said the “investigations, legal analysis, and findings were subordinate to political priorities rather than the enforcement of civil rights.”

Facing Federal Courts

Federal civil rights enforcement under the Trump administration has been dominated by inquiries and investigations that draw supporters’ likes and applause without facing close scrutiny. But the conclusion-first strategy has met a more exacting review in federal court, where the accusations and DOJ’s motives can be tested.

For instance, in United States v. City of Portland, Dhillon’s social media post helped unravel DOJ’s stated justifications for its aggressive actions toward the city’s police department. On Oct. 2, 2025, amid widespread U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) operations and corresponding protests, Portland police arrested right-wing commentator Nick Sortor outside an ICE facility. Dhillon reposted his social media account of the arrest, adding: “Portland: It’s FO time. Buckle up.” The very next day, DOJ invoked the city’s court-enforced settlement agreement, approved in 2014, over Portland police’s use of excessive force against people with mental illness to demand documents related to Sortor’s arrest and the city’s attempts to limit ICE’s use of a facility through zoning laws. DOJ’s letter strongly suggested that Portland had engaged in viewpoint discrimination that violated the First Amendment.

The timing here was telling. DOJ’s demand came as Portland police leaders supported Oregon and Portland’s lawsuit to block the deployment of the National Guard to the city. After scrutinizing DOJ’s motivation for demanding the documents, the court found that DOJ had acted “in bad faith and with unclean hands,” that its stated reasons were “pretext,” and that Dhillon’s post carried “all the hallmarks of a threat and attempted intimidation” made in response to the police leadership’s support for the National Guard litigation, rather than the “language [or] tone of a good faith investigation.”

The Cost of Substituting Political Theater for Civil Rights Enforcement

DOJ’s legitimacy was built on the expectation that allegations would be handled “in the normal course”—through impartial and rigorous investigation, principled legal analysis, and reasoned judgment. The Trump administration’s use of the Department as a rapid-response arm of partisan grievance politics has consequences.

Under aggressive federal pressure and escalating threats, institutions have preemptively curtailed programs, entered settlements, and seen a university president resign, all without a concluded investigation. Those concessions weaken protections for the communities federal civil rights laws were designed to serve.

And there’s another cost, borne by the targets themselves. They have to answer unsubstantiated and vague allegations. The ripple effects can be severe, whether or not the case ever gets to court.

Each taxpayer-funded hour spent by DOJ employees on scoring political points is also time stolen from people facing actual civil rights violations: communities confronting unlawful discrimination, voters denied equal access to the ballot, prisoners subjected to violence and abuse, people targeted by brutal hate crimes, and people seeking to access reproductive health services free from violence and intimidation.

DOJ must return to working forward from the facts, not backwards from a conclusion. Anything less is not civil rights enforcement—it’s political retribution that threatens the rule of law itself.

title: US migrant flights to Liberia evoke troubling history of sending people deemed unwanted to ...
description:
Unlike the other countries participating in the Trump administration’s efforts, Liberia has a long history with American immigration policy.
As a scholar who has written about that history, I see echoes of past U.S. efforts to move nonwhite people to Liberia in the latest removals.
The initial wave of departures was made up of African American intellectuals, church leaders and merchants.
By the end of the century, some 16,000 Black Americans made the journey, many against their will and all on the promise of a better life.

text:
The Supreme Court’s recent decision to temporarily allow the United States to resume deporting migrants to third-country destinations could see the resumption of flights to Liberia.

About the size of Ohio, the West African country is one of 35 countries the Trump administration is paying to shelter and feed Latin Americans and others living in the U.S. without proper legal status. Some of those receiving nations have a reputation for corruption and human rights abuses, and in most cases, those being deported have no links to the host nation.

The policy may ultimately be deemed unconstitutional, but on Sept. 29, 2026, the Supreme Court justices gave the green light for flights to continue while they consider the policy’s legality.

So far, at least 20 U.S. deportees have been flown to Liberia. One Colombian national who arrived in the African nation on Aug. 20 told PBS: “Honestly, I had never heard of Liberia.”

While those being deported to Liberia may not be familiar with the country, the same can’t be said for American policymakers. Unlike the other countries participating in the Trump administration’s efforts, Liberia has a long history with American immigration policy.

As a scholar who has written about that history, I see echoes of past U.S. efforts to move nonwhite people to Liberia in the latest removals. Indeed, it is those past events that gave Liberia its name.

Liberia’s American roots

In the early 1800s, Africa’s west coast attracted American leaders who were looking for a place to send those they viewed as unwanted U.S. residents: free people of African descent.

The region became the endpoint for America’s first massive removal campaign, starting in 1820, focused on relocating Black people “back to Africa.” The chief U.S. organization advocating for this effort was the American Colonization Society, created in 1816.

The initial wave of departures was made up of African American intellectuals, church leaders and merchants. The brutality and inhumanity that white Americans inflicted on free and enslaved Black people drove them out. Many abolitionists and Quakers – who fought to ban slavery – initially supported the colonization society’s removal efforts as a means for helping Black residents escape the cruelty of American laws, especially the Fugitive Slave Acts.

But the true driving force was the slaveholder class, which held a majority in Congress. Those politicians demanded the deportations because they knew the presence of free Black people gave hope to the millions in bondage — who, in some states, outnumbered white people.

These early American settlers named their new home Liberia, for liberty. And by 1847, they fought the colonization society’s control over the land and turned the settlement into the first independent republic in Africa. They set up towns and farms along the coastline, which had local indigenous communities estimated to be in the hundreds of thousands.

By the end of the century, some 16,000 Black Americans made the journey, many against their will and all on the promise of a better life. Thousands more joined them, some from the Caribbean and at least 6,000 who were rescued from slave-trading vessels, intercepted and sent to Liberia by the U.S. Navy.

A promised land

The colonization society’s mass deportation plan was a nationwide effort with powerful political leaders and slaveholders like Henry Clay, who was a U.S. senator, speaker of the House, secretary of state and three-time presidential candidate; Francis Scott Key, a famous U.S. attorney best known for writing “The Star Spangled Banner”; and Bushrod Washington, a Supreme Court justice and nephew of George Washington.

Ten Southern state legislatures endorsed the idea by passing laws that allowed the freeing of an enslaved person only when deportation out of the state was arranged and paid for. The colonization society raised the funds to pay for their removal to Liberia.

Some abolitionists and future leaders, including Abraham Lincoln, at first supported colonization because they believed it would help accelerate emancipation. But over time, and especially during the Civil War, most instead supported citizen rights for Black residents.

The effort was also opposed by powerful public intellectuals, including Frederick Douglass, who helped convince many — including Lincoln — of the need to secure freedom and justice for Black people in a country where they already lived.

At least 20% of those who made the journey to Liberia in the 1800s died of malaria. The rest dealt with supply shortages, severe weather, failed crops and hostility from indigenous communities.

But most white Americans knew none of this. They were told Liberia had fertile soil and a healthy climate; it was a promised land for Black people wishing to go home.

Harriet Beecher Stowe, in her best-selling novel “Uncle Tom’s Cabin,” furthered this notion by having her main characters, on a hair-raising and violent odyssey to escape enslavement, finally find freedom and peace on a boat headed to Liberia.

Douglass praised her novel in his newspaper, but for this last part of it, which he vehemently opposed. Douglass wrote to Stowe: “We are here, and here we are likely to remain. … We have grown up with this Republic; and I see nothing in our character … which compels the belief that we must leave the United States.”

A lingering US legacy

The American Colonization Society’s strong influence on deportations ended with the Civil War, though the organization continued raising money and influencing U.S. policy until it was dissolved in 1964.

Other independent waves of migration to Liberia followed, especially as the end of Reconstruction unleashed white-led terrorism against Black communities throughout the South. This included the Liberian Exodus Joint Stock Steamship Company, a Black-owned business that transported well-off African Americans to Liberia in 1878. Its schooner carried some of Liberia’s soon-to-be-famous families from Charleston, South Carolina, to Liberia’s capital, Monrovia.

In my view, what they accomplished along West Africa’s windward coast is astounding and, unfortunately, forgotten by most Americans. I’ve collected thousands of records from archives, including the U.S. National Archives, that show how surviving “Americo-Liberians,” as they called themselves, used grit and ingenuity to build large farming operations, grow merchant fleets, establish fisheries and spur other industries in their efforts to be integrated into Western global markets.

Yet for all the successes in difficult circumstances, Liberia in the 20th century remained in America’s shadow. After decades of fending off European attempts to absorb it into their colonial holdings, Liberia sought refuge in its historical relationship with the U.S. And in the 1920s, the two countries began a “special friendship.” At a time when Jim Crow laws ravaged the American South, U.S. business interests created a plantation economy in Liberia rooted in resource extraction that enriched large U.S. companies, including Firestone Tire and Republic Steel.

Archival records show the corruption that grew from deals benefiting the few at the expense of the many that became a long-term driver in the country’s political instability, resulting in civil strife and poverty that has wracked the country for decades.

Coming full circle

For many of the 1,200 people earmarked for deportation to Liberia in the coming months by the U.S. government, landing in the capital, Monrovia, may feel cruel. That it was once a thriving city of Black elites whose forebearers arrived there from America may feel meaningless.

The circumstances of their deportations to Liberia are obviously very different form earlier waves. Those being deported today weren’t captured and sold into bondage; many left home to escape civil war, gang violence or starvation.

But there is a common driver between American policymakers now and those in the 19th century in encouraging and enforcing deportation to Liberia: a desire to rid the U.S. of nonwhite people deemed to represent a problem at home.

In December 2026, the Supreme Court will hear arguments and ultimately decide the constitutionality of this desire, as written into today’s rapid deportation policies.

text:
On September 30, $810 million in appropriated fiscal year (FY) 2026 spending expired because of a Trump administration maneuver known as a pocket rescission. The rescission, which targeted spending that the administration correctly described as wasteful, functions as a unilateral spending cut by the executive. This makes it appealing to many who want to see less spending. However, the pocket rescission approach creates risks, and Republicans and libertarians alike should be wary of how the strategy could be exploited in the future.

The administration’s maneuver has received a mix of criticism and support. Appropriators from both parties decried the pocket rescission, calling it an illegal usurpation of congressional spending authority. Seven states have filed a lawsuit against the administration to undo the rescission. Conservatives such as Reps. Chip Roy (R-TX) and Scott Perry (R-PA) have praised the administration, focusing on the importance of cutting wasteful spending. Sen. John Kennedy (R-LA) criticized Congress for not enacting more cuts.

With the gross national debt now above $40 trillion and interest costs surging, it is easy to understand dissatisfaction with the legislative branch and a desire to see action to reduce deficit spending. There are better ways to achieve lasting savings, as seen in 2025, when the administration worked with Congress to eliminate 11 times as much spending as the FY 2026 pocket rescission did. More importantly, even though pocket rescissions can deliver a short-term policy victory (such as eliminating $810 million in wasteful spending), they open the door to larger problems down the line.

The Pendulum Always Swings Back

Supporters of the pocket rescission should beware the executive branch claiming the authority to unilaterally cut duly appropriated spending. It undermines congressional control over the federal budget. Encroachment by the president further tilts the balance of power away from the legislative branch, which is designed to be more representative of and responsive to the American public.

Libertarians consider some federal spending to be judicious. For example, federal inspectors general offices have a combined budget of roughly $4 billion per year, but their work against fraud and corruption saves taxpayers a much larger amount. The Government Accountability Office performs vital oversight on federal agencies and employees, uncovering wasteful and abusive actions. The Federal Communications Commission spends a modest amount to auction licenses for commercial spectrum, generating billions in revenue and facilitating a much larger amount of economic value in the process. All of these would be vulnerable to pocket rescissions if an administration chose to target them.

Republicans should also consider the long-term risks of the pocket rescission maneuver. A future Democratic administration could use the Trump administration’s playbook of disbursing selected funds slowly, then deploying a pocket rescission to freeze them until they expire. This would enable political victories that might be impossible to achieve in Congress, imperiling Republican priorities such as national defense and immigration enforcement.

The impulse to use escalatory tactics while in power is always present but can undermine the constitutional system and ultimately backfire when the other party regains control. Spending hawks should instead leverage today’s economic circumstances to promote a permanently leaner federal government.

Seizing Opportunities to Reduce Spending

The Trump administration secured roughly $9 billion in rescissions from Congress in 2025. Because the administration sent its rescission request to Congress on June 3, it enabled a legislative debate that drew public attention to the proposed savings. The enacted cuts were not vulnerable to legal challenge afterward, and defunding the Corporation for Public Broadcasting has permanently removed it from the federal budget. The administration could have repeated its success in FY 2026 by transmitting a rescission request in June or July rather than on September 25.

The arcane nature of pocket rescissions makes them difficult for the public to understand, dampening discussion about wasteful spending in a way that moving a rescissions package through Congress does not. Further, pocket rescissions can yield only short-term effects, so the tactic is a poor means of creating the lasting change needed to correct America’s fiscal imbalance and shrink the size of government. Congress should amend the Impoundment Control Act to prevent future pocket rescissions. Such a change would stop unilateral spending cuts while preserving the core rescission process.

With the US economy burdened by persistent inflation and debt markets demanding high yields on Treasury bonds, policymakers should work to raise public awareness about the economic costs of wasteful and unsustainable federal spending. Fiscal responsibility would be a better solution to cost-of-living concerns than harmful regulations or inflationary handouts.

While the FY 2025 and 2026 rescissions did reduce spending, total spending still increased by hundreds of billions of dollars in both years, The administration should work with Congress to enact the many worthwhile spending cuts in its discretionary budget proposals. Congress should use reconciliation to deliver dramatic savings rather than additional spending. Both branches should continue the War on Fraud by enforcing and strengthening eligibility requirements, and expand it to target deceptive spending that benefits special interests.

Pocket rescissions are a double-edged sword and poorly suited to meaningful deficit reduction. Officials should pursue lasting savings without further centralizing power in White House.
