text:
Norma Bowe pressed a stethoscope against the 10-year-old’s chest, listening to her lungs.

It was Memorial Day outside Delaney Hall, an immigration detention center in Newark, New Jersey. The child, worried about her father locked inside, was hyperventilating.

Norma, a professor and registered nurse who had previously worked in emergency rooms, told her to breathe deeply as she checked for wheezing.

Through the building’s opaque windows, Norma could make out the silhouettes of detainees pressing their bodies against the glass. Several hundred had recently gone on hunger strike over rotten food, metallic-tasting drinking water, and a lack of access to medications, toilet paper and menstruation products.

For the past year, Norma had parked her brown-and-beige camper van outside Delaney’s gates most weekends. Converted into a mobile clinic, it was stocked with sutures, glucometers and trauma and CPR kits, and offered health checks to families and protesters. That day, the clinic was busier than usual.

“Can you come over here?” someone asked.

Norma followed, thinking a person may need first aid. Instead, she encountered a wall of two dozen ICE agents in paramilitary vests, carrying batons, tasers and firearms, most of their faces masked.

Protesters faced them, some holding phones in the air to record the scene.

The sounds of drums echoed. Then, someone screamed.

Norma looked down and saw a federal agent dragging a young woman across the ground, her bright pink shirt ripping off, until she was down to a black bra.

“Help me!” the young woman shouted.

Decades earlier, as a psychiatric nurse, Norma had watched colleagues reach for restraints and sedatives when patients became violent. Her instinct was different: “No, let me talk to him.” She would sit beside them and try to calm them down.

Now that same instinct kicked in: de-escalate the situation and help the woman being dragged across the ground. Norma felt herself going into “mom mode”, moving closer.

That’s when someone from behind yanked her up. An ICE agent in a cap, black facemask, and gloved hands reached for her arms from behind her. She felt her body fling through the air.

Norma’s body barreled hard on to the sidewalk face down, as someone screamed: “Dr Bowe!”

Bystanders tried to help. One yelled: “She’s a medical professional!”

At 69, Norma knew what it felt like to be thrown like a sack of trash. She had been abused as a child, an experience that helped propel her toward a life caring for others. But now the violence came from an ICE officer, flinging her “like a javelin”, as she would later describe.

Five months earlier, Norma had been horrified by the killing of another nurse, Alex Pretti, when ICE shot him to death after he stepped in to help a woman shoved to the ground by federal agents on a Minnesota street.

As Norma felt her own face slam against the concrete, she thought about Pretti. And she thought about death.

What does it take for an ordinary person – a nurse, journalist, construction laborer or cemetery worker – to seek justice after being harmed by a federal agent?

The question is becoming increasingly urgent as ICE arrests have surged since the summer. A recent ACLU report in eight states found that over 400 of more than 1,200 incidents involved misconduct by agents, including use of force with batons or grabbing people by their necks.

But taking legal action against a federal officer – especially when ICE agents operate from unmarked vehicles, often masked and without visible names or badges – is harder and more convoluted than suing local police.

A claim against city law enforcement will typically identify the officers involved and requests police records and body-camera footage (depending on state public record laws). The municipality can take about 45 days to reply before the plaintiff can then file a lawsuit, which may lead to a jury trial.

Claims involving ICE are much more constrained. Most people must first file under the Federal Tort Claims Act and wait up to six months for a response before they can file a lawsuit.

These “are essentially negligence claims”, said Joanna Schwartz, a professor at UCLA school of law. “They’re brought against the United States, and not against individual officers.” The case is then decided by a judge, not a jury. There is no entitlement to punitive damages.

As lawyers receive more training in bringing such claims, Schwartz expects their number to grow.

It is an uphill battle. Staying the course requires a measure of courage, money and persistence. Yet an increasing number of lawyers are also taking cases pro bono as people try to exercise their rights within a narrow legal window.

In July, the ACLU simultaneously filed 54 claims in 17 states and Washington DC against the federal government on behalf of people who have suffered violence, abuse and neglect at the hands of federal law enforcement.

One of those claims was filed on behalf of Norma Bowe, whom I first met nearly two decades ago.

I first saw the video of Norma careening like a busted mannequin to the ground on Facebook. She posted it after her release from the emergency room.

Viewing the footage felt like watching someone hurt my own auntie. I met Norma in 2008, after stumbling across her “death class” at Kean University, which at the time had a three-year waiting list. I spent the next several years shadowing her classes as she took students into cemeteries, prisons, autopsy rooms and crematories, teaching them to face death in order to better understand life. In 2014, I published a book about her work.

We stayed in touch. I sent congratulations when she became a grandmother; she did the same when I became a mother. I knew she has long felt called to serve people who need care or someone to advocate on their behalf.

Ever since the 2020 pandemic, Norma had been operating the mobile clinic with grant funding and donations, offering free health checkups to undocumented and uninsured people at shelters or community hubs: Covid vaccines, checks for blood pressure diabetes, blood glucose levels or cancer, mental health screenings, stroke assessments. She spent her days at Kean University, teaching the death class, as she has every semester.

She knew it was risky to stand up to ICE, considering its rogue and aggressive tactics, and especially given the backlash she had already received.

“I am just back home after the ER,” Norma wrote that day on Facebook. “These agents have no control and they do what they want with no impunity. The conditions in Delaney Hall are horrible. The water is poisoned. The food has worms. There is inadequate medical help.”

Norma’s post received 24,000 comments, and her notifications exploded with comments from trolls.

“Stay the hell away from ICE doing their job,” one wrote. “You got all you deserved. Stupid libturd.” Another: “You should have had your fucking head bashed in with a fucking night stick.”

When I posted a comment expressing support and concern, others piled on, zeroing in on my Asian last name: “How do you think Japan would or is handling their illegal problem. Wake the fuck up.” And another wrote to me: “GO BACK TO CHINA.”

Norma signed up for DeleteMe, a service that journalists also recommend, which scrubs personal data from the internet.

The choice to take legal action against the federal government is intimidating and onerous. And as a white woman who holds tenure at her university, Norma told me she knows she has better security and protections than most.

But the vitriol against her felt minor when she thought of what was happening to others on the streets of her own state.

“If this is what they’re doing to me outside with impunity,” she said, “what the heck are they doing to the people inside?”

Last May, Norma celebrated one of her students who received magna cum laude honors. A few days later, ICE agents picked up the same student’s husband on his way to work.

He ended up at Delaney Hall, and the student went from her graduation ceremony to visit him while still wearing her cap and gown.

Delaney Hall had just reopened that same month to house more than 1,000 people under Donald Trump’s ramped up immigrant deportation initiative. The two-story site previously served as a halfway house and detention center before closing in 2023. Geo Group, one of the largest private for-profit prison operators in the US, now runs the detention center under a 15-year, $1bn federal contract.

That same month, Newark’s mayor, Ras Baraka, also visited the facility, along with other congressional state representatives, including LaMonica McIver. She stood between the mayor and agents, who yanked Baraka’s hands behind his back in handcuffs as he repeated: “I’m not resisting.”

ICE arrested Baraka for trespassing and held him in custody for five hours, later dropping charges. But the government claimed in a lawsuit that McIver had “slammed” one of the agents. The congresswoman was charged with three felony counts of assaulting federal agents, a case she is still fighting.

New Jersey’s governor, Mikie Sherrill , visited Delaney Hall the next day. “I say this as a former federal prosecutor: these are the hallmarks of a secret police,” Sherrill said in a statement. “They are acting in service to a political agenda, rather than the rule of law, and they are operating without accountability.”

As the weeks stretched on, Norma’s student shared reports from visits with her husband inside. Many of the prisoners were sick. The cells, freezing. The water tasted funny and smelled bad.

By now, Norma was visiting Delaney Hall with the mobile clinic a couple of Saturdays a month, handing out water, food, blankets and baby formula to waiting families, offering checkups, or chairs for people to sit. She listened to everyone’s stories.

One family told her they couldn’t get a man’s bladder cancer medication inside, and without it he could die soon. Norma tried to make a plea to ICE officials to let her into Delaney to administer his medication – to no avail. Another detainee had recently undergone spinal surgery, and his wife told Norma he needed antibiotics and physical therapy. Some explained to Norma that their loved ones locked inside were complaining of rashes, vomiting, or flu.

“I found myself writing a lot of medical letters,” Norma said. Families tried to carry these letters inside hoping to get treatment or medical care for detainees. But they came back defeated.

On 12 December, Norma learned that a 41-year-old, Jean Wilson Brutus, died after a day in custody at Delaney Hall on 12 December. ICE said he experienced an unexplained “medical emergency” and died from “natural causes”.

By winter, at least seven people detained inside of Delaney Hall had gone on a hunger strike. One person had been “subject to force feeding, hydration, or forced urinary catheterization, or involuntary blood draws”, according to a document published by the ICE Health Service Corps.

Delaney Hall was not an outlier. That May, ICE agents detained Elton Purvis at Boston Logan international airport. A Rastafarian priest, Purvis was taking medication for malaria and diabetes at the time. Yet in custody, Purvis said he was repeatedly denied his prescriptions, according to his federal claim.

In detention, Purvis suffered from chills, fever, and heavy sweating. Seven days after his detainment, he was hospitalized. It took several more days for him to be treated for his malaria.

Over the next six months, Purvis would move from detention center to detention center, spending the longest stretch at the South Texas ICE processing center in Pearsall, Texas, which is also operated by the Geo Group.

He would later detail how his health mistreatment had caused him to go into a hypoglycemic crash. Purvis also reported suffering bouts of diarrhea, dehydration and malnutrition, repeatedly falling unconscious.

The ACLU would file a claim on Purvis’s behalf under the Federal Tort Claims Act the same week its lawyers filed Norma’s and over four dozen others. (When I reached out to the Department of Homeland Security about the claims, a spokesperson replied: “If the AMERICAN Civil Liberties Union is this committed to the cause of criminal illegal aliens, it should change its name.”)

In detention, Purvis met a lot of people going through the same predicament, “and sometimes even worse”. Filing this claim, he told me, is for them too. “It feels like standing up for something, and I think this is the best chance I have to do so.”

Back at Delaney Hall that Memorial Day, after Norma left for treatment at the hospital, Senator Andy Kim emerged outside Delaney Hall, wearing a suit and tie, standing between a line of armed ICE agents and their armored vehicles, and a line of protesters.

With about 600 men and women surviving inside, politicians had continued to press for investigations, inspections and to speak to people inside. A woman being held inside told Kim she was forced to handle her miscarriage on her own. Another pregnant woman said she had not received any gynaecological care.

“The cruelty that you see behind me, this is the point,” the senator told a reporter on the scene. “Right now, I’m trying to have them not point guns at us.”

With Kim still wedged between the two sides, holding his hands up in a gesture of “stop”, agents shot pepper balls toward him and the crowd. The senator had to receive aid to relieve his burning eyes and throat.

It has not always been so impossible to sue federal officers for constitutional rights violations.

In 1971, the supreme court actually made it easier for people to do so in its ruling in Bivens v Six Unknown Named Agents. But in the decades since, the court has severely dismantled any remaining rights to sue them under Bivens – leaving the Federal Tort Claims Act as the primary option left to seek any legal recourse.

Last week, the family of Renee Good, the mother killed by immigration agents in January in Minneapolis, filed two federal lawsuits against the agent who shot her and several top officials in the Trump administration, under Bivens as well as the Federal Tort Claims Act. Good’s family will face the same barriers as other claimants, Schwartz told me, despite intense public attention.

The six-month clock to receive federal responses to Norma’s and the other claims is ticking. If the government then denies or ignores the claims, plaintiffs can file lawsuits. But the path forward will inevitably be lengthy and emotionally taxing for people pushing on.

Sean Beckner-Carmitchel, a journalist based in Los Angeles, filed a tort claim with the ACLU against federal immigration officers after he said they hurled a gas canister in his direction, walloping his forehead. Crystalline powder exploded across his face.

If the canister had hit his face an inch away, he said: “I could have lost an eye, or I could have died.”

He knows it is a drawn out, difficult process. But the choice to keep going, he told me, is not only about him. “I didn’t want someone else to have something even worse happen to them,” he told me. “This is the only way that I know how to prevent that.”

Two pieces of legislation – the Bivens Act and the Constitutional Accountability Act – could allow people to sue federal law enforcement officers when they violate their rights. Other states are contemplating, or in the case of Illinois and Vermont, have recently passed legislation, giving people the right to sue ICE.

The legal outcomes of such state rulings, Schwartz said, has yet to be seen. But until more legislation on the state and national level is passed making it easier for victims and their families to seek accountability, many will continue to be forced to navigate the tremendous hurdles of the Federal Tort Claims Act.

“It’s the one that exists, so we’re going to use it,” said Yasmin Cader, ACLU deputy executive director. “And we are going to win.”

On a Friday in July, Edwin López-Cornejo told his mother something was wrong.

Edwin, 39, had been detained at Delaney Hall since June. He had diabetes and high blood pressure, and as a deadly heatwave hit the region, he told Maria Cornejo that he was not receiving his medications regularly. His face and hand felt numb.

It was the last time they spoke.

The next day, Maria received a call from University hospital asking her to identify a body.

When Maria arrived, she realized her worst fears had come true: the dead person on the table was her son.

Nationwide, 48 people had died in ICE custody since Norma first began coming to Delaney Hall, according to ICE data. A June report from Physicians for Human Rights, examining 52 deaths during the first 500 days of the second Trump administration, found delays in CPR and cases in which detainees who died from sepsis had received neither blood cultures nor antibiotics.

An AP investigation that month found that hundreds of detainees in at least 33 states had alleged in federal lawsuits that immigration detention facilities denied adequate care for conditions including epilepsy, Parkinson’s, cancer and HIV.

Norma had been warning for months that more people would die at Delaney Hall. She had talked at length with members of Cosecha, an organization advocating for undocumented immigrants, which had published letters signed by dozens of detainees describing conditions inside.

One listed “inhumane” bathroom conditions, ventilation problems, urinary tract infections, beatings and the use of pepper spray inside. “If you’re sick, you have to submit a request that takes two weeks to be answered – or you never get a response at all,” another said, adding: “They only prescribe Tylenol for all ailments.”

Members of Cosecha contacted Norma and asked her to visit Maria at her Plainfield home, where she was distraught after seeing her son’s body. Maria had medical problems of her own, and they were worried the shock might worsen her condition.

Norma drove to Maria’s garden apartment. Decorated with plants and framed family photos hung on walls: Edwin in a suit and tie; his daughter, now 12, in a pink princess gown wearing a tiara and white gloves.

Maria sat slumped in a chair. Norma pricked her finger for a blood glucose screening, gently wrapping a Band-Aid around the tip. She checked in throughout the week leading up to Edwin’s funeral, bringing her protein powder, since Maria had been unable to eat.

On Saturday, 8 August, Maria wept, holding her husband’s hand as their son’s casket was lowered into the ground.

Four days later, Norma and others learned about the death of a third person who had been detained at Delaney Hall. José Chajón-Raxón had been in ICE custody since 18 July, where Department of Homeland Security officials said he suffered a seizure, before he died at the hospital.

Norma was furious, convinced that each death could have been prevented.

If the families of any of the people who died after being detained at Delaney Hall decide to seek legal compensation for damages, they too, like Norma, will likely have to resort to filing Federal Tort claims.

“I have taught students for years about the reality of death,” Norma told me. People we love die of old age and illness, or sometimes violence, homicide, accidents, suicide. It is a part of life, as she tells her classes. Long ago, her death class also reminded me how to remain attentive to life’s smallest moments, even amid the most painful challenges.

But what is happening to people at the hands of federal immigration officers in the US today is not just incomprehensible – it is preventable.

Detention centers, Norma told me, should not be death camps. For now, all she can do is keep showing up. To the places where people may need medical assistance. And to court, if that day comes.

She might never know the identities of the ICE agents who hurt her. But if she ever has a chance to face the men who grabbed her from behind, she would want to look at them, unmasked: “What if I was your mother or sister?” she would ask. “Where is your humanity?”

name: Human Rights
title: Weekly Racial Justice Update: September 27–October 3, 2026
description: Racial justice update for September 27–October 3, 2026: census race data, Black unemployment, voting rights, health care, housing, immigration enforcement, Muslim civil rights, corporate slavery disclosures, and tribal sovereignty—with analysis of impacts on specific communities.
text:
Vernellia R. Randall,
Weekly Racial Justice Update: September 27–October 3, 2026
, Racism.org (October 4, 2026).
Racial injustice operates through decisions about whose experiences are counted, whose rights are enforced, whose communities receive resources, and whose suffering requires an explanation. This week’s developments reach across those systems: census proposals, civil-rights enforcement, voting, employment, health care, housing, immigration, education, religious freedom, and tribal sovereignty.
The record includes both attacks on protections and efforts to build accountability. Federal agencies narrowed enforcement and redirected resources. Communities challenged discrimination, demanded answers about detention, and fought to preserve their political voice. California adopted corporate slavery-disclosure requirements and a future tax on private detention operators. Native communities advanced housing and cultural initiatives while defending their right to shape decisions affecting their lands.
These developments show why racial justice requires sustained attention to government action—and to the communities organizing against exclusion. Accountability depends on identifying what changed, who bears the consequences, and what must happen next.
Table of Contents
Census Comments Due October 13
Voting Rights, Intimidation, and Black Women’s Political Voice
Black Unemployment Rises
Proposed Jobs Program Targets Long-Term Unemployment

Death in ICE Custody Requires Answers
Federal Incentives and Limits on ICE Vehicle Enforcement
California Adopts a Private-Detention Tax
Advocates Challenge Asylum Referrals Without Interviews
Houston Police–ICE Cooperation Comes Under Scrutiny
DOJ Issues Discrimination Finding Against UCLA Law
Campus Racism and Institutional Accountability
Florida Muslim Organizations Challenge Terrorism Designation
Mosque Zoning and Discrimination Behind Neutral Rules
Muslim Woman’s Prison Religious-Rights Lawsuit Advances
Juvenile-Detention Agreement Requires Disability Reforms
Remembering Indigenous Boarding-School Harm

Native-Led Housing Project Advances in Chicago
Native Hawaiian Community Sponsorship Applications Open
International Discussion Examines Racism and Drug Policy
Overall Bottom Line
Search Note
1. Census Comments Due October 13
The Census Bureau’s proposed rule would prohibit questions about race, ethnicity, and sexual orientation on the decennial census short form and other enumeration questionnaires covered by the proposal. It expressly excludes the American Community Survey and administrative data from that prohibition.
Public comments are due
October 13, 2026
. Racism.org published a sample comment September 30 that readers can personalize with their experiences and concerns. Anonymous comments are permitted by entering “N/A” in required identifying fields. Readers do not need to include their telephone numbers in the comment text.
Why It Matters:
Removing census race questions would weaken the data used to identify racial disparities and enforce civil rights. Communities of color would lose a direct nationwide record of their populations.
Bottom Line:
Submit a comment by October 13 demanding the racial data needed to document exclusion and hold government accountable.
Sources:
Census Bureau,
“Decennial Census of the Population of Americans; Proposed Residence Criteria and Proposed Regulations for Demographic Questions”
, September 10, 2026. Last visited October 5, 2026.

, comment-submission page. Last checked October 5, 2026.
Back to Table of Contents
2. Voting Rights, Intimidation, and Black Women’s Political Voice
October 2 reporting documented concerns that immigration enforcement could intimidate voters. DHS said it had no plans for operations targeting polling places, while leaving open responses to threats. The reporting does not establish that ICE deployment at polling places is planned.
A civil-rights poll released September 30 found widespread concern about rights being rolled back and election officials facing pressure. Separate reporting September 29 highlighted a survey of 700 Black women registered voters: 92 percent were dissatisfied with the country’s direction, 95 percent expressed concern about changes to voting-rights protections, and 77 percent were very motivated to vote in the midterms.
Why It Matters:
Immigration-enforcement fears can discourage participation in Latino, Asian, and immigrant communities. Black women’s responses show that threats to voting protections are also driving political urgency.
Bottom Line:
Protect voters from intimidation and preserve the voting protections communities of color need to exercise political power.
Sources:
Associated Press,
Report on Immigration Enforcement and Polling-Place Concerns
, October 2, 2026. Last checked October 5, 2026.
Capital B,
“92% of Black Women Voters Are Dissatisfied With America’s Direction”
, September 29, 2026. Last visited October 5, 2026.

, September 2026. Last checked October 5, 2026.

, September 30, 2026. Last visited October 5, 2026.

3. Black Unemployment Rises
Employment figures released October 2 showed Black unemployment rising from 6.0 percent in August to 7.0 percent in September. September unemployment was 3.6 percent for white workers, 2.9 percent for Asian workers, and 4.7 percent for Hispanic workers. The overall rate was 4.2 percent, and payroll employment increased by 29,000.
The figures document a substantial racial gap. They do not, by themselves, establish the cause of the monthly increase.
Why It Matters:
Black unemployment was nearly twice white unemployment. That unequal access to work threatens Black families’ income, housing stability, and ability to build wealth.
Bottom Line:
Economic progress must be measured by whether the Black–white employment gap closes, not merely whether total employment grows.
Source:
Bureau of Labor Statistics,
“The Employment Situation—September 2026”
, October 2, 2026. Last visited October 5, 2026.

4. Proposed Jobs Program Targets Long-Term Unemployment
Senator Chris Van Hollen introduced the Ready to Work Act September 30. The proposal would support employment, training, and related services for people unemployed for at least six months. It includes support for communities experiencing persistent poverty and joblessness and for worker-owned enterprises.
The legislation is a proposal, not an operating benefit program.
Why It Matters:
The proposed program could address prolonged joblessness in communities facing racial employment barriers. Its reach will depend on who obtains the jobs and support.
Bottom Line:
Evaluate implementation by access for Black workers and other excluded communities, job quality, and reductions in persistent unemployment.
Sources:
Senator Chris Van Hollen,
“As AI Threatens American Workforce, Van Hollen Introduces Legislation to Create Jobs and Tackle Long-Term Unemployment”

5. D.C. Cuts Paid Family and Medical Leave
Changes taking effect October 1 reduced D.C.’s paid family-caregiving leave from 12 weeks to six and medical leave from 12 weeks to ten. The maximum weekly benefit fell from $1,190 to $1,100. Parental leave remained at 12 weeks, and prenatal leave remained at two.
Why It Matters:
Cutting paid leave makes caregiving depend more heavily on family savings. The racial-justice question is whether workers of color can afford the income loss or must return before care needs end.
Bottom Line:
Assess who loses benefits by race and income—and whether the cuts force workers to choose between earnings and family care.
Source:
The Washington Informer,
“D.C. Workers Lose Half of Their Paid Family Leave”
, October 1, 2026. Last visited October 5, 2026.
Back to Table of Contents
6. SBA Narrows Civil-Rights Enforcement
A Small Business Administration rule took effect September 29 removing affirmative-action provisions and ending the agency’s pursuit of Title VI disparate-impact liability against federal funding recipients. Intentional discrimination remains prohibited. Racial disparities may still serve as evidence of intentional discrimination.
Why It Matters:
Ending disparate-impact enforcement removes a way to challenge policies that exclude people of color without proving discriminatory intent.
Bottom Line:
The rollback narrows federal accountability for racial barriers in SBA-funded programs, even when those barriers produce unequal access.
Source:
Small Business Administration,
“Removing Constitutional Concerns From SBA Programs”
, September 29, 2026. Last visited October 5, 2026.

7. Minority-Health Funding Diverted to Security

Overall Bottom Line
This week shows how government decisions distribute protection and harm across racial and ethnic communities. Black workers face sharply unequal unemployment. Minority-health programs lose resources. Immigrant communities confront coverage restrictions and enforcement pressures. Muslim organizations challenge government stigma, while Native communities defend sovereignty, housing, and cultural continuity.
The responses identify concrete paths toward accountability: preserve racial data, enforce civil rights, fund legal representation, disclose corporate involvement in slavery, restore community participation, and protect tribal decision-making.
A signed law needs implementation. A settlement needs enforcement. A death in custody needs an explanation. A promise of consultation needs meaningful tribal involvement.
Racial justice requires institutions to answer for whom their decisions exclude—and to change the rules and practices producing that exclusion.

text:
WASHINGTON —

The Supreme Court begins its new term on Monday, addressing a packed docket that includes cases on climate change, immigration, and voting rights.

The justices are starting the term with a major climate change case involving energy companies seeking to block dozens of lawsuits that aim to hold them liable for damages related to climate change in Boulder, Colorado. Billions of dollars are potentially at stake in this case.

Several high-profile cases are scheduled through December, including one involving voting rights. The court will consider Arizona's push to enforce strict voting laws requiring proof of citizenship for voter registration. This follows President Donald Trump's unsuccessful attempt to pass a proof-of-citizenship bill through Congress.

The court will also hear two significant immigration cases. One focuses on the legality of the Trump administration's policy of deporting migrants to countries other than their own.

The other case examines the administration's mandatory detention policy for immigrants living in the U.S. illegally, even if they have been in the country for years. The administration argues it can hold individuals without a bond hearing, but most appeals courts that have reviewed the issue disagree.

Later in the term, the justices will also hear cases involving religious rights and an assault weapons ban.

title: First Trump Came for Immigrants. Then He Came for Their Lawyers. | Nonprofit Quarterly
authors: Kyle Paoletta, Ranada Robinson, María Constanza Costa, Camilla Richardson, Sofia Jarrin, Elizabeth Schmidt, Yamani Yansa Hernandez
description:
In the first few months of 2025, the Trump administration attempted to cancel around $267 million in federal spending on legal aid for migrants.
For legal aid groups all over America, recovery from the tumultuous early months of the second Trump administration has been excruciating.
As she prepared ImmDef staff to confront the second Trump administration in late 2024, Toczylowski put together a presentation that doubled as a highlight reel from those years.
Nevertheless, last March, the Trump administration unilaterally pulled the more than $200 million directed to those contracts.
Not only were lawyers and social workers losing their jobs, but management appeared to be in retreat, raising fears that they were capitulating to Trump.
text:
This story was originally published by Mother Jones and can be read here.

Last year, on Labor Day weekend, an immigration attorney named Cooper Richardson spent her Saturday calling the Phoenix-area shelter where one of her clients—a child from Guatemala—was being held. She was checking to see if Immigration and Customs Enforcement was on the way: Her colleagues at the Florence Immigrant & Refugee Rights Project had received word that the Trump administration was finalizing plans to summarily deport the roughly 600 unaccompanied Guatemalan children detained across the country.

Richardson made one last call before she went to bed—and that’s when she learned the shelter had been told to have her client ready to leave within two hours. She rushed to her car, then spent the half-hour drive calling colleagues to see if they had advice for how she could ensure her client wasn’t taken. “I was nervous and shaking and scared,” she says, “and I’m not the one who might have been put on a plane.”

That frantic weekend is indicative of the immense pressure that Trump’s campaign to deport roughly 14 million undocumented Americans has put on legal aid groups.

Ana Islas, who heads the Florence Project’s Tucson office, was on the other end of one of those calls. She had pulled together a rapid response team of lawyers and social workers available over the holiday weekend—a blood-pressure-spiking task in the best of times, made even more so by the Trump administration’s effort to cut off more than $200 million in federal funding for the legal defense of migrant children. Like many of its peers around the country, the Florence Project had been forced into layoffs earlier in the year, which meant the remaining attorneys were working longer hours to ensure clients got the representation they needed. “I talked to about 30 kids that Friday,” Islas says. “Including one as young as 3 years old.”

After Richardson arrived at the shelter outside Phoenix, she talked quietly with her client while the other detained children remained in their beds, trying to sleep. When a van from a company contracted to transport migrants arrived, Richardson met the drivers at the door. As soon as she explained who she was, they got on the phone. “I don’t think they were expecting to have any resistance,” she says. The contractors left; early Sunday morning, a federal judge issued a temporary restraining order against the Department of Homeland Security, which was forced to bring the children who had already been put on planes back to their shelters.

That frantic weekend is indicative of the immense pressure that Donald Trump’s campaign to deport roughly 14 million undocumented Americans has put on legal aid groups, whose work often goes beyond representation in immigration court to include giving know-your-rights presentations at shelters and employing social workers to connect migrants with housing and food assistance.

Within his first few months in office, Trump ended “humanitarian parole” for the 1.4 million refugees and migrants who entered the country during the Biden administration and appointed an acting director of ICE who pledged to make deportations as efficient as Amazon Prime, “but for human beings.” Since then, Trump has invoked the Alien Enemies Act of 1798 to remove migrants accused of a violent or drug-related crime without a trial, terminated Temporary Protected Status for 350,000 Haitian migrants, canceled the resettlement of all refugees who aren’t white South Africans, and closed ports of entry to asylum seekers. Ever more hardline policies continue to be batted around the White House, with adviser Stephen Miller pushing the president to invoke the Insurrection Act to quell anti-ICE protests and unilaterally suspend habeas corpus for the undocumented.

The impact of these policies has been amplified over the past 20 months by the Trump administration’s quieter efforts to defund the nonprofit legal aid organizations that provide free assistance and representation for migrants. Immigration law is infamous for its impossible hours and laughable salaries, but since early 2025 the sense of purpose that animates so many immigration attorneys has been tested by the federal government’s efforts to target them—and their budgets. The ensuing chaos nearly broke them.

In the first few months of 2025, the Trump administration attempted to cancel around $267 million in federal spending on legal aid for migrants. That effort was headlined by the attempt to cancel the Unaccompanied Children Program, which provides legal representation for more than 20,000 kids by attorneys at nearly 100 organizations, but the White House didn’t stop there: It also set out to kill an initiative providing legal support for families that had been separated during the first Trump administration, as well as a suite of programs that fund basic legal orientation services for immigrants in ICE detention.

Texas’ Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services was hit particularly hard by the sudden withdrawal of federal funding. In an all-staff email sent a week after the Unaccompanied Children Program was taken offline last March, then-CEO Dolores Schroeder wrote that the contract covered more than half of RAICES’ annual budget, and its cancellation would require laying off 159 employees, adding to the 61 layoffs that had been announced a month earlier, after the Trump administration eliminated funding for refugee resettlement programs.

Georgianna Pisano Goetz recalls looking up from reading that email to see colleagues in RAICES’ Houston office just as shocked as she was. “There’s no meeting with a supervisor, no inclination around the office that this is happening,” she says. The next week, the woman who oversaw operations in Houston was gone. Goetz remembers the office feeling like “a real madhouse,” with everyone comparing notes about who else had been laid off and wondering aloud “Who’s our boss?” or “What are we supposed to do?” After the smoke cleared, less than half of RAICES employees across Texas still had jobs.

For legal aid groups all over America, recovery from the tumultuous early months of the second Trump administration has been excruciating. Some organizations, like the Florence Project and the Immigrant Defenders Law Center (ImmDef) in Los Angeles, were able to quickly rebound from forced layoffs. Others have shrunk in the face of the MAGA onslaught at a time when their services have never been more needed.

After the smoke cleared, less than half of RAICES employees across Texas still had jobs.

The pressure only ratcheted up over the winter, when immigration enforcement sweeps in Chicago, New Orleans, and Minneapolis hit at the same time philanthropic sources of legal aid funding—like the Soros family’s Open Society Foundations—were being threatened with investigations from the Justice Department and the IRS. The latest body blow came in August, when a no-bid contract to administer the entirety of the Unaccompanied Children Program was awarded to a group called Our Rescue, an anti-sex-trafficking outfit that is led by a former ICE administrator and has no history of providing legal representation.

Through it all, the shifting immigration landscape has presented a succession of new hurdles. “Our work has changed dramatically,” says Lindsay Toczylowski, the leader of ImmDef. While previously much of the group’s work had been oriented around migrants claiming asylum upon reaching a port of entry, Toczylowski says the vast majority of new clients are “people who’ve lived in Southern California for 10, 20 years, most with no criminal history, many with US citizen children and grandchildren, who are being picked up through racial profiling and warrantless arrests and being thrown into detention centers.”

Pivoting from representing clients awaiting their court date while on humanitarian parole to people in detention is a massive shift, with ImmDef’s lawyers now making frequent trips to remote facilities to consult with their clients. Likewise, the summary detention of so many migrants by ICE has forced lawyers with limited expertise in immigration to learn how to file habeas corpus petitions in federal courts. Meeting so many new challenges while scrambling for funding has only made the situation feel more dire. California, New York, and other blue states have stepped up with new grants that have allowed organizations to replenish staff over the past year, but that support still hasn’t been sufficient to alter the exhausting reality every legal aid group in America is facing: more work, less money.

Meeting so many new challenges while scrambling for funding has only made the situation feel more dire.

The first significant wave of undocumented migrants crossing the southern border came in the late 1970s, when tens of thousands of Salvadorans and Nicaraguans fled civil war. Though some of these refugees initially received legal assistance from aid groups that dated to the civil rights movement, in 1980 Congress prohibited the federally funded Legal Services Corporation from offering its legal aid to anyone but American citizens. This meant that the legal aid groups geared solely to migrants that were founded in the ’80s (including RAICES and the Florence Project) initially relied on philanthropic or local government grants.

That began to change in 1993, when the Supreme Court ruled in Reno v. Flores that “the Fifth Amendment entitles aliens to due process of law in deportation proceedings.” Subsequent litigation compelled the federal government to extend due process to particularly vulnerable migrants, which it mostly did by setting up block grants that legal aid groups could apply for. The most prominent of these is the Unaccompanied Children Program, which was created after a 2008 law required the government to provide counsel to children who arrive in the United States without a guardian.

These grants helped legal aid groups become more firmly established during the Obama administration, but it was only after Trump first came to power in 2017 that they really entered the public eye. That winter, ImmDef’s Toczylowski was one of the hundreds of lawyers who showed up at LAX days after Trump’s inauguration in response to his attempt to prohibit travelers from seven majority-Muslim nations from entering the country. Airport terminals packed with protesters became an early flashpoint of public resistance to Trump’s immigration regime, and groups like ImmDef used the ensuing uproar to raise the money necessary to meet the growing need for migrant legal defense.

ImmDef was raising almost $6 million a year by 2020. It was hardly the only group to find itself flush with cash. RAICES brought in more than $25 million to support its family reunification initiatives; in California, Al Otro Lado drew national attention after filing suit on behalf of six refugees whom Customs and Border Patrol refused to admit across the southern border, leading to a $2 million jump in annual revenue for the small organization.

As she prepared ImmDef staff to confront the second Trump administration in late 2024, Toczylowski put together a presentation that doubled as a highlight reel from those years. “How did we survive and thrive in the first Trump administration?” Toczylowski asked her team, which has grown to more than 200—large enough that she needed a microphone to address them. She reviewed every phase of ImmDef’s resistance, from Remain in Mexico to family separation, to remind the organization, “We were on the front lines of all of those struggles.”

With tens of millions of dollars in funding withheld, the bottom quickly fell out of a number of organizations. Lawyers soon cut clients adrift.

Almost immediately, though, groups like ImmDef were confronting unforeseen obstacles. On day two of the new Trump administration, the nonprofit that allocates the bulk of federal funding for migrant legal aid, the Acacia Center for Justice, received a stop-work order on all of its legal orientation program grants, which totaled almost $27 million. Sara Van Hofwegen, the managing director of the Acacia Center’s legal access programs, says legal orientation initiatives previously enjoyed bipartisan support. “They made everybody’s job easier,” she explains. The funding helped aid workers guide a detainee through the legal process by giving them a presentation or materials to review so they “can come to court saying, ‘I think I’m eligible for asylum, I want to apply.’”

Though that money was briefly restored while a court challenge played out, legal orientation was fully terminated last April. Now, Van Hofwegen says, “Those programs do not exist.”

The Trump administration had more latitude to do away with the legal orientation programs than it did the three contracts with the Acacia Center that had been created by court orders or an act of Congress, including the Unaccompanied Children Program. Nevertheless, last March, the Trump administration unilaterally pulled the more than $200 million directed to those contracts. It was as shocking as it was illegal.

Several litigators, including the ACLU and ImmDef, immediately sued to reinstate all three programs administered by the Acacia Center. But with tens of millions of dollars in funding withheld, the bottom quickly fell out of a number of organizations. Lawyers soon cut clients adrift.

After the all-staff email from Dolores Schroeder, RAICES’s Georgianna Pisano Goetz says, “We had a 60-day period where they were like, ‘No new clients’—and not only no new clients, but ‘No consultations, no pro se workshops, and withdraw from every single pro bono client.’” Though the organization disseminated detailed guidelines for transferring cases, it was up to the lawyers who had been laid off to contact their clients to explain that they were going to have to withdraw from representing them.

Not only were lawyers and social workers losing their jobs, but management appeared to be in retreat, raising fears that they were capitulating to Trump.

One told me about putting together a long email detailing every case they were working on in hopes that their supervisors would find somebody to take on clients they weren’t able to personally refer to another lawyer. The attorney said they never received a response. (A RAICES spokesperson disputed this account.)

In an email, Faisal Al-Juburi, the co-CEO of RAICES wrote, “Our team’s extraordinary effort last spring kept RAICES standing to serve our communities. Within days, we established a case triage and wind-down framework, issued procedural updates, led live trainings, and built robust referral systems.” Al-Juburi said he was particularly proud that RAICES was able to maintain services for families and individuals detained at the infamous facility in Dilley, Texas. “To fulfill our mission,” he continued, “we must acknowledge that this administration is actively upending legal norms and escalating violence in communities nationwide. We bear a responsibility to adapt to this shifting landscape to safeguard our core work.”

Elsewhere, not only were lawyers and social workers losing their jobs, but management appeared to be in retreat, raising fears that they, like so many other American institutions, were capitulating to Trump. That spring, nine white-shoe law firms pledged $940 million in pro bono work to the administration, Columbia University agreed to pay $221 million to the federal government to end its probe of antisemitism on campus, and the CEOs of dozens of companies joined Trump on an official visit to the Middle East.

Meanwhile, Al Otro Lado laid off eight employees and fired two more with cause—eliminating a quarter of its unionized workforce—while also pulling out of California state grants geared toward legal representation for refugees. The employees that remained became concerned that their leaders were falling in line, too, with several theorizing that, by exclusively focusing on helping migrants on the Mexican side of the border, Al Otro Lado could avoid confrontation with the Trump administration while at the same time taking advantage of Mexico’s permissive labor laws and low cost of living (management had rejected previous campaigns by the union to equalize pay between its Mexican and American lawyers).

Melissa Flores, a spokesperson for the organization, denied that any shift in priorities away from migrants in the United States was ever on the table. “Like many organizations in our field, we’ve had to navigate difficult terrain—but our focus has never wavered,” she wrote in an email. “We remain steadfast in our mission to defend and uplift the rights of immigrants, asylum seekers, and deportees on both sides of the border.” Indeed, Al Otro Lado has begun hiring again in the United States, which union members hailed as a direct result of the pressure they’ve put on the organization’s leadership. This August, management finally agreed to negotiate with the union after 18 months of resistance.

The union-management tensions at Al Otro Lado are hardly unique. Two days before Schroeder announced that RAICES had lost more than half of its budget, the organization had agreed to a wrongful-termination settlement with a union lawyer named Maria Osornio who had been fired in December 2023. A longtime leader in the group’s appeals division, Osornio had publicly protested Schroeder’s decision to wind down her office in 2024. She was terminated shortly afterward, in part for allegedly bullying another employee.

“It’s such a disservice to the people who really need our help to put ego before talent,” Osornio says. “We were spending so much time fighting with our bosses instead of focusing on the issues.” The organization found itself paying $225,000 to Osornio, and trying to heal internal tensions, at the same time the government tore a multimillion-dollar hole in its balance sheet.

Asked about the settlement with Osornio, a spokesperson for RAICES declined to comment on “specific personnel matters,” but called the timing “purely coincidental.”

A similar situation transpired in New York City last spring, when the nonprofit Bronx Defenders put an attorney named Sophia Gurulé on unpaid leave for “multiple recent performance failures,” namely a handful of late court filings. Gurulé had never faced any disciplinary action before, and soon 24 colleagues signed a protest letter to Bronx Defenders’ executive director, Juval Scott, alleging that she’d been suspended for her vocal union advocacy. “We’ve witnessed a mind-boggling number of changes in federal regulations, agency precedent, and circuit case law that radically reshaped an already complex area of law,” the lawyers wrote. “Suspending Sophia at a time where the Immigration Practice…is hanging on by a thread is inappropriate, concerning, and harmful to staff and clients alike.”

A spokesperson for Bronx Defenders said that while the organization doesn’t comment on personnel matters, “what we can say is that every decision we make is guided by our responsibility to the people we represent and the Bronx communities we serve.” The spokesperson specifically objected to the characterization that the organization’s immigration practice had been hampered by the suspension of Gurulé, pointing out that around the same time it had secured emergency funding from New York’s city council, hired new immigration attorneys, and provided training on filing habeas corpus petitions.

The simmering tension at Bronx Defenders, RAICES, Al Otro Lado, and other organizations hasn’t stopped them from playing crucial roles in the broader fight to defend migrants in court. Still, their inability to speedily resolve whatever personnel issues arise has been a counterproductive distraction. “I want to be out there helping,” Osornio says. “That’s what’s so heartbreaking: I want to be out there advocating, but I essentially lost my job for calling out the C-suite.”

“It’s an assault from all angles on the organizations that serve immigrant communities.”

Ana Islas, from the Florence Project, was one of the few dozen supervising attorneys from all over the country who attended an Acacia Center conference in Atlanta the same weekend that the administration pulled funding for the Unaccompanied Children Program. Midway through a presentation in a hotel conference room, everyone’s phone lit up. The agenda had to be put on hold as attorneys ducked into the hall to confer with their colleagues. Waiting for her flight home to Tucson, Islas remembers sitting in the terminal with her mind racing: “The kids are here and they need to know their rights even if we’re not representing them. And if we are representing them, we can’t just drop them like a hot potato.”

By and large, immigration attorneys have remained focused on that mission. “We are winning cases despite all the terrible stuff that’s happening out there,” says Chiqui Sanchez Kennedy, the leader of the Galveston-Houston Immigrant Representation Project. “We are gaining asylum for our clients. We’re getting clients released from detention.”

For many attorneys, the sense of momentum felt like it began to turn in their favor last September, when the Acacia Center was finally able to begin restoring funding for the Unaccompanied Children Program after a series of court orders ended six months of uncertainty. I talked to Van Hofwegen when the last suspended grants had been restored, but she sounded less triumphant than steely, acknowledging that more threats lay on the horizon. “I think the cuts to federal funding are really clearly happening in this larger context of a federal government that wants to make it as difficult as possible for immigrants to navigate their legal process and who wants to remove legal access and due process as much as possible from folks,” she says.

ImmDef’s Toczylowski agreed, telling me, “It’s an assault from all angles on the organizations that serve immigrant communities.” One of the more alarming vectors of that assault is the demand by the former chairman of the House Homeland Security Committee, Rep. Mark Green (R-Tenn.), that 215 NGOs provide records to the panel about how they “benefited from the border crisis created by the Biden Administration.”

In this climate of ever-changing rules and constant threats of funding cuts, legal aid organizations cannot afford to allow internal backbiting and score settling detract from their core missions. In May, an arbitrator found that Sophia Gurulé had been unlawfully terminated under the terms of her union’s collective bargaining agreement with the Bronx Defenders, even as the arbitrator didn’t dispute the organization’s reasons for suspending her. “I feel vindicated,” Gurulé told me. She added: “It is sad that a public defender nonprofit located in the South Bronx, historically one of the poorest congressional districts in the country, spent a year and who knows how many thousands of dollars to try to justify their bad behavior.”

“Where are the lawyers for the kids? They’re at the nonprofits doing this work without pay, and that’s because we are qualified, dedicated, mission-driven people.”

Aside from a few notable exceptions, most legal aid organizations have managed to get out of their own way this year and settled into a grinding legal war with the Trump administration. That made them better prepared for the most recent assault, an overhaul of the Unaccompanied Children Program that Roxana Avila-Cimpeanu, from the Florence Project, calls “monumental.” Under a new plan proposed by the Department of Health and Human Services, pro bono representation would be prioritized—a cost cutting measure that would mean detained children were working with attorneys with little immigration expertise—and all lawyers would be limited to virtual consultations with detained children. Avila-Cimpeanu says these changes could be devastating because there’s no substitute for “being able to meet in person with the child and really having them know that we don’t work for the shelter, we don’t work for the government. We’re there for them.”

In August, the administration awarded a $158 million contract to administer the entirety of the new version of the Unaccompanied Children Program to a group called Our Rescue, whose operations are devoted to stopping sex trafficking and do not currently include any sort of legal assistance. Notably, the group is led by a former ICE official named Derek Benner and was founded by another former ICE employee, Tim Ballard. The latter is best known for being portrayed in a popular QAnon-backed anti-sex trafficking film, Sound of Freedom, which came out shortly before he himself was accused of sexual coercion by seven women. (Ballard has denied the allegations, even as he resigned from Our Rescue after they became public. Our Rescue did not respond to emailed questions about its capacity for providing legal representation to migrant children.)

At a virtual event organized by the Acacia Center a month after funding for the Unaccompanied Children Program lapsed, Michael Lukens, the head of the Amica Center for Immigrant Rights, rejected the idea that Our Rescue can provide the same services as organizations like his. “Our Rescue does not do this work,” he said. “They are not qualified, and there has been no indication that that contract has been signed, that work has started, that Our Rescue has made any move to actually help a child.” That puts Lukens and his peers in the unsustainable position of working pro bono for the foreseeable future. “Where are the lawyers for the kids? Right now, they’re at the nonprofits who are doing this work without pay, and that’s because we are qualified, dedicated, mission-driven people.”

At the same time the old system for funding legal aid for migrant children has been detonated, the administration has spent the past few months illegally withholding payment for work done under the old Unaccompanied Children Program contract. This means that, yet again, nonprofits are scrambling to provide needed services. Avila-Cimpeanu says that Florence Project will find a way to continue representing its clients on a pro bono basis, a resolve shared even by lawyers at nonprofits without the same resources.

Melissa Lopez, the head of a small group in Texas called Estrella del Paso, posted a “heartbreaking update” in late July, saying that she had been forced to lay off 13 staffers because the administration was overdue on nearly $1 million in payments for completed work. Still, Lopez said, “We currently represent about 243 unaccompanied children. We have an ethical, legal, and moral obligation to continue representing these children, and with or without money from the federal government, we must do that.”

Nearly every lawyer I spoke with over the past year reflected on the reality that the Trump administration will keep finding ways to deny migrants their legal rights for as long as they’re in power. For many, finding the motivation to continue fighting requires staying connected to the clients themselves. Sanchez Kennedy, from the Galveston-Houston Immigrant Representation Project, makes a point of commemorating every case with her team, even the unsuccessful ones. “We call them hard-fought losses,” she says. “Every time we help a client access due process and actively participate in their immigration case, help them defend themselves against deportation—that means that they are getting a fair shot. That alone is worth celebrating.”

name: Human Rights
title: On immigration, Democrats should look to the Nordic model
authors: Will Marshall, opinion contributor, Will Marshall, opinion contributor
description:
Stopping illegal immigration has been President Trump’s most reliable rallying cry.
Since the Social Democrats came to power in 2019, they have slowed the pace of immigration while speeding up deportation of uninvited gate crashers.
Sweden’s Social Democrats, historically a working-class party, also have executed a U-turn on immigration.
Democrats, who have long admired the Nordic economic model, should learn from the new Nordic model on immigration.
Voters won’t trust Democrats to enforce immigration laws until they break emphatically with progressive demands for “decriminalization” and open borders.
text:
As Democrats and other center-left parties struggle to understand why working-class voters have turned against them, they reach readily for economic explanations. Yet most flinch from confronting another potent driver of blue-collar anger — uncontrolled immigration.

Of course, that’s partly an economic issue too. But it also illuminates the deep rift between elite and popular opinion on emotive questions of national sovereignty, cultural identity and democratic agency in deciding who can enter one’s country and become a citizen.

Stopping illegal immigration has been President Trump’s most reliable rallying cry. His call to wall America off from a flood of “criminal aliens” in 2016 helped him forge a strong bond with non-college voters. He went back to the immigration well in his 2024 comeback, when those voters again ranked the issue as a top concern, second only to high living costs.

Hostility to mass migration also is the rocket fuel propelling neo-nationalist populists in Europe. These include the far-right Alternative for Germany party, which recently made startling gains in state elections; France’s National Rally, now leading polls ahead of next year’s presidential election, and the United Kingdom’s fast-rising Reform Party.

Across the West, working-class voters feel betrayed by political elites who lecture them about the aggregate economic benefits of more immigration and belittle their doubts as nativist if not racist. Despite the issue’s enduring salience, few center-left parties have figured out how to defuse it.

Denmark is a conspicuous exception. Since the Social Democrats came to power in 2019, they have slowed the pace of immigration while speeding up deportation of uninvited gate crashers. They have also moved aggressively to integrate migrants into Danish society, passing “parallel society” laws to prevent their concentration in segregated communities.

European progressives have decried the shift as a concession to right-wing xenophobia. But Mette Frederiksen, who won her third term as prime minister last June, maintains that a restrictive migration policy is integral to her party’s historic commitment to social solidarity.

“Being a traditional Social Democratic thinker means you cannot allow everyone who wants to join your society to come,” she told the New York Times. With porous borders, “it’s impossible to have a sustainable society, especially if you are a welfare society, as we are.”

Fredericksen believes admitting fewer migrants and speeding their assimilation into Danish life are key to sustaining public support for the high taxes necessary to support Denmark’s generous welfare state, which corrects for economic inequality. That approach has enabled her party to stem working class defections while marginalizing the hard-right Danish Peoples’ Party.

She also emphasizes a critical point that seems to elude many on the U.S. and European left: The economic and social costs of large-scale immigration — competition for jobs and downward pressure on blue collar wages, gang-related violence, strains on schools, housing, public health and other services — are not distributed evenly. They fall more heavily on wage earners than highly educated and well-heeled Danes.

Center-left governments in other Scandinavian countries are following Denmark’s lead. Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store’s “Plan for Norway” includes calls for “clearer and stricter” immigration laws that tighten rules around family unification, speed up deportation of immigrants who don’t qualify for asylum and combat criminal gangs that help people enter the country illegally.

Sweden’s Social Democrats, historically a working-class party, also have executed a U-turn on immigration. “We had one of the most generous asylum systems in Europe, and that was wrong,” admits the party leader Magdalena Andersson, who is working to form a center-left governing coalition.

Democrats, who have long admired the Nordic economic model, should learn from the new Nordic model on immigration. It offers a humane path to curbing illegal migration in contrast to the cruel and violent tactics of Trump and his sadistic henchman Stephen Miller.

The party, however, has yet to reckon with the Biden-Harris administration’s immigration debacle. Biden loosened asylum and parole rules and until 2024 made little effort to secure the border. Migrants saw the green light and surged across it in record numbers.

Voters won’t trust Democrats to enforce immigration laws until they break emphatically with progressive demands for “decriminalization” and open borders. They should recall that Presidents Barack Obama and Bill Clinton kept illegal immigration under control despite taking flak from the left and immigrant rights’ groups for robust deportation programs.

Democrats are keenly attuned to how economic and technological change have undermined working Americans’ prospects for upward mobility. The same forces have sparked the mass migrations of the 21st century — and a furious popular backlash.

To keep faith with their traditional working-class constituents, center-left parties need to show they can control borders, restrict illegal entry and assimilate newcomers in ways consistent with liberal and social democratic principles. The Nordic Model shows that’s not a mission impossible.

text:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents arrived in southwest Kansas on September 22 and departed three days later, leaving fear, uncertainty and anger.

Many in the Hispanic and Latino communities in Dodge City, Garden City and Liberal, where most ICE activity was located, returned to work this week. But their fear persists and they aren’t yet leaving their homes or returning to regular activities, multiple immigrants said.

The fear was contagious. In Manhattan, about 225 miles east of Dodge City, social media posts blasted warnings of possible ICE agents on Thursday because of a large presence of law enforcement vehicles in a store parking lot. It turned out to be a training session for local police, according to a store employee.

Here are a handful of glimpses into the lives of Kansans affected by the raids.

Viridiana Boron, volunteer

Viridiana Boron spent several days last week delivering meals to Dodge City families whose members were scared to leave home because ICE was in the area.

Her mother and sister cooked meals for about 200 people, and Boron delivered them, she said.

“I was the one that was on the street and watching everything, watching all the suffer the families was having,” she said, pausing to apologize for her English. “I saw the reality, the truth. They were scared. They were sad. They were worried. I saw families with no water.”

Boron started crying.

“It was something that I’ve never seen in my life,” she said. “How can people not have heart and just do things like that? Because I mean, there I know could be a lot of immigrants over here that are like criminals, but a lot of people that I saw, they were not criminals. They were people working hard for their kids.”

This week, many people she knows have returned to work, but they aren’t eating out or shopping as the fear lingers, Boron said.

Boron came to the United States at age 24, receiving a visa because she and her family were threatened in Mexico. She has since married and is a legal permanent resident. Despite knowing she had the correct documentation, she was scared during the ICE operation.

Others who stayed home also had documentation, she said. But they have seen instances where it didn’t matter, and ICE agents stopped cars to check paperwork just because someone looked Hispanic or Latina, Boron said.

The affect on the community was “huge,” she said. It was difficult explaining to her 11-year-old son why people were scared because he didn’t understand the difference a paper could make, Boron said.

“We are all the same,” she said.

Julie Barraza, volunteer and activist

Julie Barraza smiled at everyone approaching the table she set up at a downtown Dodge City protest on September 24. She patiently answered questions about a petition to reform the country’s immigration system.

“I was born and raised here, and I’ve never seen such a cloud over the town,” she said during a break. “The first morning, they (ICE) were waiting for me to get out of my car, and I didn’t know what was going on. I didn’t get out of my car.”

Barraza drove on to work at Rattlesnake Grill. She said ICE agents came in to eat but employees didn’t realize they were with ICE because they wore regular clothing.

“Once we figured out they were ICE agents, because a customer had alerted us, I stepped out and decided to tell them to leave, and they refused,” she recalled. “I was scared, but I still did it.”

The agents did get up and leave, Barraza said, adding that several restaurants in town refused to serve agents and others closed because there weren’t employees to work.

Patrick Lopez, immigrant and educator

Patrick Lopez stood in the midst of a Dodge City protest on September 24, holding a sign and nodding to people he knew. He was there, he said, to “show solidarity with people who are being persecuted by ICE.”

“I’m here to defend my immigrant brothers and sisters. I’m here to stand up for them, and I hate that they have to live in fear right now,” Lopez said. “I can’t sleep last night. I’m offended as an American. I’m embarrassed as an American. I’m indignant. I can’t believe that this is happening right now.”

While acknowledging the economic costs to town — restaurants closed, businesses slowing or stopping work — Lopez said they weren’t what made him toss and turn at night.

“I also wish that people remembered the human rights effect,” he said. “People’s families should be protected. I don’t care what the issue is. You can’t destroy people’s families like that and hopefully get away with it.”

He tried unsuccessfully to reach a friend who drives a cab and worried that he was detained.

“He works every day, and that’s the thing. The people that ICE is after are hardworking people around town,” Lopez said. “Many of them are putting their kids through school. They’re just trying to make a living.”

Sarahí Aguilera, therapist and immigrant

Sarahí Aguilera is a licensed social worker, and she works as a mental health therapist. Advocating for the immigrant community, she said, is at the foundation of her personal and professional life.

She knows the challenges well. Aguilera is part of the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals program, which allows young people who arrived during specific time periods to apply and work in the country.

DACA has been under fire during President Donald Trump’s administration, she said, but she was fortunate that her permit didn’t expire when the program was temporarily halted. Since then, it has been a “consistent uphill battle” to keep the program active, Aguilera said.

Other family members weren’t so lucky. Aguilera’s sister had just been to an immigration appointment after turning 15, which is the age that people can apply for the DACA program, Aguilera said.

“We had started her paperwork. She had been approved. She had gone to her biometrics. I lived at Wichita at the time because that’s where I was getting my education,” she said. “And she got approved. She just never received her work permit.”

It was frustrating because when the family looked her up in the system, it said she was approved, Aguilera said. But she never physically received the approval that would allow her to receive her driver’s license or continue her education.

Her sister eventually married and is in the process of acquiring her documentation, Aguilera said. The experience reminds her how difficult it is to go through the immigration process and how different it is for each person, she said.

“Especially seeing me and believing she was going to have the same opportunity,” Aguilera said. “It really impacted her mental health and her motivation to further her education and just work on herself.”

Aguilera volunteers with New Frontiers, a nonprofit organization that works with young people in southwest Kansas to create a grassroots movement focused on political, social and economic power.

The group has a rapid response team that becomes active when events like ICE raids in the area occur, she said. Volunteers watch for ICE agents and try to verify information before releasing it to the community.

“Fear already does a lot to someone,” Aguilera said. “So fear and the wrong information — we want to make sure that we’re just prepared and grounded with what information we’re trying to share.”

Fear of the unknown is a problem for southwest Kansas immigrants, Aguilera said, along with how overwhelming information coming out could be.

While ICE was in the area, she saw about four clients because most were afraid to go out. Typically, her schedule is full every day.

Aguilera said she understands why some people are critical of immigrants who don’t have documentation.

“There is so much misinformation. I believe as a society we need to do a better job of understanding what the immigration process looks like,” she said. “Of understanding what are the barriers, what are the circumstances? Because there is not a system that is going to work for all of us.”

DACA recipients, for instance, don’t have a pathway to citizenship unless they marry or their jobs petition for them, Aguilera said.

Whatever a person’s belief system, she said, she hopes people are careful with their words.

“I do think it’s important to be mindful of the comments and what they can do to the mental health of someone overall,” she said, adding that people are easily influenced by social media and political figures, who she believes often don’t understand the process either.

Does she think significant immigration reform is likely?

“My heart wants to say that it’s hopeful. My uncertainty and anxiety that I’ve experienced for the past 10 years wants me to have a different answer,” Aguilera said. “I do believe people are opening their eyes. I believe we are getting a lot more information and more attention. Although I think we are creating great awareness and sharing information and education, I don’t believe we will see the impact and the change we want to see until people get out and vote.”

description:
DILLEY, Texas -- Last month, Kelly Ocampo believed she received good news: Her 21-year-old pregnant sister had finally been granted bond and was going to be released from the family immigration detention center in Dilley, Texas.
"This notice confirms that the immigration bond ordered by the Immigration Court has been successfully paid through an official payment method authorized by the U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS)," the letter stated.
SEE ALSO: 21-year-old pregnant mom detained at Texas immigration facility for over a month, family says When Ocampo received the letter, her sister had been in detention for a few weeks.
But now, a month after she believed the bond was approved, her sister -- who is five months pregnant -- is still in federal immigration custody.
Ocampo and her family spent all their savings on the alleged lawyer to try to get her sister released, she said.
text:
DILLEY, Texas -- Last month, Kelly Ocampo believed she received good news: Her 21-year-old pregnant sister had finally been granted bond and was going to be released from the family immigration detention center in Dilley, Texas.

The letter she received from a lawyer to whom she had paid more than $3,000 was written on U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement letterhead and stated that the ICE bond for Maria Alejandra Gomez-Quiroz was approved.

"This notice confirms that the immigration bond ordered by the Immigration Court has been successfully paid through an official payment method authorized by the U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS)," the letter stated.

SEE ALSO: 21-year-old pregnant mom detained at Texas immigration facility for over a month, family says

When Ocampo received the letter, her sister had been in detention for a few weeks. But now, a month after she believed the bond was approved, her sister -- who is five months pregnant -- is still in federal immigration custody.

"It was a scam," Ocampo told ABC News.

Ocampo believes she was scammed by an individual posing as an immigration attorney, and said her sister has now been detained for over 40 days. Ocampo and her family spent all their savings on the alleged lawyer to try to get her sister released, she said.

ABC News reached out to the person Ocampo says claimed to be a lawyer, but did not receive a response.

Ocampo told ABC News that her sister and partner were fleeing violent guerrillas in Colombia and were planning on applying for asylum in the U.S.

Gomez-Quiroz was arrested by U.S. Border Patrol at the border in June.

She is one of at least 500 people detained at Dilley and one of four pregnant women being held there as part of the Trump administration's ongoing immigration crackdown, according to lawmakers.

Her detention comes as a federal district judge in California has ordered the appointment of a special master and independent monitor to examine "time in custody" at the Dilley facility to ensure that the government is complying with guidelines established in previous legal settlements.

Immigration lawyers have argued that the administration is detaining people longer than allowed by previous court settlements.

Immigrant advocacy groups have also said that arrests and detentions of pregnant women violate an ICE directive stating that the agency should not "detain, arrest, or continue to detain individuals known to be pregnant, postpartum, or nursing" except under exceptional circumstances.

ABC News previously reported on a different 21-year-old pregnant woman who has been detained at Dilly for more than 50 days with her 2-year-old son.

Immigrant advocates, medical professionals and lawmakers have previously raised concerns about conditions at the South Texas facility.

The order from the California judge also calls for the special master and independent monitor to monitor compliance with "adequate access to medical care" at Dilley.

DHS officials have previously disputed any allegations of substandard medical care at the detention facility.

A spokesperson for DHS said Gomez-Quiroz was convicted of illegal entry on July 6 and stated that she remains in ICE custody pending the outcome of her removal proceedings.

In response to concerns from Gomez-Quiroz's family that she has been experiencing lower abdominal pain, a DHS spokesperson said, "It is a longstanding practice to provide comprehensive medical care from the moment a person enters ICE custody."

"She's been very depressed," Ocampo told ABC News. "My mom is desperate ... this is a very hard situation.
