text:
WASHINGTON, Oct 5 (Reuters) - The US Supreme Court is set on Monday to hear a bid by oil companies ExxonMobil and Suncor Energy to thwart a lawsuit by officials in Boulder, Colorado, seeking monetary damages for harms caused by climate change, as the justices open a new nine-month term.

US-based Exxon and Canada-based Suncor appealed after the Colorado Supreme Court let Boulder's lawsuit accusing them of state law violations proceed. President Donald Trump's administration has backed Exxon and Suncor, arguing that the federal government's authority to regulate air pollution precludes Boulder's claims.

The top US judicial body opens its new term on the first Monday in October, as is its custom. It also has major cases involving Trump's hardline immigration policies and state-level bans on assault-style rifles, among others, lined up for the term.

Boulder's city and county governments have accused Exxon and Suncor of helping drive climate change and misleading the public about the risks of fossil fuels. Boulder aims to hold the companies liable for past and future costs associated with climate change such as infrastructure repairs, environmental damage, emergency management and harms to public health.

The burning of fossil fuels releases greenhouse gases including carbon dioxide into the atmosphere, trapping heat and raising average global temperatures over time.

Nearly 60 state and local governments have brought similar suits seeking billions of dollars from fossil fuel companies, with more continuing to be filed, Exxon and Suncor told the justices. A ruling by the Supreme Court siding with the companies could lead to many of those cases being dismissed.

Monday's arguments mark the latest example of energy-sector companies asking the justices to block climate-related liability or limit federal environmental regulation.

Backers of the oil companies argue that if Boulder's most far-reaching claims are allowed to proceed, it could give states sweeping power over conduct occurring far outside their borders.

Energy companies and trade groups, along with states allied with them, have built a largely winning record before the justices over the past two decades in cases involving climate liability and the reach of federal environmental regulation.

The current court has a 6-3 conservative majority.

Exxon and Suncor argue, among other things, that Boulder's claims intrude on an area controlled by the federal government as well as the Clean Air Act.

Justice Samuel Alito has recused himself from participating in the case. Alito owns stock in several oil and gas companies but not Exxon or Suncor, according to his financial disclosure forms.

The Supreme Court's decision is expected by the end of June.

(Reporting by John Kruzel; Editing by Will Dunham)

text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Supreme Court's new term begins Monday with cases on climate change, religious rights and President Donald Trump’s crackdown on immigration high on the agenda.

Here’s a look at what's in store:

Climate change

The high court is starting its term with a major climate change case. The justices will hear an appeal from energy companies trying to block dozens of lawsuits seeking to hold them liable in court for damage related to climate change.

Billions of dollars are potentially at stake in a case out of Boulder, Colorado, where local officials say the industry should help shoulder the escalating costs of disasters linked to climate change.

The companies, Suncor and ExxonMobil, say lawsuits aren't the way to deal with the global issue. They have the backing of the Trump administration, which argues the litigation is a power grab intended to impose regulations on emissions.

Assault weapons bans

About a dozen states have banned semiautomatic rifles like AR-15s, which are often called assault weapons. They say the guns are disproportionately used in mass shootings, and banning them helps reduce gun violence.

Challengers say those laws violate the Second Amendment. They argue that AR-15s and other similar weapons are among the most popular and commonly owned guns in the country.

The conservative-majority court has expanded gun rights in recent years, and four justices had signaled that it was only a matter of time before the court took up the issue. The case will be considered in December.

Immigration

The court will hear two significant immigration cases with potentially big implications for Trump's wide-reaching crackdown.

One is about deportations of migrants who can't be quickly sent back to their home countries. The Trump administration has been sending thousands to other countries where they have no ties, under a series of often-secret agreements.

The Supreme Court will consider overturning lower court orders allowing them a chance to object. The justices have allowed the flights to continue in the meantime.

The other case is over the administration's mandatory detention policy for immigrants who have been living in the U.S. illegally, even if they've been in the country for years.

The administration argues it can hold people without a bond hearing, but most appeals courts that have considered the issue disagree.

Voting

A Republican push to enforce strict Arizona voting laws will also come before the justices this term.

One measure requires people to show proof of citizenship when registering to vote using a state form, and another calls for regular purges of the voter rolls to remove people if their citizenship could not be confirmed.

It comes as Trump has failed to get legislation requiring documentary proof of citizenship for registering to vote through Congress. Arguments are set for December.

Religious rights

Catholic preschools that can't take part in a taxpayer-funded program in Colorado will come before the court in November. It's the justices' latest case involving religious rights.

St. Mary Catholic Parish says it's been left out of the state's universal preschool program over its faith-based admissions policies, which exclude kids from LGBTQ+ families.

Colorado says religious schools are welcome to participate but have to follow nondiscrimination laws. The program was created by a 2020 ballot measure and provides public funding for preschool at schools selected by parents.

title: Under Trump, immigration arrests and detentions surge in Tennessee
description:
Since Donald Trump was sworn into office for a second time, immigration arrests have surged nationwide as his administration carries out an unprecedented mass detention and deportation agenda.
At the current pace of arrests and detentions, ICE is on track to arrest and detain an even greater number of immigrants in Tennessee this year.
Hundreds of the Tennessee arrests during Trump’s second term stemmed from large-scale, targeted operations highlighted in ICE news releases.
Before Trump retook office, just two Tennessee sheriffs had entered into so-called 287(g) agreements with the federal government to cooperate with the federal government in immigration enforcement.
While immigration arrests and detentions are occurring across Tennessee, Memphis has seen the largest number, followed by Nashville/Davidson County, Knox County, Rutherford County and Hamilton County.
text:
Since Donald Trump was sworn into office for a second time, immigration arrests have surged nationwide as his administration carries out an unprecedented mass detention and deportation agenda.

In Tennessee, the number of people arrested and detained began to climb almost immediately after the president’s January 2025 inauguration.

In total, the number of immigrant arrests and detentions multiplied nearly four-fold in Tennessee during the president’s first year in office, compared to the final year of the Biden administration, according to data the Tennessee Lookout analyzed from the Deportation Data Project at U.C. Berkeley and U.C.L.A. The Deportation Data Project obtained the data from U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE, through Freedom of Information Act litigation.

At the current pace of arrests and detentions, ICE is on track to arrest and detain an even greater number of immigrants in Tennessee this year.

Tennessee’s Republican leaders have largely applauded the heightened immigration enforcement activities across the state

Tennessee House Speaker Cameron Sexton, a Crossville Republican, openly talked about working with Trump’s White House to pass a slate of legislation targeting immigrants without legal status, calling it a “model for the nation.” Several laws prevent immigrants without legal status from accessing the limited public benefits that immigrants without legal status are entitled to, such as public health clinic access.

“Tennessee will not become a sanctuary state for illegal immigration,” Sexton said in a news release last touting recent ICE deportations. “We will ensure our public benefits are only for those who are citizens and who come into our country legally.”

Among state Republican actions was establishing a first-of-its-kind Centralized Immigration Enforcement Bureau in Tennessee whose mission is to “oversee state and local collaboration with federal immigration authorities.”

At the same time, immigrant advocates have sprung into action to provide legal services, organize public protests, organize aid to families left behind by the detentions and train volunteers to monitor and document ICE arrests in real time.

“The Trump administration has aggressively imposed a brutal campaign of mass detention and deportation, sparing no one,” Spring Miller, senior director of legal strategy at the Tennessee Immigrant and Refugee Rights Coalition wrote in a recent op-ed highlighting the impact of ICE detentions on mothers and children.

Hundreds of the Tennessee arrests during Trump’s second term stemmed from large-scale, targeted operations highlighted in ICE news releases.

ICE announced 196 arrests in Nashville during a weeklong traffic stop dragnet in May 2025 dubbed “Operation Flood the Zone,” conducted in partnership with the Tennessee Highway Patrol.

In May 2026, ICE in partnership with Sevierville police and sheriffs arrested and detained 117 immigrants in east Tennessee in “Operation Smoky Mountain.” In the initial weeks after Trump created the crime-fighting Memphis Safe Task Force in October ICE data shows more than 400 arrests and detentions of immigrants in that city.

Partnerships between ICE and local police and sheriffs have also driven increasing immigration arrests that have taken place largely out of public view.

Before Trump retook office, just two Tennessee sheriffs had entered into so-called 287(g) agreements with the federal government to cooperate with the federal government in immigration enforcement.

Today there are more than 120.

While federal officials have pledged to target the “worst of the worst” in immigration enforcement, data shows the majority of immigrants detained in Tennessee since the beginning of 2025 had not been convicted of any crime. Two-thirds of those detained had either no criminal mark on their record or faced pending charges.

While immigration arrests and detentions are occurring across Tennessee, Memphis has seen the largest number, followed by Nashville/Davidson County, Knox County, Rutherford County and Hamilton County.

text:
Three transgender women who have been detained for months at a male-only central Louisiana immigration detention center allege that they have faced abuse and transphobia at the hands of staff and other detainees.

In interviews with Verite News, they allege that they have been assaulted by officers, forcibly detransitioned, verbally harassed and kept in solitary confinement.

“Everywhere they call us men, faggots, very offensive words,” Camila Toro de Paula, one of the detainees, told Verite News. The officers “let it happen. We don’t have a right to anything here; we trans women don’t have rights” at the facility, she added.

Two of the women — Estephany Rivas and Sofia — have spent months at Central Louisiana ICE Processing Center in Jena. The third, Camila Toro de Paula, has been there for more than a year. The three women are in protective custody, separated from other detainees. Verite is only using Sofia’s middle name because she is worried about the conditions at the detention center continuing or worsening.

The Trump administration forces trans women to be housed with men in detention centers. U.S. Immigration and Enforcement (ICE) houses the women in solitary confinement for their protection, but the women say the isolation has not prevented them from enduring death threats, humiliating pat downs and physical abuse by staff.

The Jena facility is run by GEO Group — a for-profit corporation that is one of the country’s largest private prison operators — which has been criticized for its treatment of detainees. A 2024 report (PDF) on ICE detention centers in Louisiana by Robert & Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center, the American Civil Liberties Union and other leading human rights organizations recorded “systemic human rights abuses,” as they called it, at the facilities. At the Jena facility, they reported that there had been detainee deaths, people being shackled for more than 24 hours, contaminated food, filthy cells and bathrooms, physical abuse – such as spraying detainees with pepper spray, sexual harassment and assault, medical abuse and neglect, and the use of solitary confinement as retaliation.

Other organizations, such as Immigration Equality and Southeast Dignity Not Detention, have found similar conditions for detainees at the facility.

“There is nothing in the system that is built to recognize their full humanity as trans people, and now there’s no mechanisms in place to protect them from transphobic violence, from abuse of solitary confinement,” Mich González, a New Orleans-based immigrant rights attorney who has represented trans women in detention, said about the Trump administration ending protections for transgender detainees.

The three women had all been living in the U.S. for several years. Like most immigrant detainees, they do not have active criminal charges against them. Rivas had misdemeanor traffic offenses that were resolved before her detention, according to court records and her attorney Mauricio Sierra. Toro de Paula had one previous conviction for a low-level misdemeanor as well as two felony charges stemming from a 2025 arrest that were dismissed, according to her attorney and a New York Times report.

Media reports and court records also show that Toro de Paula, who is Venezuelan, and Rivas, who is Honduran, were taken by ICE agents in New York and in Baton Rouge, Louisiana, respectively, then taken to Central Louisiana. Sofia was taken by Border Patrol agents in Mississippi and transferred to ICE custody before being sent to Central Louisiana.

They are seeking asylum in the U.S. after facing death threats and attempted rapes in their home countries due to being transgender, and at least one has been persecuted by cartels.

It is not uncommon for people to be detained for months in poor conditions, but as the experience of these detainees, which has been corroborated by legal documents, records from the detention facility, medical records, interviews with the detainees’ attorneys and emails from the attorneys to the facility indicate, LGBTQIA+ immigrants face additional discrimination on the basis of their sexual and gender identity — often the very reason they are seeking asylum in the United States. Transgender women in particular are at a high-risk of gendered and sexual abuse due to being housed in male-only facilities.

Verite News reviewed court documents, emails, medical records and incident reports from their time at the Central Louisiana facility, and spoke with the women and their attorneys.

“What they are doing to us is torture,” Toro de Paula said.

Humiliating pat downs and use of force

The women say that they’ve faced physical abuse because they have refused to undergo pat downs and strip searches that expose their bodies in front of male guards.

According to a June 25 incident report, a group of guards — which included men and at least one woman — approached Rivas and asked her to stand up and submit to a pat down. It is not clear from the report why they were searching her. The female guard said she touched Rivas’ shoulder. The officer then alleged that Rivas “aggressively turned towards me swinging his arm around.” Rivas turned around, “swung the towel in his hand, striking my neck, and said ‘Don’t fucking touch me,’” according to the officer. The report refers to Rivas using he/him/his pronouns instead of her preferred pronouns.

The guard went on to say that another Correctional Emergency Response Team (CERT) member at the facility put her in the prone position and handcuffed her.

On June 26, a “Unit Disciplinary Committee Report of Findings and Actions” written by a member of the Unit Disciplinary Committee — tasked with investigating incident reports — detailed Rivas’ account of the incident. Verite News has part of the report and requested the full document from the U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) which has yet to respond.

According to the report, Rivas “stated his shirt began to rise, that’s when he told the officer ‘Don’t touch me’.” In an interview with the committee, Rivas said that she refused to be searched because there were several men present, and she denied that she ever hit the officer with a towel. Rivas said that “a view of camera footage” would show she never swung a towel.

“They threw me to the ground, and all the men were on top of me. [The female sergeant] tried to lift up my shirt to search me. And I told her, ‘No, no, don’t touch me —don’t touch me because I don’t want you to lift up my shirt,’” Rivas alleged in an interview with Verite News.

Sofia also alleged she had previously allowed the same female guard to search her, but after Rivas was restrained, the guard pushed her against the wall again, taunted her and pulled her hair.

“After they punished [Rivas], she slammed me against the wall again and searched me once more,” Sofia alleged. “‘No touch you?’ ‘No touch you?’, she’d say to me. She was kind of trying to make me angry to see if I’d do something so she could punish me too. And I told her, ‘It’s okay.’ I told her. And she grabbed my hair and pulled it.”

According to the disciplinary report document, the findings were based on the credibility of the officer, the investigation report and Rivas’ version of the incident. Although only Rivas’s testimony is available in the document, DHS said that “all staff provided the required documentation for the incident” and that a use of force review “was conducted by GEO and ICE Leadership and found to be justified.”

Verite News provided Sarah Decker, a senior staff attorney at the Robert & Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center Center, with the reports. Decker said that the description of Rivas arrest as her being “assisted to the prone position and handcuffed by another CERT member” was a “sanitized” way to describe a takedown — when officers use force to place someone face-down on the floor.

“We’ve had a number of clients who have been beaten and permanently disabled by takedowns, so we routinely see that they’re not actually following the use of force guidelines; that they’re using an indiscriminate amount of force when they’re taking people down,” Decker said.

ICE’s own National Detention Standards (PDF) handbook classifies a “take-down” as a “hard technique” and stipulates that “officers should first issue verbal commands” because it carries a high risk of injury.

Decker also pointed out the CERT members, who handcuffed Rivas, typically have high-risk security training and are brought in for takedowns.

Rivas’ attorney Mauricio Sierra, who is challenging her detention and seeking her release through a habeas corpus lawsuit, confirmed her account.

“There was no justifiable reason to … attack my client, to confine my client in that way, ” Sierra said. Sierra added that when he met with her, she was in a yellow-colored jumpsuit, a change from her blue-colored jumpsuit, indicating that the facility was classifying her as a higher level threat to the guards at the detention center. DHS confirmed her uniform color was changed because the charge of “Assault on Staff” is more severe.

Due to the conflicting allegations, Rivas was scheduled to have a hearing with an investigative panel on June 29. She alleges that the hearing never took place and that the video footage of the incident she requested was not handed over, while DHS says that the hearing did take place and she provided a verbal statement using the translator line. It is not clear from the documents available to Verite if there were additional findings as a result of the investigation.

Decker added that, in her experience working on use of force cases at detention centers, it is extremely difficult for detainees to hold officers responsible.

“The accounts of the detained people are the most reliable source of information. The video footage is great, but you often can’t get it, and I think the officers’ accounts are just not accurate,” Decker said. Verite asked for the video but it was not provided at the time of publication.

Protective custody

Beyond the allegations of physical abuse, the detainees said they have suffered emotionally from months of isolation.

At the detention facility in Jena, the women are confined in administrative segregation for their protection because they are transgender. It is the same unit as disciplinary segregation, where people are sent for infractions. Both administrative and disciplinary segregation are types of solitary confinement.

Experts, including the United Nations (PDF), say that any type of prolonged solitary confinement amounts to torture, despite its use being widespread in the U.S.

“They say that where they’re keeping us here for our protection, but this isn’t protection, it’s torture,” Sofia said.

Detainees in administrative segregation are supposed to have greater privileges to those who are there for disciplinary reasons, such as getting more time in the yard or being able to use a tablet, but court documents indicate they are still locked up for twenty hours a day.

And the women at the Jena detention center also allege that the few privileges they have are curtailed arbitrarily. According to medical records, Sofia once suffered a mental health crisis due to an officer cutting off time outside her cell.

“Sofia approached the sergeant with the intent to explain how she and other queer detainees felt this was discriminatory,” a psychologist who, in coordination with Humanitarian Outreach for Migrant Emotional Health, provided a mental health evaluation for Sofia’s asylum case. “According to Sofia, the sergeant told her to ‘shut up,’ followed by ‘shut your mouth.’”

“She went to her cell, grabbed a razor, and ‘cut [her]self, just to feel relief,” the report continued.

“Sofia elaborated that the superficial “scratch” relieved her frustration,” the psychologist wrote. “She believes there is a difference between clinical symptoms of depression and her experience of being ‘rightfully stressed for being [detained] so long under unfair conditions.’”

DHS responded that both Central Louisiana facility staff and medical staff deny the incident occurred, despite their own records showing Sofia had been transferred to a mental health hospital for self-harm.

Jeremy Jong, a staff attorney with the immigration advocacy nonprofit Al Otro Lado, told Verite News that detention centers are not equipped to deal with detainees who have complex needs, and often opt to simply place people in solitary confinement.

Additionally, DHS responded that “recreation privileges have never been revoked, and that they are offered recreation daily,” but that the women have at times been moved from the general population yard to the Special Management Unit due to rules infractions.

Despite being in protective custody, the women have faced transphobic abuse and threats from other detainees, they allege. In emails reviewed by Verite News from November and December 2025, Laura Berger, an immigration staff attorney at The Legal Aid society representing Toro de Paula, repeatedly wrote to the Jena facility’s supervisory detention and deportation officer, Christopher Rabe, about a detainee who continually verbally harassed and threatened Toro de Paula.

“One of the other detainees in her unit attempted to assault her and loudly accused her of having AIDS. The detainee threatened to harm my client and said that he had killed people before,” Berger wrote in the email. Although the facility provides a way for detainees to make complaints, Berger says that staff either brushed off Toro de Paula’s complaints or are unable to understand the threats since they were made in Spanish.

When asked for comment, DHS responded that the allegations were “FALSE” and that “no staff at [Central Louisiana ICE Processing Center] witnessed the conduct being described by Toro de Paula’s attorney.” However, emails from Rabe to Berger acknowledge the facility had to separate the other detainee from Toro de Paula.

The agency also said that “staff cannot control what other detainees may verbalize,” but “they are trained to hold detainees accountable for misconduct should it occur with internal disciplinary reports.”

Forced detransition and medical neglect

All three women say they are being denied treatment for medical ailments like stomach aches, blood in their urine and skin rashes, and are also denied trans health care.

When asked for comment, DHS responded that detainees “have been sent to see a urologist on multiple occasions and other specialists as part of their care plan.” The agency added that it “is the best healthcare many aliens have received in their entire lives” and that “meals are certified by dieticians.” The women also allege that the food is contaminated, undercooked and inedible.

The facility had at least two deaths that were due to an improper medical response, according to a 2017 investigation (PDF) by the DHS’ Office for Civil Rights and Civil Liberties.

While medical neglect is widespread in detention facilities nationwide, specifically denying trans health care fits into a nationwide trend of forced detransition in detention centers.

At Central Louisiana, Sofia and Rivas say that they are being denied hormone replacement therapy, which they both were taking before they were detained. According to a DHS statement to Verite News, DHS segregates the women by biological sex because of Trump’s 2025 executive order. The order also explicitly states that the Bureau of Prisons and federal funds cannot be “expended for any medical procedure, treatment, or drug for the purpose of conforming an inmate’s appearance to that of the opposite sex.”

The women also say that they are also being denied feminine clothes and makeup, both of which would help them feel more comfortable in their bodies.

“They don’t let us wear makeup, so what we do is use a pencil to paint on our faces. Just because we do that, they get mad and report us. What harm are we doing to them by” using pencils to replace makeup, Rivas said.

DHS says the allegations that undergarments have been changed is false. Regarding their use of colored pencils as makeup, DHS says that “detainees are not permitted to utilize colored pencils outside their intended use” because it is considered contraband.

“[Detention] is now encouraged because mistreating people puts them in a more desperate situation, to then seek voluntary departure and under duress give up legal rights they may have to stay in the country”, Nora Ahmed, who is ACLU of Louisiana’s legal director, told Verite News.

Transgender immigrants in detention

The women at the Central Louisiana ICE Processing Center who are alleging transphobic harassment, physical and emotional abuse aren’t the only ones in Louisiana in recent years.

In 2023, Vicky, a transgender woman who was detained in Pine Prairie ICE Detention Center — also operated by the GEO Group — filed a civil rights complaint (PDF) describing the culture of the facility. In a press release announcing the filing of the complaint, the group Immigrant Justice said the facility had a “culture of transphobia, harassment and medical negligence.”

In September 2025, the ACLU of Louisiana, Robert & Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center and the National Immigration Project filed complaints on behalf of four immigrants who were detained at the South Louisiana ICE Detention Center in Basile — also run by the GEO Group. The complaints alleged that two trans men and one nonbinary person, all housed in a female-only facility, were subject to sexual abuse, forced labor, retaliation and denial of medical care.

And this type of alleged mistreatment is happening in other states as well. A 2016 Human Rights Watch report that included interviews with former trans detainees, found that they were subjected to abusive strip searches in front of male guards, and a peer reviewed study that analyzed ICE audits found that strip searches of transgender detainees occurred in violation of ICE policy from 2014 to 2019 in at least three states: Washington, Arizona and California.

Yet, it is difficult to estimate how many people are affected by transphobic abuse in immigrant detention centers.

Under the second Trump administration, ICE is excluding the number of transgender detainees from constitutionally mandated detention center reports. The last report issued by the Biden administration in January 2025 recorded that there were 47 transgender people in immigration detention. But according to the Vera Institute of Justice, the government is not counting transgender people due to the administration’s hostility towards trans people’s lives and rights.

The 2025 executive order that President Donald Trump signed equated gender with biological sex and mandated federal agencies to remove “all statements, policies, regulations, forms, communications, or other internal and external messages” which recognized transgender and gender non-conforming people. The order also prohibited trans women from being housed in women’s prisons or detention centers. In effect, they can only be housed in male facilities.

Shortly after, the 2015 “Transgender Care Memorandum” was taken offline. It was last available in February 2025 from ICE’s website, according to the Internet Archive (PDF). The memo — signed by Tom Homan, then the executive director for ICE under the Obama administration — established basic care requirements for transgender detainees. (Homan is now Trump’s “border czar.”) For example, it mandated limiting solitary confinement to 72 hours, to consider placing a detainee in housing consistent with their gender identity, and to conduct strip searches in private, among other rules. Additionally, contracts with some detention facilities had their transgender care requirements removed.

While past complaints indicate that these transgender care requirements were often violated by facilities (PDF), the memo still gave trans detainees a degree of recognition, as well as a way to challenge discriminatory treatment.

“We know that the government is making it impossible to even be yourself in prison,” Déa Thatcher, an organizer with Trans & Queer Community Fund, a mutual aid group that provides commissary support for trans immigrant detainees, said. “When I tell you the amount of times I’ve gotten on a video with someone and they have put their hands over their face because they don’t want me to see their beard, it’s like they are being forced to look a certain way and present a certain way.”

‘I am practically signing my death warrant‘

According to Rivas’ habeas corpus petition, she is seeking asylum due to being targeted by the Honduran Los Zetas cartel, who she claims murdered her brothers after she refused to traffic drugs for them. She had been harassed by them for years due to being transgender, the petition says. Mexican cartel members later kidnapped and assaulted Rivas on her journey to the U.S.-Mexico border.

“If I go back to my country, I am practically signing my death warrant,” Rivas said.

Sofia and Toro de Paula are also seeking asylum after being subjected to transphobic physical violence in their home countries. They both had their asylum petitions denied and are appealing the decision.

“In general, trans women had a shot at winning [asylum] because of how our asylum laws are written and because trans people are targeted in many countries for being trans,” Jong told Verite News.

But immigration detention makes it harder for their legal team to prepare an asylum case or an appeal because they can only meet with detainees for a few hours each week, making it more difficult to prepare a strong case. It is then much more likely that they will lose their case and be deported.

“You have to collect all this evidence, where your main person to help you is locked up, with little to no access to the outside world, and where everyone outside is grappling with their absence,” immigration attorney Mich González said. He added that immigrants have cases that could determine life or death yet are being tried in an administrative court inside a facility that is actively harming people.

The women could be detained indefinitely. The U.S. Supreme Court has agreed to review a case determining whether immigrants can be denied bond and kept in detention while they challenge their removal. If the court rules in favor of the Trump administration, the women will have no clear path out of immigration detention, barring deportation or being allowed to legally remain in the country.

“We want them to treat us with dignity and to treat the next trans people who come to this center well, with respect,” Rivas said.

title: The U.S. deported a former political prisoner to Nicaragua. He's now in prison again
authors: Kate Linthicum, Ismael López, www.latimes.com, kate-linthicum
description:
A former political prisoner who said he was tortured for leading protests against Nicaragua’s authoritarian government was arrested and jailed immediately after he was deported there from the United States last week, according to relatives and human rights advocates.
Jarquín was imprisoned for nine months, and later told journalists and human rights investigators that guards burned his genitals with cigarette butts.
He was released in 2019, spent a short period in Costa Rica and later sought political asylum in the United States.
But other Nicaraguans are being sent home, despite warnings from human rights advocates that such deportations may violate the international ban on “refoulement” — returning someone to a country where they face persecution or torture.
“The United States government knows Nicaragua is one of the most authoritarian governments in the hemisphere and should take robust steps to ensure nobody is sent back to torture or abuse.”
text:
A former political prisoner who said he was tortured for leading protests against Nicaragua’s authoritarian government was arrested and jailed immediately after he was deported there from the United States last week, according to relatives and human rights advocates.

Jeffrey Jarquín, 35, was taken directly from the deportation flight to Nicaragua’s notorious Modelo prison, where he had been held previously for participating in pro-democracy marches that were violently repressed by President Daniel Ortega.

Jarquín was among thousands of Nicaraguans who took to the streets in 2018 to demand Ortega’s resignation and free elections. He helped occupy two public universities, and later took refugee inside a small Catholic church as it came under fire from pro-government militia forces — an incident that became emblematic of the country’s embattled protest movement.

Jarquín was imprisoned for nine months, and later told journalists and human rights investigators that guards burned his genitals with cigarette butts. He was released in 2019, spent a short period in Costa Rica and later sought political asylum in the United States.

The Trump administration has levied sanctions on Ortega and his family members and has repeatedly criticized his government, with Juan Pablo Segura, deputy assistant secretary of State for Western Hemisphere affairs, describing it recently as a “brutal dictatorship that is stealing, lying and murdering.”

Yet journalists, human rights advocates and political dissidents who were persecuted for promoting democracy in Nicaragua are increasingly being targeted for deportation as the Trump administration narrows access to asylum and expands the pool of migrants eligible for removal.

U.S. immigration agents have recently begun arresting members of a high-profile group of Nicaraguan political prisoners who were freed in a 2023 State Department deal, flown to the U.S. and granted temporary humanitarian parole and the chance to apply for asylum.

The U.S. has sent some Nicaraguan migrants as far away as Africa under a Trump administration program that deports asylum seekers and others to “third countries” where they have no ties.

But other Nicaraguans are being sent home, despite warnings from human rights advocates that such deportations may violate the international ban on “refoulement” — returning someone to a country where they face persecution or torture.

“The United States sent him to the very prisons where he had already been tortured,” said Muriel Sáenz, an activist who represented Jarquín during an immigration bond hearing.

Jarquín, she said, is a victim of political persecution who has been sent “back into the hands of his tormentors.”

Jarquín was arrested in Miami in February after being accused of assault. A judge dismissed the case, but while Jarquín was detained, immigration agents initiated deportation proceedings against him. An immigration judge denied him asylum, according to his advocates.

They said Jarquín agreed to be deported but asked to be sent to a third country. Instead he was put on a plane to Managua last week.

U.S. deportations to Nicaragua have risen sharply under Trump. An analysis of government data by Human Rights Watch found that the U.S. deported more than 6,300 Nicaraguans between January and July of this year, compared with 3,323 during the same period in 2025.

In Miami’s Nicaraguan community, Jarquín was known as a vocal opponent of the Sandinista regime, often carrying a megaphone to protests. He posted photos on social media of himself alongside U.S. Republican leaders who have also criticized Ortega, including U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

At 81, Ortega is the longest-serving leader in the Americas. He rules the country with his co-president and wife, Rosario Murillo.

The pair, former revolutionaries who decades ago helped overthrow a brutal right-wing dictatorship, have tightened their grip on power in recent years, closing media outlets and nongovernmental organizations and jailing or expelling virtually all of their political opponents. Nicaragua’s government did not respond to inquiries about the Jarquín case.

His friends and family members say they don’t know when they will see him again.

“His life is in danger back in Nicaragua,” said Ronmell López, a friend. “We demand that the dictatorship ... respect his life and safety.”

“For Nicaraguan deportees, the risk of persecution is real,” said Juan Pappier, deputy director of the Americas division at Human Rights Watch. “The United States government knows Nicaragua is one of the most authoritarian governments in the hemisphere and should take robust steps to ensure nobody is sent back to torture or abuse.”

text:
The Supreme Court's next chapter begins Monday, with the justices set to decide key questions involving President Trump's immigration agenda, climate-change litigation and gun control in their new term.

The big picture: But one of the most closely watched fights may be on Truth Social, rather than the docket, as an increasingly agitated Trump chastises the high court he helped shape.

The executive and judicial branches are set for another round in the white-columned ring with a president who moves at breakneck speed.

State of play: The court recently agreed to hear two major immigration cases, one over mandatory detention for certain immigrants and another over deporting immigrants to third countries where they lack ties.

On the latter, the high court allowed the administration to restart its fast-tracked third-country deportations late last month while it considers the underlying legal questions in December.

The court agreed Thursday to take up the detention case, setting the stage to test the Trump administration's legal interpretation that noncitizens who entered the country illegally, but have been living in the U.S., are to be held without bond.

While federal appeals courts have been divided on the issue, a vast majority — nine of the 11 — have rejected the Trump administration's interpretation.

Flashback: While the Supreme Court shot down Trump's attempt to undermine birthright citizenship last term, it handed him a number of immigration wins and green-lit policies on its shadow docket.

Those victories for Trump allowed the administration to end temporary protected status, enforce stricter asylum rules and use a revamped tool to check voters' citizenship.

Zoom out: Before those cases come to the bench, the court will hear arguments Monday in a key climate case that could determine the fate of state-court lawsuits nationwide seeking climate damages from oil giants, Axios' Ben Geman reports.

The court also added two other cases to its lineup Thursday, on top of the mandatory detention debate: One is about a federal law protecting land use by religious groups brought by a missionary organization, and the other is about military benefits in divorce settlement agreements.

Later this year, the court will weigh the constitutionality of bans on AR-15-style weapons and consider whether Arizona can mandate proof of citizenship for people registering to vote.

More disputes over other Trump policies are sure to reach the court this term.

Friction point: Though the high court has inflated executive power and gave the president a number of summer shadow docket wins, it also checked some of his most audacious actions last term. He didn't like that.

After the justices blocked the administration's pre-midterm attempt to rewrite mail-in voting rules, the president raged against his own Supreme Court picks.

"These are not the people I interviewed to serve on the United States Supreme Court, they are merely a shell of their original selves," he wrote on Truth Social.

In a recent interview with Time, the president said he regretted nominating them, saying, "I gave them the chance of a lifetime, and it's unfortunate what they did."

authors: Brian Sharp, Jose Sandoval, www.wxxinews.org, brian-sharp, jose-sandoval
description:

ICE does not have a detention facility for women in Western New York, so it otherwise contracted with jails or moved female detainees out of state.

text:
Updated plans to expand the ICE detention facility at Batavia now describe a $17 million soft-sided or tent project — all or part of which is to house women.

The Department of Homeland Security previously announced a 100-bed hard-sided facility described as a “temporary detention structure.” The Buffalo Service Processing Center in Batavia already is the largest Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention facility in New York state, typically operating well over its 650-bed capacity but — until now — only housing men.

The latest contract modification appears to add $7 million to the project, bringing it to its current total, and states the intent is to establish a “soft-sided facility and support services for detained female aliens,” records show. Funding would cover two years of operation, and includes $5 million for contingencies.

“While this approach may be more expensive, it is necessary to meet the immediate and urgent bedspace requirements in the Buffalo area of responsibility,” wrote Charles Wall, deputy director with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, in a June 15 letter seeking contract approval for the tent facility.

U.S. Rep. Timothy Kennedy, a Democrat whose Western New York district includes Batavia, released the letter and other documents Friday. Kennedy, who is a member of the House Committee on Homeland Security, reiterated his opposition to the expansion saying the Trump Administration mislead Americans when they said they were going after " the worst of the worst."

"More than 70 percent of the people held in Batavia have no criminal record, and DHS says that doesn't matter," Kennedy said in a prepared statement.

Kennedy referenced a response he recently received from Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, included in the documents released Friday, stating that 28% of the detainees at Batavia had a criminal history but that "known criminal history is not a prerequisite for immigration enforcement action and never has been."

Federal officials have tied the expansion to New York state prohibiting local law enforcement from cooperating with immigration authorities. That was signed into law in May and took effect in August. Fifteen county sheriffs are currently suing the state over the new law.

The state’s prohibition includes housing detainees in county jails. ICE does not have a detention facility for women in Western New York, so it otherwise contracted with jails or moved female detainees out of state.

Exactly what is to be built at Batavia, though, is unclear.

Walls’ letter cites the $17 million, two-year project cost, and was penned two-and-a-half months before Homeland Security awarded a sole-source or no-bid contract purportedly for the 100-bed hard-sided expansion. That contract went to Akima Infrastructure Protection, LLC. The U.S. firm has ties to human rights abuses at Guantanamo Bay, and also has been put in charge of running the Batavia facility.

In his letter, Walls sought approval “as soon as possible" while estimating the tent or soft-sided expansion would take six months or less to build. He included additional "medical infrastructure" including exam, consultation and airborne infection isolation rooms, a multipurpose room, offices and a nurses station. Mullin listed a need for added staffing, ranging from nurses and a dentist to recreation coordinators.

The facility has previously been cited for insufficient medical care and staffing shortages.

The modification with added funding that described the soft-sided women’s facility was filed on Tuesday, Sept. 29. That same day, Mullin wrote to Kennedy, referencing only a hard-sided facility — also for women, though possibly for men but not to include children — and stating that construction had yet to begin.

The documents Kennedy released had details, including total capacity of the expansion, redacted. Kennedy declined an interview request. A spokesperson for Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer said his office was compiling information but was not prepared to comment. Immigration and Customs Enforcement did not respond to questions seeking clarification after initially re-releasing its statement from this summer referring to the hard-sided facility.

title: The Immigration and Asylum Bill risks weakening our right to family life - Liberty
description:
The Immigration and Asylum Bill is a major new piece of legislation making its way through Parliament, covering everything from asylum appeals to modern slavery.
What the Bill would change The Bill defines “family life”, as partners and children under 18 who live together.
We are being asked to weaken a fundamental human right on the basis of an argument that the Government’s own analysis can’t support.
The Immigration and Asylum Bill moves us away from that principle by narrowing who counts as family and narrowing what judges are allowed to consider.
We should be deeply cautious about weakening fundamental rights on the basis of myths, political pressure, or uncertain evidence.
text:
The Immigration and Asylum Bill is a major new piece of legislation making its way through Parliament, covering everything from asylum appeals to modern slavery. MPs approved its main principles back in July; it’s now at Committee Stage, where a small group of MPs go through it line by line, checking the detail and considering changes. After that it returns to the Commons for further votes, then faces the same process again in the House of Lords – so there’s still time for it to change before it becomes law.

This blog focuses on Part 2 of the Bill, which would rewrite how courts apply Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR): the right to private and family life.

Where this came from

Part 2 didn’t come out of nowhere. The Government first introduced these plans in its November 2025 Restoring Order and Control policy statement. In May 2026, the UK and 45 other Council of Europe states signed a political declaration giving states more room to weigh Article 8 family rights against deportation. This Bill brings that agenda home, writing it into UK law.

The UK has a new Prime Minister, but not a new direction on immigration. One of Andy Burnham’s first votes back in Parliament was in favour of this Bill, even after nearly 80 Labour backbenchers wrote urging him to rethink the reforms. As PM, he’s kept the Bill’s architect, Shabana Mahmood, on as Home Secretary – suggesting we shouldn’t expect a major shift on immigration any time soon.

Rewriting a fundamental right

The Government says these reforms will restore public confidence, but we disagree. Article 8 protects families, privacy, and homes far beyond the immigration system, and there’s little proof these changes will even work.

Weakening a fundamental right doesn’t build confidence in it – it just leaves it weaker for everyone. How it’s treated here sets a precedent for how it can be treated elsewhere.

What the Bill would change

The Bill defines “family life”, as partners and children under 18 who live together. Anything else – a grandparent raising a grandchild, an adult caring for an elderly parent – has to prove additional dependency, and the Bill explicitly rules out financial dependence and emotional support as proof on their own. Judges would no longer ask whether separating a family is fair, only whether it fits the definition.

Children will pay the price

The Bill narrows when it’s considered unreasonable to expect a British or settled child to leave the UK, and raises the threshold for keeping a family together when a parent faces removal – requiring proof that separation would cause the child a “very significant and long-lasting adverse effect”. In practice, that means more children being uprooted from their homes, schools and communities, or separated from a parent who provides their care and stability.

Where’s the evidence that this is necessary?

Article 8 has become one of the most misunderstood rights in public debate. Politicians from across the political spectrum have argued it stops the UK controlling immigration and deporting foreign criminals – but the evidence tells a different story. The Bonavero Institute found that more than 75% of media reports mentioning the ECHR focused on immigration control, with many misreporting the cases they covered. For deportations of foreign national offenders, successful Article 8 appeals amounted to just 2.5% of the number deported over the same period.

The Government’s own impact assessment estimates these changes could cost as much as £46 million over 10 years – driven largely by the cost of appeals, removals and lost visa revenue, before any savings materialise. Any offsetting saving rests largely on a deterrent effect it admits is “unknown and not quantified”, with other impacts “not estimated due to an absence of evidence”.

We are being asked to weaken a fundamental human right on the basis of an argument that the Government’s own analysis can’t support.

Article 8 protects all of us

Article 8 is not just about immigration. It protects privacy, homes and family relationships across many contexts: keeping families together in care settings, protecting women fleeing domestic violence, safeguarding medical autonomy and personal data. Its strength lies in allowing judges to balance individual circumstances against wider public interests and reach proportionate decisions.

The Immigration and Asylum Bill moves us away from that principle by narrowing who counts as family and narrowing what judges are allowed to consider. We should be deeply cautious about weakening fundamental rights on the basis of myths, political pressure, or uncertain evidence. Human rights must not be conditional protections applied only to those deemed ‘deserving’.

Once a right can be narrowed for one group, any of our rights can be narrowed too, whenever it’s politically convenient.

The Government must drop these proposals. Protecting Article 8 means protecting the principle that human rights belong to everyone.

name: Human Rights
title: It's time to abolish ICE | Amy Fischer - The Guardian
description:
That’s the conclusion we at Amnesty International have reached after documenting the chilling pattern of human rights violations across the US during immigration enforcement operations.
We documented abuses inside detention facilities as well.
The United States has an obligation to respect and protect the human rights of all of us.
Immigration enforcement does not exempt any government from that responsibility.
It is past time to build an immigration system grounded in human rights and human dignity.
text:
ICE must be abolished.

That’s the conclusion we at Amnesty International have reached after documenting the chilling pattern of human rights violations across the US during immigration enforcement operations.

ICE’s record of violating human rights has been documented for more than two decades, but our latest findings show that the abuses go well beyond a series of incidents. Instead, under the Trump administration, there is a clear pattern that has reached a new and dangerous scale.

In large-scale immigration enforcement operations in Chicago, Minneapolis-St Paul, New Orleans and Washington DC, we documented federal agents repeatedly racially profiling and arbitrarily detaining people based on their perceived race. Agents also targeted workplaces and neighborhoods that they associated with Black and brown immigrant communities. I spoke with dozens of people – including Indigenous people, Black and brown US citizens, and people with legal immigration status who were also racially profiled, stopped and arbitrarily detained.

In all of the cities, people told me about federal officers using intimidation and unlawful force, including lethal force, against people they were attempting to detain, as well as community members observing or defending their neighbors. Agents broke down doors with guns drawn, smashed vehicle windows without justification and threw people to the ground. They used teargas and pepper spray against protesters and observers in public places, often impacting children and the surrounding neighborhoods. They also used facial recognition technology, drones and helicopters to unlawfully surveil people and intimidate them at the same time. As a Washington DC resident, I remember the helicopters shaking the windows of my home.

We documented abuses inside detention facilities as well. I heard harrowing stories from people who were held for prolonged periods in overcrowded and unsanitary facilities not designed for long-term detention, with minimal food, no access to healthcare, and severely restricted access to lawyers. We have concluded that these conditions constitute cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment and, in some circumstances, may amount to torture. We also documented unlawful incommunicado detention and possible acts of enforced disappearance, including cases in which families and lawyers could not locate people in ICE custody. I listened to panicked family members desperately seeking their loved ones who had been snatched by masked men in their communities, without a trace and no way to locate them.

The significance of our findings is not simply the brutality of individual incidents. It is their consistency. These violations were committed across four cities, involving different communities, operations and agents, yet they were strikingly similar. They are characteristic of the Trump administration’s cruel mass detention and deportation machine, including an immigration enforcement system in which safeguards have been weakened, oversight dismantled and accountability having become nothing more than a buzzword.

When a pattern of human rights violations is so undeniably occurring and completely embedded within an institution, for decades, and with pervasive impunity, the only solution is to start over. That’s why we are calling for ICE to be abolished.

The Trump administration’s deliberately cruel and racist practices have left entire communities across the US living in fear. Families are being torn apart. My friends are being deported. People are afraid to leave home to go to work, take their children to school or seek medical care.

The United States has an obligation to respect and protect the human rights of all of us. Immigration enforcement does not exempt any government from that responsibility. Yet the Trump administration has turned the country’s immigration enforcement system into a monster which repeatedly violates people’s rights.

ICE is not an inevitable feature of the US government. It was created in the aftermath of 9/11 to turn immigration into a national security issue, and has been problematic since.

However, the scale and horror that we have witnessed since January 2025, fueled by billions of new dollars and persistent impunity, has reached new levels. It has become clear that no amount of defunding, training or disciplinary measures will be enough. The extent and scale of the abuses and failures we documented lead to only one possible road to justice: ICE must be abolished.

But we can’t stop there. A future without ICE is not the end of the work. It’s a threshold step toward building an immigration system that complies with international human rights law and standards, centers family unity and compassion, and does not rely on cruelty and fear.

In fact, across the four cities we investigated, communities have refused to accept cruelty and fear as inevitable. People have built rapid-response networks and hotlines. They walk neighbors to school and work. They provide food, financial assistance, legal support and medical care. They document abuses. They support families who have been torn apart. They protect one another. Their solidarity shows us what communities can do when people refuse to abandon one another.

We don’t have to look farther than these communities to know that we can create a future where all of us are cared for, ICE agents don’t have free rein to terrorize our communities, where government power is subject to accountability, and where every person can enjoy their human rights.

It is past time to build an immigration system grounded in human rights and human dignity. It starts by abolishing ICE.

title: Haitian college student Pierre Damas Bel remembered for his hard work, kindness, and love ...
description:
Family and friends remembered Pierre Damas Bel as a hard-working, loving, and dependable young man who had hopes of building a hospital in Haiti.
Hundreds of people attended Damas Bel’s funeral at St. John’s Missionary Baptist Church in Springfield, Ohio on Saturday.

text:
This story discusses suicide. If you or someone you know is contemplating suicide, please call or text the National Suicide and Crisis Lifeline at 988.

Family and friends remembered Pierre Damas Bel as a hard-working, loving, and dependable young man who had hopes of building a hospital in Haiti.

Hundreds of people attended Damas Bel’s funeral at St. John’s Missionary Baptist Church in Springfield, Ohio on Saturday. The obituary, prayers, and remembrances were spoken in a mix of Haitian Creole and English.

“We come to mourn Pierre Damas Bel, but also to remember with gratitude the life that he lived, the people who he loved,” said Carl Ruby, pastor of Springfield’s Central Christian Church.

Damas Bel died in an apparent suicide on Aug. 31. His family said that happened because he was forced to wear an ankle monitor by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement after the U.S. Supreme Court allowed President Donald Trump to end temporary protected status for the 330,000 Haitians who’ve fled violence in their home country.

“We come because his life matters, because this family matters,” said Ernie Brown, senior pastor of St. John Missionary Baptist Church.

“May we remember not only how life ended, but also how life (was) lived, the relationships he formed, the moments he shared, the laughter, the memories, and the love surrounding him,” Brown said.

Many who spoke urged those in attendance to remember Damas Bel for the life he lived.

“Pierre Damas Bel deserves to be remembered for more than the tragedy that ended his earthly journey,” Ruby said.

Legal protected status for Haitians officially ended on July 27 and Haitians living in Springfield have been required to report to the ICE offices in Blue Ash or Westerville to accept ankle monitors.

“Our dear friend and brother might have died by suicide, but he was killed by the system,” said Guerline Jozef, executive director of the Haitian Bridge Alliance.

“Pierre’s legacy leaves a mark in our lives forever, and how the criminalization of Haitian immigrants can be an unnecessary death sentence,” said Yola Lamarre, an advocate with the Haitian Community Network.

Damas Bel, 20, was born in Tiburon, Haiti and came to the United States in 2021.

He was a first-year student at Wright State University studying neuroscience who had hopes of going to medical school. He also worked at Texas Roadhouse.

Damas Bel graduated from Springfield High School in May. He participated in the Junior Reserve Officers’ Training Corps and played on the high school soccer team.

“Damas was not simply a student with ambitions,” Ruby said.

“He was a young man who believed in helping people. His family remembers him as loving, obedient, dependable, compassionate.”

Damas Bel was raised by his father and stepmother, and had two younger siblings. Damas Bel’s father Pierre Ronal Bel described the deep relationship he had with his son in a statement that was read aloud during the service.

“He knew everything about me. … Whenever someone opens the front door, I have the sense that it is him coming home.”

Damas Bel’s stepmother Landy St. Juste shared how he helped her with job applications, interpreted for her, and checked on her regularly.

“He was loving and kind. May his beautiful soul rest in peace.”

His younger brother Bradley Bel said Damas Bel was always there for him.

“You always made me feel like I was never alone. You are someone I could always count on.”

When talking about Damas Bel’s father, Ruby mentioned Mamie Till-Mobley whose son Emmett Till who was lynched in Mississippi in 1955.

“He too died a violent death that galvanized the attention of the world and helped to fuel the Civil Rights Movement,” Ruby said.

“Like Emmett Till, Pierre Damas died under the weight of a racialized system that did not provide him with equal liberty and equal justice. He died under a way of governing that did not recognize his inalienable rights to life, liberty, and happiness. … May Pierre Damas Bel’s death start a movement of justice for all Haitian people.”

Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine attended the funeral and talked to Damas Bel’s family seated in the front row.

“Fran and I lost a 22-year-old daughter, Becky, so we have some understanding of the great trauma and sorrow that they face,” DeWine said. “I just want to be there for the family.”

Springfield Mayor Robert Rue was also at the funeral and sat next to DeWine during the service.

Ohio state Rep. Latyna Humphrey, D-Columbus, spoke on behalf of the Ohio Legislative Black Caucus.

“(Damas Bel) played a part in the American dream,” she said. “He was willing to work for his family. He was willing to create community. He was willing to make sure that he was educated because he too had dreams, he too had aspirations, he too wanted to save his community.”

Some in attendance at the funeral might not have known Damas Bel, Ruby said, but wanted to show support for his family and the Haitian community in Springfield.

“This group wants you and other Haitians who have come to Springfield to know that you are a blessing, not a burden to our community,” Ruby said.

“You have made our city better. You have not made it worse. This group wants you to know that you are not guests in Springfield. … You are a part of our community, and we do not want you to be ripped away.”

About 15,000 Haitians live in Springfield, with a mixture of temporary protected status, citizenship and other legal status.

Five Haitians from Springfield, Ohio have been deported back to Haiti and nearly 75 Haitians living in Ohio have been detained since July 27 at one of four Ohio detention facilities that contract with ICE.

text:
The Supreme Court justices return to the bench Monday for their new term, and their docket is already filling up with new confrontations on President Trump’s immigration agenda, among other major cases.

The term begins at a moment when the court’s public approval stands near record lows and in the shadow of a fraught relationship between Trump and the justices — namely the conservatives he appointed to the bench who have at times ruled against him.

“They voted against me too often,” Trump told Time magazine in an interview last week, referencing Justices Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett. “I gave them the position of a lifetime, and they vote against me often. They vote for me, too.”

It’s that mixed record that has fueled questions about how Trump’s agenda will fare this term at the Supreme Court, as lower court judges repeatedly block the president’s policies, prompting the disputes to continually reach the justices in a barrage.

In just the past week, the justices cranked up their docket by adding two major appeals brought by the administration concerning the president’s immigration agenda.

The court will review whether officials are giving enough due process before deporting migrants to third countries where they have no ties. They’ll also rule on the legality of Trump’s mandatory detention policy, which has fueled a tsunami of litigation in the lower courts. Decisions in both cases are expected by summer.

“Because of the vast number of illegal immigrants — particularly during the Biden administration, but for many years up until now — that just creates an incredible backlog of issues and concerns,” said Carrie Severino, president of the Judicial Crisis Network and a former law clerk to Justice Clarence Thomas. “Particularly as this president is trying to actually enforce the immigration laws.”

“So, immigration is definitely an issue,” she noted.

It leaves groups that have prolifically fought the president in court, like the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU), gearing up for another major year at the Supreme Court.

“Last term, OT25 [October Term 2025], was one of the ACLU’s busiest ever,” Cecilia Wang, the group’s national legal director, told reporters during a briefing call last week. “This term may top that.”

Left-leaning groups have remained optimistic in their chances before the conservative-majority court after last term produced a mixed outcome for the president.

The court delivered Trump major wins on executive control over independent agencies and immigration but also struck down his signature tariff policy, thwarted his efforts to restrict birthright citizenship and blocked him from immediately firing Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook.

Trump’s foes have also found relief in the justices’ recent emergency decisions that kept the president’s mail-in voting plan blocked ahead of the midterms.

It’s some of those decisions that have left the president reeling. Trump, in one recent social media post, called his nominees “merely a shell of their original selves.”

In an interview with CBS News set to air Sunday, Justice Samuel Alito brushed off any notion the justices have a political agenda and pointed out the bipartisan nature of court criticism.

“He has his own way of saying things,” Alito said of Trump. “But the criticism of the court, I mean, I want to be even-handed on this. The criticism of the court by [former] President Biden and justices by President Biden and his administration was very harsh. And President Trump has been very harsh.”

The public attacks didn’t stop the president from inviting Kavanaugh and Barrett to join him at the recent state dinner hosted for Chinese President Xi Jinping, however.

It’s not just Trump being critical. The Supreme Court’s public approval stands near record lows. A record-high 43 percent of Americans believe the court is too conservative, according to a Gallup poll conducted in early September. Just a little more than one-third of those surveyed said it was “just about right” ideologically, and 17 percent said it was too liberal.

Beyond the upcoming cases that directly implicate Trump’s agenda, some touch on political issues about which Trump’s base cares deeply.

The justices will hear challenges to an Arizona law that requires documentary proof of citizenship when registering to vote, a policy Republicans want implemented nationwide for federal elections. They’ll also take up several religious liberty disputes and examine the constitutionality of state bans on semi-automatic weapons, specifically AR-15s.

“We have a more exciting docket than we often do at this point,” said Severino.

“At the beginning of the Supreme Court term, some terms you would look at the list of the cases they’ve accepted already, and say, ‘Oh, it’s going to be kind of a snoozer,’” she added.

ACLU is asking the Supreme Court to add more cases to its plate. Among its pending requests is one that seeks to declare as unconstitutional Texas’s law requiring public school classrooms to post the Ten Commandments. The justices are set to consider taking up the case at a closed-door meeting after Texas responds in writing this fall.

“Our fundamental civil rights and civil liberties are under unprecedented attacks from all quarters,” Wang told reporters. “And many of those fights are poised to potentially make it up to the Supreme Court this term.”

On Monday, the term is set to begin with a bang as the justices consider a blockbuster case involving the fossil fuel industry. The Supreme Court will decide if cities and groups can use state law to force companies to pay potentially billions in damages over accusations they contributed to climate change and misled the public.

The case took an unanticipated turn last week when the court announced Alito’s last-minute recusal. Alito had faced pressure to exit the case due to perceived conflicts of interest related to his stock holdings in the oil and gas sector, but he told Bloomberg that his recusal was “prudent” — not required.

It’s a big week for Alito for unrelated reasons. On Tuesday, he’s set to release his first authored book since joining the bench, titled, “So Ordered: An Originalist’s View of the Constitution, the Court, and Our Country.”

His CBS News interview is at the beginning of a rare media tour to promote it.

“It’s part of the job that you’re going displease people by making decisions on controversial matters, because one side or the other is going to really dislike you,” Alito told the outlet.

text:
By LINDSAY WHITEHURST

WASHINGTON (AP) — The Supreme Court’s new term begins Monday with cases on climate change, religious rights and President Donald Trump’s crackdown on immigration high on the agenda.

Here’s a look at what’s in store:

Climate change

The high court is starting its term with a major climate change case. The justices will hear an appeal from energy companies trying to block dozens of lawsuits seeking to hold them liable in court for damage related to climate change.

Billions of dollars are potentially at stake in a case out of Boulder, Colorado, where local officials say the industry should help shoulder the escalating costs of disasters linked to climate change.

The companies, Suncor and ExxonMobil, say lawsuits aren’t the way to deal with the global issue. They have the backing of the Trump administration, which argues the litigation is a power grab intended to impose regulations on emissions.

Assault weapons bans

About a dozen states have banned semiautomatic rifles like AR-15s, which are often called assault weapons. They say the guns are disproportionately used in mass shootings, and banning them helps reduce gun violence.

Challengers say those laws violate the Second Amendment. They argue that AR-15s and other similar weapons are among the most popular and commonly owned guns in the country.

The conservative-majority court has expanded gun rights in recent years, and four justices had signaled that it was only a matter of time before the court took up the issue. The case will be considered in December.

Immigration

The court will hear two significant immigration cases with potentially big implications for Trump’s wide-reaching crackdown.

One is about deportations of migrants who can’t be quickly sent back to their home countries. The Trump administration has been sending thousands to other countries where they have no ties, under a series of often-secret agreements.

The Supreme Court will consider overturning lower court orders allowing them a chance to object. The justices have allowed the flights to continue in the meantime.

The other case is over the administration’s mandatory detention policy for immigrants who have been living in the U.S. illegally, even if they’ve been in the country for years.

The administration argues it can hold people without a bond hearing, but most appeals courts that have considered the issue disagree.

Voting

A Republican push to enforce strict Arizona voting laws will also come before the justices this term.

One measure requires people to show proof of citizenship when registering to vote using a state form, and another calls for regular purges of the voter rolls to remove people if their citizenship could not be confirmed.

It comes as Trump has failed to get legislation requiring documentary proof of citizenship for registering to vote through Congress. Arguments are set for December.

Religious rights

Catholic preschools that can’t take part in a taxpayer-funded program in Colorado will come before the court in November. It’s the justices’ latest case involving religious rights.

St. Mary Catholic Parish says it’s been left out of the state’s universal preschool program over its faith-based admissions policies, which exclude kids from LGBTQ+ families.

Colorado says religious schools are welcome to participate but have to follow nondiscrimination laws. The program was created by a 2020 ballot measure and provides public funding for preschool at schools selected by parents.
