text:
As students arrived at Turman Elementary School on the morning of Sept. 25, many were met by an unsettling scene: a group of masked men in unmarked vehicles toting firearms outside their school.

After numerous parents and students’ reports, Harrison District 2 and school leadership confirmed that the men were immigration officials. The incident occurred as those officials have increased their presence throughout southeast Colorado Springs.

Recommended Stories

▶

Some described them as “guys with guns looking for someone,” and others reported them identifying themselves as U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers, according to D-2 Chief Communication Officer Christine O’Brien.

The ICE interaction with children and families outside their school was a first in D-2, but O’Brien noted they were aware of prior operations in their neighborhoods. She added that there have been officials in neighborhoods surrounding D-2 schools this past week, with activities often occurring while students are heading to school.

On Monday, multiple ICE agents in three unmarked vehicles rammed into a truck along Lexington Village Lane in southeast Colorado Springs, following a high-speed chase around 6:30 a.m.

In an email to Turman families, D-2 Administration noted that the officials “never ventured onto the school grounds and did not communicate with the school or the district.” District security and an administrator responded and brought students into the building during the morning drop-off.

“Our students are safe, our staff is here and learning is continuing as usual,” Turman Principal Mickee Witt wrote to families in a separate email. “We know situations like this can bring questions or concerns for families. Please reach out to us if you would like to talk. We are here to support our Turman community.”

ICE officers can speak with families as long as they remain off school property, but their proximity to Turman appeared to impact attendance for the day. O’Brien confirmed that 39 students were absent that day, which accounts for 26.71% of the school’s population. The average daily attendance prior was 94.44%.

When reached for comment, a spokesperson for ICE Denver Public Affairs told The Gazette in an email that, “There’s nothing further to add.”

D-2 community members have responded to the recent ICE activity in their neighborhoods. Colorado House District 17 representative and former D-2 Board of Education member Regina English called the incident “deeply disturbing and unacceptable,” in a statement shared on social media.

“Children should be able to walk to school without encountering masked, armed federal officers in unmarked vehicles and wondering whether they are safe,” she wrote.

Last month, D-2’s Sierra High School participated in a statewide walkout specifically protesting recent ICE activity. Hundreds of students marched around the school, touting signs and screaming chants under school supervision in what was their latest demonstration.

Sierra Junior Angel Cardenas helped organize and promote the walkout in the week leading up to it and told the Gazette he decided to participate after witnessing the effects ICE has had on his community.

“I hear a lot of talk about how local Hispanic places have seen a decline in business because of these ICE raids,” he said.

“Also, I know people with a low criminal record or no criminal record at all who have gotten stopped by ICE or arrested by ICE. I know someone who was waiting on their green card and got arrested by them. So, it’s just been an upsetting situation that’s made me very passionate.”

State law requires public schools to accept all students, regardless of citizenship or immigration status, but doesn’t require them to track or report this information to the Department of Education, so it’s not known how many immigrant students currently attend D-2 schools. El Paso County’s most diverse school district, D-2 reported that 53.77% of last year’s students were Hispanic and 8.25% were multiple races. Students also spoke 52 languages last year.

Sierra Junior Annabel Wenzl contacted the Colorado Youth Coalition, which coordinated the walkout, to add her school to the list of participants after watching various actions by ICE across the country on social media.

The deaths of U.S. citizens Renee Good and Alex Pretti during anti-ICE demonstrations in Minneapolis and the conditions of detention facilities were what spurred her call to action. She said that the Sierra students organized three walkouts last year, against both ICE and gun violence, and two during her freshman year.

“We all care about these issues (at the school) and a lot of people showed up to those ones, but this was something else,” she said of the most recent demonstration. “There was like half the school there.”

Following any incidents involving ICE officers, O’Brien said that two local advocacy groups visit the impacted neighborhoods to assist with community information and support. For the students, school counselors check in with them throughout the day when they are impacted. No further actions have been taken at the administrative level in response to the events at Turman.

Going forward, she said the district hopes that immigration officials provide the same level of collaboration they have with other law enforcement agencies. This could include reporting when they will conduct operations near schools, avoiding drop-off and pickup times and identifying themselves as ICE officials.

“I am sure you have seen the photo, but it would also be nice for them to avoid standing on top of the truck with a mask and gun,” O’Brien added.

title: Nearly 20 minors held in Korea's immigration detention facilities: lawmaker
description:
Seventeen foreign nationals under the age of 18 were being held in immigration detention facilities in Korea as of August, according to a lawmaker’s office.
The facilities hold foreign nationals who lack valid immigration status in Korea pending deportation.
But experts have warned that detention could have a negative impact on children’s mental health, citing international research.
According to a separate statement by Save the Children, 84 people under the age of 18 were detained at immigration detention facilities across Korea between 2022 and July this year.
However, legislative efforts to revise current rules, which do not distinguish between minors and adults in immigration detention, have stalled since multiple bills were proposed last year.
text:
Seventeen foreign nationals under the age of 18 were being held in immigration detention facilities in Korea as of August, according to a lawmaker’s office.

According to the office of Rep. Park Eun-jung of the Rebuilding Korea Party, eight foreign nationals under the age of 18 were being held at the Foreigners’ Protection Center in Hwaseong, Gyeonggi Province, while another nine were being held at a center in Cheongju, North Chungcheong Province.

The facilities hold foreign nationals who lack valid immigration status in Korea pending deportation.

But experts have warned that detention could have a negative impact on children’s mental health, citing international research.

According to a separate statement by Save the Children, 84 people under the age of 18 were detained at immigration detention facilities across Korea between 2022 and July this year. Of them, 79 were unaccompanied by family members or guardians.

The youngest, accompanied by a guardian, was less than 1 year old.

In some cases, minors were detained for as long as 197 days.

The issue has prompted multiple recommendations from UN bodies, including the Committee on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination and the Committee on the Rights of the Child, calling for revisions to the Immigration Act to end the detention of children. Korea’s National Human Rights Commission also issued a similar recommendation in 2024.

However, legislative efforts to revise current rules, which do not distinguish between minors and adults in immigration detention, have stalled since multiple bills were proposed last year.

Lee Sang-hyun, a lawyer with public interest law organization Doroo, said the prolonged legislative delay continues to leave minors at risk, as they remain subject to the same detention environment despite requiring special care in areas including health and education.

“While there is a legal basis for providing education, it is hardly implemented in practice,” Lee said in a phone interview with The Korea Herald. “They are not effectively separated from adults in their daily lives and are forced to follow the same detention routine.”

Lee called for authorities to formally recognize their responsibility to protect detained children and for the passage of legislation establishing special standards based on children’s vulnerability.

Immigration The court will hear two significant immigration cases with potentially big implications for Trump's wide-reaching crackdown.
Religious rights Catholic preschools that can't take part in a taxpayer-funded program in Colorado will come before the court in November.
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Supreme Court's new term begins Monday with cases on climate change, religious rights and President Donald Trump’s crackdown on immigration high on the agenda.

Here’s a look at what's in store:

Climate change

The high court is starting its term with a major climate change case. The justices will hear an appeal from energy companies trying to block dozens of lawsuits seeking to hold them liable in court for damage related to climate change.

Billions of dollars are potentially at stake in a case out of Boulder, Colorado, where local officials say the industry should help shoulder the escalating costs of disasters linked to climate change.

The companies, Suncor and ExxonMobil, say lawsuits aren't the way to deal with the global issue. They have the backing of the Trump administration, which argues the litigation is a power grab intended to impose regulations on emissions.

Assault weapons bans

About a dozen states have banned semiautomatic rifles like AR-15s, which are often called assault weapons. They say the guns are disproportionately used in mass shootings, and banning them helps reduce gun violence.

Challengers say those laws violate the Second Amendment. They argue that AR-15s and other similar weapons are among the most popular and commonly owned guns in the country.

The conservative-majority court has expanded gun rights in recent years, and four justices had signaled that it was only a matter of time before the court took up the issue. The case will be considered in December.

Immigration

The court will hear two significant immigration cases with potentially big implications for Trump's wide-reaching crackdown.

One is about deportations of migrants who can't be quickly sent back to their home countries. The Trump administration has been sending thousands to other countries where they have no ties, under a series of often-secret agreements.

The Supreme Court will consider overturning lower court orders allowing them a chance to object. The justices have allowed the flights to continue in the meantime.

The other case is over the administration's mandatory detention policy for immigrants who have been living in the U.S. illegally, even if they've been in the country for years.

The administration argues it can hold people without a bond hearing, but most appeals courts that have considered the issue disagree.

Voting

A Republican push to enforce strict Arizona voting laws will also come before the justices this term.

One measure requires people to show proof of citizenship when registering to vote using a state form, and another calls for regular purges of the voter rolls to remove people if their citizenship could not be confirmed.

It comes as Trump has failed to get legislation requiring documentary proof of citizenship for registering to vote through Congress. Arguments are set for December.

Religious rights

Catholic preschools that can't take part in a taxpayer-funded program in Colorado will come before the court in November. It's the justices' latest case involving religious rights.

St. Mary Catholic Parish says it's been left out of the state's universal preschool program over its faith-based admissions policies, which exclude kids from LGBTQ+ families.

Colorado says religious schools are welcome to participate but have to follow nondiscrimination laws. The program was created by a 2020 ballot measure and provides public funding for preschool at schools selected by parents.

title: Supreme Court heads into new term with one eye on President Trump | Politics - KTEN
description: (CNN) — When the Supreme Court kicks off a new, nine-month term on Monday, one key player will be noticeably absent: President Donald Trump.
text:
(CNN) —
When the Supreme Court kicks off a new, nine-month term on Monday, one key player will be noticeably absent: President Donald Trump.
After months of
near-constant confrontation
with the White House, the nine justices will retake their seats behind the court’s mahogany bench without a docket full of Trump-driven, separation-of-powers blockbusters that defined the last term — from
tariffs
to
birthright citizenship
to the firing of once-
independent government officials
.
The respite is unlikely to last.
In the coming weeks, the justices will decide whether to wade into Trump’s messy defamation brawl with
magazine columnist E. Jean Carroll
, his mass cancellation of
federal research grants
, whether the
Department of Government Efficiency
must provide records detailing its slashing of federal agencies last year, and the administration’s ban on
transgender Americans
serving in the military.
Those and other cases could be added to a term that already includes an important Second Amendment challenge to
bans on AR-15 rifles
, the most significant case dealing with
climate change
to reach the justices in nearly two decades, and a fight over whether religious preschools receiving taxpayer money may decline to enroll the children of same-sex couples.
So far this next term, the court has granted 28 cases, less than half of what the justices will likely decide by June.
“There’s a very good chance that the 35 or so that the court is likely to grant in the remainder of the year will be the ones that are really the highlights,” Masha Hansford, an attorney at Davis Polk & Wardwell and a former assistant to the solicitor general, said at a recent event organized by the National Constitution Center.
One area where the court is already delving into Trump’s policies this term is immigration. The court has announced in recent days that it will hear arguments over the president’s
mandatory detention policy
and his push to deport migrants to countries other than their homeland. While important, neither of those cases has drawn the same level of attention as last year’s birthright citizenship case.
Dance with Trump
After Trump and his allies launched a rhetorical war against lower courts in early 2025, the president and the Supreme Court seemed to slide into a détente by the middle of the year — a delicate dance in which Trump has abided by the losses handed to him by the high court even as he has occasionally lashed out against the justices who supported them.
The court overwhelmingly sided with Trump on its emergency docket — the fast-track cases that are usually decided without argument. And it also backed the president in major regular cases that were argued during the last term and resulted in full opinions. One of those included the blockbuster decision allowing him to fire the leaders of
agencies like the Federal Trade Commission
. But the court was also willing to push back against Trump in some of those cases, such as by rejecting his emergency global tariffs and his push to undo birthright citizenship as it had been understood for more than a century.
Still, Trump has not shied away from railing against the 6-3 conservative court this past summer, including the three justices — Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett — whom he named to the bench during his first term.
Trump told Time Magazine
last week that he regretted nominated them.
“I gave them ​the position of a lifetime,” the president lamented, “and they vote against me often.”
The justices themselves have largely demurred when asked about Trump’s unusually personal attacks on the court. Justice Samuel Alito, a conservative who spoke to CBS as he prepares to publish a new book this week, said there has been a “great change in what presidents have said about the court when they are unhappy about our decisions.”
But, Alito said, that “very harsh” criticism has been “bipartisan.”
Pressed on Trump’s harsher statements, Alito said, “he has his own way of saying things.”
Girding for an election
Before the court decides any of the regular — or merits — cases it has granted, there’s a chance it will have to deal with a flood of litigation tied to next month’s midterm election. Whether that is a deluge or a trickle may be in voters’ hands.
Derek Muller, a law professor and election law expert at Notre Dame, said he believes the likelihood of post-election litigation will be low “because there probably won’t be enough decisively close cases where litigation would really matter.” But, he said, “if it does happen, it could significantly transform the upcoming Supreme Court term.”
The court has already juggled a series of redistricting disputes spun off from the president’s push for a mid-decade
redrawing of House district boundaries
. And last month it shut down
Trump’s controversial proposal
to give the US Postal Service a role in screening — and potentially rejecting — mail ballots sent to voters across the country.
Also waiting in the wings are several important non-Trump merits cases that could define the 2026-2027 term. It seems almost inevitable that the court will review state laws requiring the
Ten Commandments
to be posted in public school classrooms. Moreover, a legal battle raging between prediction sites like Kalshi and Polymarket and state governments
has already reached the high court
and could make its way to an oral argument sometime next year.
Banning AR-15 rifles
The court’s conservative majority has been steadily expanding gun rights under the Second Amendment for years. It have a huge opportunity to do so again this term.
In December, the court will hear arguments in cases challenging bans on AR-15 rifles enacted in Connecticut and Cook County, Illinois. Gun rights groups say the semi-automatic rifles are widely owned by Americans and are permitted in the vast majority of states. Gun control advocates counter that the weapons have been frequently used in mass shootings and should not receive Second Amendment protection because they are more “dangerous” and “unusual” than other types of guns.
The case draws heavily on a landmark 2008 decision from the Supreme Court,
District of Columbia v. Heller
, which stood for the prospect that arms “in common use” are protected under the Second Amendment.
“I think we know how this case is going to come out,” Deepak Gupta, a veteran appellate attorney, said at a recent event hosted by the Georgetown Law Center, suggesting that the court would likely strike down the AR-15 bans. “We know the outcome, but we don’t know
how
it’s going to be decided.”
Suing Exxon for climate change
On the very first day of the term, the justices will confront a long-running dispute about whether cities and states may sue fossil fuel companies for billions of dollars in damages caused by climate change. The appeal before the court deals with one such suit from Boulder, Colorado, but the decision will almost certainly play into dozens of other pending cases filed by cities and states attempting to hold oil companies accountable.
ExxonMobil and Suncor, the two companies that brought the case to the high court, argue that climate pollution is inherently a federal issue, in part because emissions waft across state lines. That understanding of federal control, they say, should effectively supersede state law. But Boulder says that there’s nothing in the Constitution or in federal law that backs up ExxonMobil’s position, and that the Supreme Court should let the lawsuit proceed.
Particularly notable is
Alito’s decision to recuse
himself from the case because of stock he owns in fossil fuel companies such as ConocoPhillips and Phillips 66. That opens the possibility of a 4-4 split,
a rare outcome
that would uphold the decision by Colorado’s Supreme Court that allowed Boulder’s lawsuit to proceed without setting a precedent.
Immigration emerges as a theme
One important Trump-related case that has reached the docket deals with the administration’s policy of
imposing mandatory detention
without bond hearings for people who entered the country illegally and who are targeted for deportation. Though the cases are lower profile than birthright citizenship, the court’s decision in the detention case could have enormous consequences for the president’s push to round up migrants living in the United States.
Trump broke with decades of past practice – including that of his first administration – and reinterpreted an immigration law Congress enacted in the 1990s to find that people in the country illegally should be subject to mandatory detention without bond hearings. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has recorded a massive increase in the number of migrants held in detention, from just under 38,000 at the end of the Biden administration to more than 65,000 this past summer.
The detention case is one of several dealing with immigration this term. Late last month, the court granted another important immigration case dealing with the Trump administration’s policy of removing certain people to
countries other than their homeland
– despite human rights concerns raised about some of those countries.
Religious schools v. LGBTQ rights
The Supreme Court in recent years has repeatedly
sided with religious schools
seeking public funding. Now it will answer a question it has largely avoided in those earlier cases: How to handle a religious school that declines to work with LGBTQ families.
The
case comes out of Colorado
, which enacted a ballot provision in 2020 that provides state funding for a universal preschool program. While the program allows religious preschools to take part, it also includes a nondiscrimination provision that requires each school receiving public money to provide eligible children an equal opportunity to enroll, regardless of race, religious affiliation, sexual orientation, gender identity and other factors.
Two Catholic parishes in Colorado that operate preschools sued over the policy and brought the case to the Supreme Court in November. They argue that honoring that anti-discrimination provision in the program would require them to violate their faith.
“The tea leaves are pretty good for the challengers generally,” Roman Martinez, a Latham & Watkins partner who regularly appears before the Supreme Court, said at the Georgetown event.
“What’s driving the court is a commitment to a type of pluralism,” he said. “The court, I think, is very concerned about religious groups sort of having equal access and being treated equally as a matter of practice, not just as a matter of formalism.”

title: CBP tests walk-through facial recognition for long-elusive land-border biometric exit
description:
Land exit remains the difficult piece CBP already uses facial comparison extensively at airports, seaports, and pedestrian land-border entry lanes.
But CBP acknowledged that it still lacked a feasible solution for broad biometric exit deployment in the land and sea environments.
CBP said it had implemented comprehensive facial biometric processing at air, sea, and pedestrian land entry, but only at air exit.
The agency said it would publish another Federal Register notice before undertaking large-scale biometric exit implementation at land or sea ports.
The agency then said it was still searching for a feasible way to perform biometric exit at land borders.
text:
U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) has taken another step toward closing one of the government’s biggest remaining gaps in its biometric entry-exit system by testing facial recognition systems that can capture pedestrians as they walk out of the U.S. at a busy Texas border crossing.

The Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) Science and Technology Directorate (S&T) said it tested three industry solutions at the Progreso International Bridge after CBP asked the directorate in October 2025 for technology that can securely and efficiently confirm pedestrian departures using biometrics.

More than 1.1 million pedestrians leave the U.S. for Mexico through the crossing annually, according to the bridge director.

The demonstration is particularly significant because pedestrian land exit has remained one of the unfinished portions of a biometric entry-exit system Congress first mandated decades ago.

It also comes as CBP has access to a large new pool of money to move such technology beyond testing.

The Secure America Act, signed into law on June 10, appropriates $3.45 billion to CBP through September 2029 for border security, technology, and screening.

Among the purposes Congress specifically authorized are “necessary expenses, including the deployment of technology,” for the biometric entry and exit system required by the Intelligence Reform and Terrorism Prevention Act of 2004.

The money is not exclusively earmarked for biometrics and can also support inspection equipment, AI, surveillance technology, air and marine systems, and other border operations.

Biometric Update reported in June that the account sits within nearly $70 billion in new DHS funding through 2029, although Congress did not specify how much of the technology money CBP must spend on facial recognition or other biometric systems.

The Progreso field test took place in May, shortly before Congress enacted the new funding. The work now provides a clearer picture of one capability that could eventually draw on that money, although DHS has not said it will purchase any of the tested systems.

Land exit remains the difficult piece

CBP already uses facial comparison extensively at airports, seaports, and pedestrian land-border entry lanes. Exit has been much harder at land crossings because travelers generally are moving away from U.S. inspection facilities, and stopping large volumes of pedestrians or vehicles to collect biometrics could create significant congestion.

That problem was still unresolved when DHS finalized sweeping biometric entry-exit regulations last year.

The final rule, effective Dec. 26, 2025, removed regulatory limits that had confined biometric exit to pilot programs and provided that all non-U.S. citizen travelers subject to the rule may be photographed upon entry and departure.

But CBP acknowledged that it still lacked a feasible solution for broad biometric exit deployment in the land and sea environments. CBP said it had implemented comprehensive facial biometric processing at air, sea, and pedestrian land entry, but only at air exit.

The agency said it would publish another Federal Register notice before undertaking large-scale biometric exit implementation at land or sea ports.

The Progreso test appears aimed squarely at that gap.

S&T initially invited six companies to the Maryland Test Facility for capability demonstrations early this year. CBP and S&T selected three systems for additional testing, two from NEC National Security Systems and a joint solution from Paravision and AiFi.

The work was conducted through Cooperative Research and Development Agreements, with the companies covering their own participation costs.

Before moving to Texas, S&T constructed a replica of the Progreso pedestrian exit environment in Maryland so the vendors could install and refine their systems under controlled conditions.

They moved to the actual crossing in May.

Faces captured without stopping pedestrians

The operational problem was considerably different from capturing a face at an airport kiosk or boarding gate.

Systems had to obtain usable images of people walking through an outdoor corridor while handling different heights and walking speeds, hats, sunglasses, and umbrellas, as well as changing daylight and nighttime lighting.

NEC demonstrated its SmartID Express and NeoFace Express systems. NEC National Security Systems President Todd Morris said the systems captured what the company characterized as high-quality facial images of thousands of pedestrians per day under outdoor conditions.

The Paravision-AiFi approach combined facial recognition with AiFi’s spatial-analysis technology to analyze pedestrian movement through the capture area and select facial images suitable for biometric matching.

DHS said the vendors used AI and other technologies to construct a three-dimensional model of the capture zone, observe pedestrian movement, and select facial images suitable for matching against CBP’s Traveler Verification Service, the agency’s cloud-based facial matching system.

Cameras were positioned at different heights and locations around the pedestrian walkway, and testing continued after dark with different lighting configurations.

U.S. citizens were told through English- and Spanish-language signs that they could decline biometric collection, and a separate opt-out lane was provided. DHS said the biometric entry-exit mandate applies to non-U.S. citizen travelers.

CBP Biometrics Program Office Director Larry Panetta said image capture “exceeded expectations” during both daytime and nighttime testing and said the technology could serve as a “force multiplier,” allowing CBP to deploy its resources more effectively.

In its September 1 account of the test, DHS did not publish quantitative recognition or capture-success rates, false-match figures, demographic performance results, or comparative scores for the three systems.

That leaves the Progreso trial as an operational assessment rather than a procurement decision.

Still, it marks a notable progression from where CBP stood when it issued the biometric rule less than a year ago.

The agency then said it was still searching for a feasible way to perform biometric exit at land borders.

It has now tested multiple walk-through facial capture systems under live border conditions, while Congress has separately provided a multibillion-dollar technology account that expressly allows money to be used to deploy the biometric entry-exit system.

CBP has already said that before it implements large-scale biometric exit at land ports, it will publish the details in the Federal Register and seek public comments.

description:
The family proceedings had not concluded at the time of the immigration appeal.
A key issue was therefore whether he had a right to remain in the UK under Article 8 ECHR, pending the conclusion of the family proceedings.
Judgment and outcome The Court of Appeal also dismissed Mr Ahmed’s appeal, in a unanimous judgment.
Each case will turn on its specific facts and will require careful preparation, including potentially coordination with the Family Court for disclosure of relevant material.
Family practitioners should take note that where a client’s immigration status is not secure, their ability to remain in the UK while family proceedings run their course should not be assumed.
text:
Background

The case Jakir Ahmed v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2026] EWCA Civ 509 involved a father who had applied for a Family Court Order permitting contact with his British daughter, shortly before applying for permission to stay in the UK on the basis of that relationship. Success in such an application requires at least direct access to the child, as well as evidence of taking an active role in the child’s upbringing, and an intention to continue doing so. His immigration application was refused on the basis that he didn’t meet those requirements, and the refusal was appealed. The family proceedings had not concluded at the time of the immigration appeal. A key issue was therefore whether he had a right to remain in the UK under Article 8 ECHR, pending the conclusion of the family proceedings.

The First-Tier Tribunal had dismissed the appeal, finding that Mr Ahmed had no such right to remain. His subsequent appeal to the Upper Tribunal was also dismissed. Mr Ahmed appealed to the Court of Appeal.

Judgment and outcome

The Court of Appeal also dismissed Mr Ahmed’s appeal, in a unanimous judgment. It emphasised that in cases where there are concurrent immigration and family proceedings and a decision must be made about which takes priority, the factors set out in RS v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2012] UKUT 218 (IAC) apply.

These include:

whether the outcome of the family proceedings is likely to be material to the immigration decision;

whether there are compelling public interest reasons to exclude the individual irrespective of the outcome of the family proceedings; and

where contact proceedings are instigated in an immigration appeal, whether there is reason to believe they have been instituted to delay removal rather than to promote the child’s welfare.

Immigration judges are therefore required to engage with the question of the child’s welfare – though they must not prejudge the decision on that issue, which remains for the Family Court.

In assessing the questions above, a judge will usually want to consider the degree of the claimant’s previous interest in/contact with the child; the timing of contact proceedings and the commitment with which they have been progressed; when a decision is likely to be reached; and what materials are or can be made available to identify pointers as to where the child’s welfare lies.

In Mr Ahmed’s case, it was found that he had little interest in contact with the child (having had no direct contact for over 3 years), and that he was not committed to the family court proceedings, which were being used to delay the immigration process. The CA noted that there was nothing in the evidence to indicate that the welfare of the child pointed to the renewal of direct contact, and that if anything, it pointed against direct contact. Mr Ahmed therefore did not have a right to remain in the UK on the basis of Article 8 ECHR, pending conclusion of the family proceedings.

Key takeaways

The case provides a helpful reminder that family proceedings may well be relevant to an individual’s ability to remain lawfully in the UK, but they will not in and of themselves be sufficient to secure status. Each case will turn on its specific facts and will require careful preparation, including potentially coordination with the Family Court for disclosure of relevant material.

It also provides helpful clarification that the principles set out in RS will apply to concurrent immigration and family proceedings, even where there is no immediate question of removal or deportation (as had been the case in RS itself).

Family practitioners should take note that where a client’s immigration status is not secure, their ability to remain in the UK while family proceedings run their course should not be assumed. Immigration advice should be taken as early as possible so that both aspects can be managed in a coordinated way.

text:
Human Rights Watch (HRW) on Friday reported that US immigration authorities detained 8 Nicaraguan exiles who were previously granted protected status in 2023 after fleeing political prosecution.

On February 9 2023, the Nicaraguan government declared 222 political prisoners as “traitors” and expelled them to the United States, stripping 94 government dissenters and critics of their nationality. The US government announced that it was welcoming the 222 individuals as “parolees” and granted them “a two-year humanitarian parole into the US” subject to certain conditions.

HRW reported that, three years later, “after offering refuge to these critics of the Nicaraguan government…the United States is now detaining and threatening to deport them.” It reported that at least 8 of the Nicaraguan exiles, including those without nationality and with pending asylum claims, have been detained.

HRW confirmed that two of the 8 individuals were arrested during either “a court appointment of asylum interview between April and September 2026”, and according to their legal teams and family members who spoke with HRW, “it appears that five of the 8 men are still in detention”.

Among those detained by ICE is Marlon Gerardo Sáenz. Sáenz was formerly part of the Nicaraguan paramilitary, however he defected and became a vocal critic of the government. He was imprisoned in 2022, and stripped of his citizenship before arriving in the US as one of the 222 people. Sáenz’s case is especially complex due to his prior paramilitary involvement and allegations of human rights abuses at that time. Sáenz’s lawyer, Tucker Sandler, commented that “Mr. Sáenz deserves respect, dignity and a fair shot at asylum because that is the democratic promise of our great country.”

Humanitarian parole was previously granted under the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA), and empowered the Secretary of Homeland Security to grant discretionary and temporary entry or remain in the US under emergency humanitarian circumstances. However, the Trump administration suspended or terminated humanitarian parole programs for migrants from Cuba, Haiti, Nicaragua, and Venezuela in 2025. According to Democracy Now, “the detention of Haitians has surged by 142%” as the Trump administration continues a mass deportation campaign.

Over the last five years, Nicaragua has faced human rights abuses and systematic oppression under the Ortega-Murillo government. Rights groups such as Amnesty International report arbitrary detentions, inhumane prison conditions, political repression, enforced disappearances, torture, extrajudicial executions, arbitrary deprivation of nationality, and brutal crackdowns on free speech and dissent.

HRW warned against the US sending deportees to a country where they face “a risk of prosecution and torture there…nor should it deport people to third countries where they face such risks, including through onward deportation to Nicaragua.” Americas director at HRW, Juanita Goebertus advised that “international law prohibits the United States from returning anyone to face the threat of prosecution or torture.”

text:
THANLYIN: Nearly 1,500 Myanmar migrants from Malaysia returned to their war-ravaged home country on Sunday under an opaque repatriation scheme that rights monitors say cannot assure their safety.

Dozens of migrants were transported on buses to a Buddhist monastery hall for immigration and health checks, AFP journalists saw, after the returnees arrived by Myanmar Navy ships that docked at the nearby base in Thanlyin.

"I haven't met my family yet," said Kyaw Swar Thein, 53, who worked in a coffee shop in Malaysia before he was arrested there.

He said he suffered scabies while in detention for a year and eight months -- one reason he wanted to come home. Now his future seemed unclear.

"I do not hope for anything," he said among the rows of men sat cross-legged on the floor, some wearing T-shirts reading "We love Myanmar".

The United Nations has warned conditions in Myanmar, which has been consumed by civil war since a 2021 military coup, mean safe homecomings cannot be guaranteed as required under international law.

Malaysia insists all returnees agreed to voluntary repatriation from detention centres, but the UN and rights groups have raised concerns that Myanmar migrants had little choice.

Hundreds of families with vehicles gathered at dawn to collect their relatives outside the naval base, some holding up paper signs with photographs or the names of their loved ones.

While some were allowed past the base gates to welcome their family members, a naval official dashed hopes of immediate reunions for most.

"You cannot take them right away," he shouted into a megaphone, saying returnees would first be brought to different locations in the Yangon region.

One woman said she was looking for her 19-year-old brother who was arrested in Malaysia soon after he arrived there three months ago.

"We saw his name on the list of returnees but we couldn't go inside to find him," said the woman, who declined to give her name for security reasons.

Kyaw Myint, 55, said he worried his three grandchildren, who were detained in Malaysia for more than a year, could now be conscripted in Myanmar -- "not only by the military but also by ethnic armed groups".

Three Myanmar Navy ships carrying migrants docked at the Thanlyin base early Sunday, said a naval official whom AFP has kept anonymous as he was not authorised to speak to media.

The ships left Malaysia on Tuesday carrying 1,476 migrants, according to the Myanmar government -- the first of 5,000 that Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim says Myanmar agreed to take back.

The arrivals were due to include mostly men, as well as 27 children and 79 women, Malaysian media said.

"Our main concern is his arrival won't be safe," said the sister of one migrant who had told his family he expected to be sent aboard the ships.

There are also concerns members of the persecuted Rohingya are among the returned group after Anwar announced the repatriations in July against a backdrop of rising xenophobia towards refugees, particularly the Rohingya.

Members of the ethnic group fled Myanmar en masse following a military crackdown starting in 2017, which rights experts say amounted to genocide.

Rohingya make up the majority of Myanmar refugees and asylum seekers in Malaysia, but Kuala Lumpur has not responded to an AFP query about the number onboard.

Myanmar says the returnees completed sentences for immigration offences in Malaysia.

Monitor organisations such as Fortify Rights report dire conditions in the detention centres.

The UN refugee agency said this past week its staff were not allowed to meet migrants to confirm whether their decisions to return "were genuinely free and informed".

Malaysia is already moving ahead with plans to return a second group of more than 3,500 migrants, saying they have caused financial, social and security burdens.

Myanmar's Min Aung Hlaing, the coup leader who was installed as civilian president in April, is expected to visit Malaysia soon to discuss the repatriation scheme.

Myanmar pledged last month that returns will be "safe and dignified".

But Yap Lay Sheng, a senior human rights specialist with Fortify Rights, told AFP: "There's no telling how the regime would treat returnees."

Myanmar's civil war has killed more than 100,000 people since the coup, according to monitor ACLED -- including 50 in a military airstrike late last month.

"This is no time to return anyone forcibly to a country plagued by egregious human rights violations and abuses," UN rights chief Volker Turk said Tuesday. - AFP

text:
(CNN) — When the Supreme Court kicks off a new, nine-month term on Monday, one key player will be noticeably absent: President Donald Trump.

After months of near-constant confrontation with the White House, the nine justices will retake their seats behind the court’s mahogany bench without a docket full of Trump-driven, separation-of-powers blockbusters that defined the last term — from tariffs to birthright citizenship to the firing of once-independent government officials.

The respite is unlikely to last.

In the coming weeks, the justices will decide whether to wade into Trump’s messy defamation brawl with magazine columnist E. Jean Carroll, his mass cancellation of federal research grants, whether the Department of Government Efficiency must provide records detailing its slashing of federal agencies last year, and the administration’s ban on transgender Americans serving in the military.

Those and other cases could be added to a term that already includes an important Second Amendment challenge to bans on AR-15 rifles, the most significant case dealing with climate change to reach the justices in nearly two decades, and a fight over whether religious preschools receiving taxpayer money may decline to enroll the children of same-sex couples.

So far this next term, the court has granted 28 cases, less than half of what the justices will likely decide by June.

“There’s a very good chance that the 35 or so that the court is likely to grant in the remainder of the year will be the ones that are really the highlights,” Masha Hansford, an attorney at Davis Polk & Wardwell and a former assistant to the solicitor general, said at a recent event organized by the National Constitution Center.

One area where the court is already delving into Trump’s policies this term is immigration. The court has announced in recent days that it will hear arguments over the president’s mandatory detention policy and his push to deport migrants to countries other than their homeland. While important, neither of those cases has drawn the same level of attention as last year’s birthright citizenship case.

Dance with Trump

After Trump and his allies launched a rhetorical war against lower courts in early 2025, the president and the Supreme Court seemed to slide into a détente by the middle of the year — a delicate dance in which Trump has abided by the losses handed to him by the high court even as he has occasionally lashed out against the justices who supported them.

The court overwhelmingly sided with Trump on its emergency docket — the fast-track cases that are usually decided without argument. And it also backed the president in major regular cases that were argued during the last term and resulted in full opinions. One of those included the blockbuster decision allowing him to fire the leaders of agencies like the Federal Trade Commission. But the court was also willing to push back against Trump in some of those cases, such as by rejecting his emergency global tariffs and his push to undo birthright citizenship as it had been understood for more than a century.

Still, Trump has not shied away from railing against the 6-3 conservative court this past summer, including the three justices — Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett — whom he named to the bench during his first term. Trump told Time Magazine last week that he regretted nominated them.

“I gave them ​the position of a lifetime,” the president lamented, “and they vote against me often.”

The justices themselves have largely demurred when asked about Trump’s unusually personal attacks on the court. Justice Samuel Alito, a conservative who spoke to CBS as he prepares to publish a new book this week, said there has been a “great change in what presidents have said about the court when they are unhappy about our decisions.”

But, Alito said, that “very harsh” criticism has been “bipartisan.”

Pressed on Trump’s harsher statements, Alito said, “he has his own way of saying things.”

Girding for an election

Before the court decides any of the regular — or merits — cases it has granted, there’s a chance it will have to deal with a flood of litigation tied to next month’s midterm election. Whether that is a deluge or a trickle may be in voters’ hands.

Derek Muller, a law professor and election law expert at Notre Dame, said he believes the likelihood of post-election litigation will be low “because there probably won’t be enough decisively close cases where litigation would really matter.” But, he said, “if it does happen, it could significantly transform the upcoming Supreme Court term.”

The court has already juggled a series of redistricting disputes spun off from the president’s push for a mid-decade redrawing of House district boundaries. And last month it shut down Trump’s controversial proposal to give the US Postal Service a role in screening — and potentially rejecting — mail ballots sent to voters across the country.

Also waiting in the wings are several important non-Trump merits cases that could define the 2026-2027 term. It seems almost inevitable that the court will review state laws requiring the Ten Commandments to be posted in public school classrooms. Moreover, a legal battle raging between prediction sites like Kalshi and Polymarket and state governments has already reached the high court and could make its way to an oral argument sometime next year.

Banning AR-15 rifles

The court’s conservative majority has been steadily expanding gun rights under the Second Amendment for years. It have a huge opportunity to do so again this term.

In December, the court will hear arguments in cases challenging bans on AR-15 rifles enacted in Connecticut and Cook County, Illinois. Gun rights groups say the semi-automatic rifles are widely owned by Americans and are permitted in the vast majority of states. Gun control advocates counter that the weapons have been frequently used in mass shootings and should not receive Second Amendment protection because they are more “dangerous” and “unusual” than other types of guns.

The case draws heavily on a landmark 2008 decision from the Supreme Court, District of Columbia v. Heller, which stood for the prospect that arms “in common use” are protected under the Second Amendment.

“I think we know how this case is going to come out,” Deepak Gupta, a veteran appellate attorney, said at a recent event hosted by the Georgetown Law Center, suggesting that the court would likely strike down the AR-15 bans. “We know the outcome, but we don’t know how it’s going to be decided.”

Suing Exxon for climate change

On the very first day of the term, the justices will confront a long-running dispute about whether cities and states may sue fossil fuel companies for billions of dollars in damages caused by climate change. The appeal before the court deals with one such suit from Boulder, Colorado, but the decision will almost certainly play into dozens of other pending cases filed by cities and states attempting to hold oil companies accountable.

ExxonMobil and Suncor, the two companies that brought the case to the high court, argue that climate pollution is inherently a federal issue, in part because emissions waft across state lines. That understanding of federal control, they say, should effectively supersede state law. But Boulder says that there’s nothing in the Constitution or in federal law that backs up ExxonMobil’s position, and that the Supreme Court should let the lawsuit proceed.

Particularly notable is Alito’s decision to recuse himself from the case because of stock he owns in fossil fuel companies such as ConocoPhillips and Phillips 66. That opens the possibility of a 4-4 split, a rare outcome that would uphold the decision by Colorado’s Supreme Court that allowed Boulder’s lawsuit to proceed without setting a precedent.

Immigration emerges as a theme

One important Trump-related case that has reached the docket deals with the administration’s policy of imposing mandatory detention without bond hearings for people who entered the country illegally and who are targeted for deportation. Though the cases are lower profile than birthright citizenship, the court’s decision in the detention case could have enormous consequences for the president’s push to round up migrants living in the United States.

Trump broke with decades of past practice – including that of his first administration – and reinterpreted an immigration law Congress enacted in the 1990s to find that people in the country illegally should be subject to mandatory detention without bond hearings. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has recorded a massive increase in the number of migrants held in detention, from just under 38,000 at the end of the Biden administration to more than 65,000 this past summer.

The detention case is one of several dealing with immigration this term. Late last month, the court granted another important immigration case dealing with the Trump administration’s policy of removing certain people to countries other than their homeland – despite human rights concerns raised about some of those countries.

Religious schools v. LGBTQ rights

The Supreme Court in recent years has repeatedly sided with religious schools seeking public funding. Now it will answer a question it has largely avoided in those earlier cases: How to handle a religious school that declines to work with LGBTQ families.

The case comes out of Colorado, which enacted a ballot provision in 2020 that provides state funding for a universal preschool program. While the program allows religious preschools to take part, it also includes a nondiscrimination provision that requires each school receiving public money to provide eligible children an equal opportunity to enroll, regardless of race, religious affiliation, sexual orientation, gender identity and other factors.

Two Catholic parishes in Colorado that operate preschools sued over the policy and brought the case to the Supreme Court in November. They argue that honoring that anti-discrimination provision in the program would require them to violate their faith.

“The tea leaves are pretty good for the challengers generally,” Roman Martinez, a Latham & Watkins partner who regularly appears before the Supreme Court, said at the Georgetown event.

“What’s driving the court is a commitment to a type of pluralism,” he said. “The court, I think, is very concerned about religious groups sort of having equal access and being treated equally as a matter of practice, not just as a matter of formalism.”

Newly unsealed court records showing how information collected on people observing immigration arrests in Maine later contributed to a border stop offer a real-world example of the kind of subject data ICE is now migrating into a broader Palantir case-management and analytics system.

The records show an HSI agent photographed observers, collected vehicle information and entered subject records into Palantir’s Investigative Case Management system. The government has acknowledged that information entered about plaintiff Carlyn Williams later led to enhanced screening at the Canadian border.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is requiring existing ICM data to be migrated into a new Palantir architecture designed to combine case management, attached media and investigative analytics in an Enterprise Lakehouse linked to Customs and Border Protection (CBP) and other federal systems.

ICE also requires both transactional case data and “derived analytical data” within the platform to remain wholly owned by the agency. That raises a question not addressed in the public privacy documentation reviewed by Biometric Update: what happens to analytical relationships and other derived information when the underlying subject record is later corrected, archived or deleted?

The question is no longer abstract.

WIRED reported that court records in Hilton show an HSI agent created ICM records on people observing immigration arrests in Maine during January’s Operation Catch of the Day.

The government says the agent, identified as “J.C.”, created records on eight people he believed posed potential threats to law enforcement so law enforcement could access their information if they encountered them again. The plaintiffs say observers were photographed, vehicle information was collected, and facial recognition searches were conducted.

One of those records later had a tangible consequence.

The government has acknowledged in a September 18 filing that J.C.’s entry of Carlyn Williams’ name and vehicle information into ICM led to the March 2026 border stop. The amended complaint says Williams and her spouse, fellow plaintiff Polyxenia Pantos, faced enhanced screening while returning from Canada.

ICE is moving ICM data into a new Palantir system

The timing is significant because ICE is in the middle of a major ICM overhaul.

ICE awarded Palantir a roughly $45.8 million order in June to modernize HSI’s investigative case management and investigative analytics capabilities on the agency’s Case Management and Analytics platform.

The agency’s limited-sources justification describes a system considerably broader than traditional case management. ICE requires a single integrated platform combining investigative case management with investigative analytics.

An Enterprise Lakehouse will combine case records, subject information covering people, businesses, and vehicles, investigative reports, approval workflows, and attached media with outside law enforcement information.

ICE says the lakehouse can become an authoritative data source and is expected to support analytics and information sharing with CBP for lookout and seizure tracking.

The platform must be interoperable with CBP, the Department of Justice, the Federal Bureau of Investigation’s Criminal Justice Information Services, the National Law Enforcement Telecommunications System, and the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) Office of Biometric Identity Management.

ICE says existing investigative information must remain accessible and accurate, and it makes the contractor responsible for ensuring all data is migrated and accounted for without exceptions or errors.

The same requirements separately identify both transactional case management information and “derived analytical data” as data that must remain under ICE ownership.

The documents do not establish whether the eight Maine records have already been migrated.

But they place the kinds of records at issue in Hilton within a much larger body of historical ICM information that ICE has directed Palantir to preserve while building a system capable of generating new analytical products from the underlying data.

ICM records already reach CBP

The Williams border stop also illustrates that information stored in ICM has never necessarily remained inside HSI.

A 2016 DHS Privacy Impact Assessment says an ICM Interface Hub allows ICE-created subject records to be continually published and updated in CBP’s TECS Platform.

The records can concern people, vehicles, aircraft, and other subjects of ICE law-enforcement interest. DHS said they “serve as ‘lookout records’” that CBP uses to screen travelers entering and leaving the country.

The same architecture sent daily ICM updates into the HSI Data Warehouse for reporting and analytical use.

That does not mean every ICM subject record automatically becomes a formal TECS lookout requiring a border officer to take action.

CBP’s TECS privacy documentation describes a specific Lookout Record that authorized users can create and place “on Primary,” allowing CBP officers to receive instructions when they encounter a traveler, including referral to secondary inspection.

The public record does not identify which TECS object, flag or referral mechanism caused Williams’ March inspection. What is established is that her ICM information reached beyond HSI: the government says J.C.’s entry led to the border stop.

Among other things, they are seeking to have Williams’ records archived and to prevent DHS from using information collected about the plaintiffs against them.

But an analytical environment can generate information beyond the source record itself – links among people, vehicles, addresses, cases and other entities, as well as visualizations, alerts and other analytical products.

ICE has previously addressed that problem explicitly in another analytics system.

A 2023 privacy assessment for the Data Analysis and Research for Trade Transparency System (DARTTS), as it transitioned to ICE’s Repository for Analytics in a Virtualized Environment (RAVEn), spells out how source-data retention and analytical products are supposed to be handled.

When underlying records are deleted during a source-system refresh, associated analytical products are also supposed to be deleted automatically because they are tagged back to the source records.

An exception applies when an analyst identifies a product as connected to an active investigation or case. It can then be moved into the relevant case-management system and becomes subject to that system’s retention rules.

The new Palantir architecture combines case management and analytics much more directly.

Yet ICE’s publicly available ICM privacy documentation still reflects an older architecture.

The August 2021 ICM privacy assessment predates the Case Management and Analytics platform and Enterprise Lakehouse.

The public documentation reviewed by Biometric Update does not explain the equivalent lineage rules for the new architecture – including whether archiving or correcting an underlying subject record automatically changes analytical relationships, derived information, or copies previously transmitted to another DHS component.

Mobile Query may have created another data trail

The photographs sent for facial recognition in Maine raise a separate biometric retention question.

The court record identifies the CBP application used to search the photographs as Mobile Query.

CBP has long used that name for a broader mobile application.

A CBP contracting document describes Mobile Query as an all-purpose tool that can search agency databases, scan travel documents, review flight manifests, and identify passengers through fingerprints.

But separate federal litigation has produced testimony suggesting the terminology is not always precise.

Biometric Update separately identified federal litigation in Oregon that bears directly on the terminology. In M-J-M-A- v. Wamsley, a CBP official testified that she used what she called a “facial recognition mobile query for CBP.”

U.S. District Judge Mustafa Kasubhai’s subsequent opinion, citing the same encounter and testimony, identifies the application as Mobile Fortify.

Mobile Fortify is a CBP mobile biometric identification app that lets officers use a government-issued phone to capture a person’s face or fingerprints and run them against DHS identity and immigration databases in the field.

Judge Kasubhai’s ruling does not establish that the “Mobile Query” identified in the Maine litigation was necessarily Mobile Fortify, but it shows that the terminology immigration enforcement officers use is not dispositive.

A DHS Privacy Threshold Analysis says every new photograph or fingerprint submitted through Mobile Fortify, whether or not it produces a match, becomes an encounter record stored in CBP’s Automated Targeting System for 15 years. The document says CBP retains all photographs, including nonmatching images of U.S. citizens and lawful permanent residents.

If Mobile Fortify was used in Maine, each photograph submitted through it therefore would have created a CBP encounter record separate from the observers’ ICM subject records. The currently available court documents do not establish that Mobile Fortify was the application used there.

ICE records can encompass people who are not arrest targets

ICE’s formal records policies also show that its information systems can contain information about people beyond those arrested or suspected of crimes.

A July 2025 update to ICE’s Search, Arrest, and Seizure System of Records expanded the categories of individuals covered to include witnesses, people with knowledge of alleged activity and witness bystanders, as well as people whose images or audio are captured incidentally during searches, arrests, or seizures.

For those incidentally recorded individuals, the notice says they fall within the system of records when ICE retrieves the information by a personal identifier in its normal course of business.

The same notice expanded the categories of information maintained in the system to include biometric information, geolocation, commercial data, and information derived from new surveillance and information technologies, in addition to photographs, identifying information, and vehicle-related records.

DHS nevertheless argues in Hilton that the Maine encounters do not demonstrate a wider retaliatory surveillance policy.

The government says department policy prohibits targeting people merely for exercising First Amendment rights and says J.C. created the records because he believed the individuals posed operational or safety concerns.

The plaintiffs dispute that characterization and argue the surveillance and record collection chilled their constitutionally protected observation of immigration enforcement.

Whatever the court ultimately decides, the litigation supplies something the Palantir procurement documents alone could not: a view of what an ICM subject record can look like at the beginning of its lifecycle.

It can begin with a photograph, a vehicle, a name and an agent’s characterization. The Maine case shows how that information can later affect border screening, while ICE is building an analytical environment designed to combine those source records with information derived from them.

text:
CAPE TOWN, South Africa (AP) — A Laotian citizen deported by the United States to Eswatini under the Trump administration's immigration crackdown was released from a maximum-security prison in the African nation on Sunday after being held there for more than a year, his lawyer said.

Phone Chomsavanh was among five immigrants deported to Eswatini — where he has no ties — in July 2025 in the early days of the Trump administration's secretive and highly contentious third-country deportation program.

Chomsavanh's U.S.-based lawyer, Tin Thanh Nguyen, said in a statement announcing his release that he had only been informed that he was being deported to Eswatini shortly before a military cargo plane carrying him and other deportees landed there more than 14 months ago.

Chomsavanh was now being deported to Laos, Nguyen said.

Chomsavanh and the four other immigrants he was deported to Eswatini with were convicted of serious crimes in the U.S., but had served their sentences by the time they were sent to the Matsapha Correctional Complex near Eswatini's administrative capital, Mbabane.

“He had already served his time. Instead they put him on a plane without telling him where it was headed and left him in a prison in a country he had never heard of, where nobody ever accused him of anything," Nguyen said. “He sat there for more than a year. No notice, no hearing, no chance to object. That is not due process by any definition.”

He said in separate messages to The Associated Press that Chomsavanh had left Eswatini and landed in Johannesburg en route to Laos.

An Eswatini government spokesperson didn’t immediately acknowledge Chomsavanh’s release.

Chomsavanh was born in a refugee camp in Thailand after his parents fled Laos, and his family moved to the United States when he was 7, his lawyer said.

Chomsavanh is one of around 500 immigrants who have been deported from the United States to African countries that aren't their home nations since the third-country program began last year, according to advocacy groups Human Rights First and Refugees International, which have been monitoring the deportations.

Around a dozen African countries have accepted third-country deportees from the U.S., some in exchange for millions of dollars in payments. Eswatini, which is Africa's last absolute monarchy and is ruled by a king, was paid $5.1 million by the Trump administration to take deportees, according to the agreement between the countries. Eswatini has received around 30 deportees so far.

The program, which results in immigrants being held in countries they have no ties to and where they haven't been charged with any crime, has been fiercely criticized by rights groups and lawyers. It has been the subject of legal challenges in the U.S. and in some of the countries where immigrants have been sent.

The Trump administration has defended the policy as a way to quickly remove immigrants who have final deportation orders from the U.S. when their home countries might not immediately take them back.

Last month, a U.S. appeals court upheld a judge's ruling to halt the program, because it didn’t give immigrants facing removal from the U.S. time to challenge their deportation to a third country if they fear persecution or torture there.

The U.S. Supreme Court ruled last week to temporarily allow U.S. President Donald Trump's administration to continue swiftly removing immigrants to third countries, though it will hear arguments in the case in December.

The program has largely been carried out in secrecy, with little transparency over how many immigrants have been deported to third countries, and where and in what conditions they are being held.

description:
While it sounds like a spectacular place, I’ve never been to Big Bend National Park in West Texas.
By the summer, the bulldozers were rolling—including, incredibly, in untouched areas of the park.
You can barely see the Big Bend Sector (brown) on this chart of migrant apprehensions.

text:
Last Friday, I sat in a witness box in El Paso answering questions about a place I’ve never visited.

While it sounds like a spectacular place, I’ve never been to Big Bend National Park in West Texas. WOLA’s work on border security and migration has taken me to eight of the nine sectors into which Border Patrol divides the U.S.-Mexico border—but not to the agency’s Big Bend Sector, even though it makes up a quarter of the border.

Almost nothing happens there, security- or humanitarian-wise. By migrant entries, drug seizures, violent incidents, and other indicators, the wild, remote Big Bend isn’t in the same league as even the sectors ranked seventh and eighth.

Someday, I hope to get in a boat and tour the Rio Grande through the canyons of one of the National Park system’s crown jewels. But I could never justify using WOLA’s resources—we’re independent and depend on donations—to pay for “field research” there.

Big Bend “barrier infrastructure” contracts, and a lawsuit

Earlier this year, DHS announced plans to build border barriers and other infrastructure near the river in the pristine park, and 30-foot-high walls outside it. Local leaders from across the political spectrum sounded the alarm: tour operators, ranchers, historical preservationists, environmentalists, and county and city officials, including law enforcement.

A tour operator said he would probably have to close his decades-old business. A local nonprofit leader worried that construction equipment vibrations would damage a centuries-old adobe church. “This land is a part of me,” said a rancher whose home and cattle would be cut off from the river.

They filed suit to stop the project, even as DHS rapidly signed contracts with private builders worth over $7 billion, including $1.7 billion within the park itself. By the summer, the bulldozers were rolling—including, incredibly, in untouched areas of the park.

I was humbled and honored when this coalition’s attorneys, from the Center for Biological Diversity and the Texas Civil Rights Project, asked me to help. Border security and migration have been part of my work at WOLA for 15 years, and I’ve carved out a niche as a compiler and explainer of data on the U.S.-Mexico border and the U.S.-bound migration route through the Americas. You can find many charts, graphs, and tables in our reports and weekly Border Updates, as well as on my social media accounts.

Pulling up obscure border data is an oddball skill, but it was a great fit for the Big Bend litigation, where the plaintiffs needed to stop the harm while the case proceeds.

“High illegal entry”

Normally, the federal government couldn’t just sign contracts and start building in a wild area, in a matter of weeks, without weighing impacts and consulting affected communities. Dozens of environmental laws, indigenous rights laws, and cultural and historical preservation laws would block that.

The border wall is different, though. A 2005 amendment to a 1996 law (Section 102 of the “Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act”) allows the Secretary of Homeland Security to waive all other laws to build border barriers. Nearly the entire border is now covered by waivers as the Trump administration spends $46.6 billion in construction money Congress appropriated through the so-called “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” last year.

But there’s a catch.

The waiver authority, section 102(a) spells out, only applies “in areas of high illegal entry into the United States.” And Big Bend is emphatically not one.

That’s where data nerdery comes in. Proving that Big Bend isn’t “busy” enough to justify waiving laws takes detailed, credible information—and I have a lot of official data. Since July I’ve provided it in two extensive “expert reports” to back up the plaintiffs’ argument. The short version: since 1960, the Big Bend Sector—one-quarter of the border—has accounted for about one-sixtieth of migrant apprehensions and one-one-hundredth of non-marijuana drug seizures (and marijuana, legal in three of four border states, is low and declining). You can barely see the Big Bend Sector (brown) on this chart of migrant apprehensions.

A hearing for a preliminary injunction to stop work

In late September, after a bipartisan local outcry led it to call a pause, DHS announced that it would resume construction in Big Bend National Park. The plaintiffs asked Federal District Judge Kathleen Cardone to issue a preliminary injunction to stop the work while the case proceeds, and she quickly scheduled an October 2 hearing in her El Paso courtroom.

I was the second of eight witnesses called to testify, right after the park’s 2018-2023 superintendent. So there I was on Friday morning, seated to the Judge’s left in a full room in El Paso’s modern federal courthouse, my head bursting with numbers because I couldn’t bring any devices to prompt me.

Unless I’m talking to congressional staff or reporters who need the information, conversations about border security and migration data usually result in glazed-over eyes and a subject change. But here, I got to go into excruciating detail about migrant encounters, checkpoints, drug seizures, asylum, the effect of the 2020-2023 Title 42 policy, and much else.

I don’t recall it all: after at least 45 minutes on the stand, I think I went into a bit of a fugue state. I’m told that I did well, though, decimating any notion that Big Bend is an area of high illegal entry. I can only describe the Justice Department’s cross-examination as “desultory.”

Here’s a kind assessment from Big Bend Sentinel and Texas Tribune reporter Sam Karas, one of several mutual social-media follows I met in person for the first time:

As I left the stand, there were smiles from community leaders and plaintiffs present, most of whom hadn’t known who the easterner in the dark suit and tie was when we showed up at court that morning.

The outcome

After four hours of proceedings and brief closing arguments, Judge Cardone said she was ready to issue her order. It really could have gone either way: she is a 2003 Bush appointee who ran a tight courtroom, even warning those in attendance when some witnesses’ comments elicited chuckles.

The Judge prefaced her decision with a caution against any displays of emotion, as the case is highly charged. As she went on to grant the plaintiffs’ request for an injunction, halting all construction and suspending the DHS waivers on other laws, we all stayed as silent as we could, slowly exhaling, avoiding eye contact, and wiping our eyes until the gavel banged. Once outside the courtroom, we erupted. The rest of the afternoon was celebration, review of what went well and how to do better, and reading all the national press coverage rolling in.

For now, the bulldozers are silenced, and the contractors at the “man camps” near the construction sites are paused until Judge Cardone decides the case on its merits after further arguments, which are not scheduled yet. The only thing that might restart construction now is a Supreme Court reversal, which the justices could do on their “shadow docket”—but even that seems unlikely, at least right away, given how unpopular this border barrier project is in Texas.

It’s an understatement to say we haven’t had many wins in the border and migration space lately. This one felt especially sweet.

WOLA isn’t a direct-service organization: we’re trying to change policy and shape debates at their source, in the U.S. capital, which means we rarely see how our work immediately affects people’s lives. But on Friday I got to celebrate with local leaders, business owners, landowners, environmental defenders, and others—all from a part of the country I’ve never even seen—who just got a reprieve from real harm.

I’ll have this warm memory for the rest of my days, and some new friends who can show me around when I finally visit the Big Bend.

Postscript: I can’t end this without a big shout-out to the lead legal team, from the Center for Biological Diversity, who marshaled the witnesses and arguments in this case. Law schools could teach a case study based on the work of Zeynep Graves, Emma Yip, and Shannon Labuschagne, who assembled a diverse team of experts and witnesses: a former park official, a tourist business owner, a rancher, a nonprofit leader restoring a fragile historic site, an ecologist, a community leader, an activist documenting the harms—and me, a Washington data nerd. The legal team’s guidance made my declarations and testimony infinitely stronger.
