title: California Just Made History Taxing ICE Detention Centers - Here's What Changes
description:
A Financial Penalty Aimed at an Expanding Industry The law formally establishes the Private Detention Facility Tax Law, though it will not take effect immediately.
The measure arrives as California's private detention infrastructure has expanded rapidly under the Trump administration's enforcement push.
Two Corporations, Eight Facilities, and a $1.5 Billion Complication Two companies hold the largest share of California's private detention capacity.
CoreCivic manages the 1,994-bed Otay Mesa Detention Center in San Diego County and the 2,560-bed California City Detention Facility in Kern County, the largest immigration detention complex in the state.
More than 50 people died in ICE custody during Trump's second term — a figure that Human Rights Watch and Physicians for Human Rights characterize as the highest mortality rate recorded in federal immigration detention in over a decade.
text:
California Gov. Gavin Newsom signed AB 1633 into law on September 29, 2026, positioning the state as the first in the nation to impose a dedicated tax on for-profit companies that manage immigration detention facilities under federal contract. The bill, carried by Assemblymember Matt Haney (D-San Francisco), places a 25% tax on the gross receipts of private detention operators — a rate significantly lower than the 50% written into the legislation when it was introduced in January 2026 but still without precedent anywhere in the United States.

A Financial Penalty Aimed at an Expanding Industry

The law formally establishes the Private Detention Facility Tax Law, though it will not take effect immediately. The 25% levy on gross receipts kicks in July 1, 2028, giving affected operators time to mount legal challenges or restructure their California footprint. Revenue generated under the law flows into the newly created Due Process for All Fund, which — subject to legislative appropriation — would pay for immigration legal services and support programs for detained individuals and their families.

The measure arrives as California's private detention infrastructure has expanded rapidly under the Trump administration's enforcement push. According to reporting that cites Department of Homeland Security data, the state now hosts eight ICE-contracted private immigration detention facilities — all operated by for-profit corporations with documented histories of dangerous conditions, inadequate medical care, and sustained regulatory failures.

Two Corporations, Eight Facilities, and a $1.5 Billion Complication

Two companies hold the largest share of California's private detention capacity. CoreCivic manages the 1,994-bed Otay Mesa Detention Center in San Diego County and the 2,560-bed California City Detention Facility in Kern County, the largest immigration detention complex in the state. Those two facilities, however, changed hands in July 2026: CoreCivic completed the sale of both properties to the U.S. Department of Homeland Security for a combined $1.5 billion, while retaining management contracts with ICE for both sites. The federal government now holds the underlying real estate — a development that raises unresolved questions about whether a state tax can constitutionally reach facilities the federal government itself owns, even when a private company manages day-to-day operations.

The GEO Group, meanwhile, operates the Adelanto ICE Processing Center in San Bernardino County's high desert — a facility that became central to legislative hearings on detention conditions following a federal lawsuit in January 2026 documenting patterns of neglect and abuse. Four people died at Adelanto between September 2025 and March 2026, according to a California Department of Justice report. A gross receipts tax — applied before expenses or deductions — could meaningfully compress margins for both GEO Group and CoreCivic on their California operations, regardless of whether a given facility performs well in any individual year.

The Push to Sign — and What Could Unravel It in Court

The California Immigrant Policy Center, the bill's lead sponsor, gathered more than 10,000 letters and postcards from residents across the state, pressing Newsom to act before the September 30 signing deadline. Faith communities, labor unions, and civil rights organizations held a Capitol rally during the final weeks of the session. Haney, in a signing statement, called the detention industry one "built on heartbreak" and said California had chosen to hold corporations financially accountable for the consequences their operations impose on immigrant families.

The law enters a legal environment shaped by recent defeats. In April 2026, the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals issued an injunction blocking two California immigration laws: the "No Secret Police Act," which banned law enforcement officers — including ICE agents — from wearing face coverings, and a companion measure requiring agents to display visible identification. The court held that both laws unconstitutionally directed how the federal government could conduct its enforcement operations. Private prison companies are expected to mount analogous arguments against AB 1633 — that a state tax reaching federal contractors effectively obstructs a federal government function. California's attorneys will need a theory for why this tax survives constitutional scrutiny where those laws did not.

Part of a Broader Legislative Push

AB 1633 is one measure within a larger package. Newsom signed 21 immigration-related bills in the September 29 session. A companion bill, AB 2465, carried by Assemblymember Liz Ortega, bars businesses with financial ties to immigration detention and enforcement from accessing certain state tax credits, grants, and loans — a parallel financial restriction operating through a different mechanism in California's tax code.

Newsom also signed legislation banning electric shock gloves, prohibiting all law enforcement officers — including federal ICE agents operating in California — from using electroshock wearable devices until at least 2030. The move came in direct response to a $16.7 million federal contract ICE awarded to a Kentucky company for 6,000 pairs of the devices. The Department of Homeland Security has signaled it does not plan to comply with the ban, setting up another front in the state's ongoing confrontation with the administration.

Deaths, Conditions, and the Urgency Behind the Package

The political drive behind the legislative package draws on a grim body of evidence. More than 50 people died in ICE custody during Trump's second term — a figure that Human Rights Watch and Physicians for Human Rights characterize as the highest mortality rate recorded in federal immigration detention in over a decade. Inspections at Adelanto, cited repeatedly in legislative hearings, found conditions that California officials described as dangerous and inconsistent with basic standards of humane care.

Whether AB 1633 ultimately survives federal litigation will determine its real-world impact. But as the first law of its kind enacted in the United States, it creates a model that other Democratic-led states will likely examine — and marks California's most aggressive use of its tax code yet as a tool to shape a federal immigration enforcement system it has consistently sought to constrain.

text:
Ben Shapiro is at it again in his quest to conquer cinema. The Daily Wire's next film has started production in Montana, and if the goal was to grab headlines, mission accomplished.

The film is called "Pawn Shop," a pro-ICE thriller that has already drawn local protestors in Livingston, Montana. It comes from Shapiro and producer Dallas Sonnier and follows "Run Hide Fight: Infidels," starring Jonathan Majors, which also drew protests during production. At this point, protesters might as well be part of the Daily Wire crew.

Now here's the part not many have zeroed in on: the cast. Apparently, the three leads are Harvey Keitel, Danny Trejo and Henry Thomas. That's Mr. White from "Reservoir Dogs," Machete himself, and Elliott from "E.T." — a kid who hid an undocumented alien from federal agents. So this checks out.

The director is Michael Polish ("Twin Falls Idaho"), and the script comes from Jake Harlen, who doesn't seem to have an IMDb page.

Here's the official synopsis:

When chaos hits the streets of Minneapolis, a young federal agent is left alone after his partner is seriously hurt and must find a way to survive an increasingly dangerous situation. Seeking shelter inside a neighborhood pawn shop, he becomes trapped with a traditional Hispanic father and his progressive college-age son, forcing three very different men to confront fear, conflicting beliefs and a crisis that tests their courage and humanity.

What's more, the film's opening scene has been revealed through a leaked script, and there's no hiding the inspiration. The sequence dramatizes the fatal ICE shooting of Renée Good in Minnesota this past January. Harlen's script describes Good's stand-in, a character named Melanie, as "a fat blue-hair." It then lingers on the killing: "The first shot takes Melanie in the neck, below her covid mask. The second in the head, above her covid mask." It goes on to describe blood splattering onto her passenger's forehead and "matching covid mask."

Shapiro has spent years complaining that Hollywood won't make movies for conservatives. This is one way to fix that.

While we're at it, and as previously reported, Shapiro isn't done with his quest. He's going arthouse, having written the screenplay for "Confession," the new film from "The Painted Bird" director Václav Marhoul. The 1938 Moscow interrogation drama, starring Rob Lowe, Jennifer Jason Leigh, Nick Nolte, Emile Hirsch and James Franco, world premieres this month at the Warsaw Film Festival.

text:
CAPE TOWN, South Africa (AP) — A Laotian citizen deported by the United States to Eswatini under the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown was released from a maximum security prison in the African nation on Sunday after being held there for more than a year, his lawyer said.

Phone Chomsavanh was among five immigrants deported to Eswatini — where he has no ties — in July 2025 in the early days of the Trump administration’s secretive and highly contentious third-country deportation program.

Chomsavanh’s U.S.-based lawyer, Tin Thanh Nguyen, said in a statement announcing his release that he had only been informed that he was being deported to Eswatini shortly before a military cargo plane carrying him and other deportees landed there more than 14 months ago.

Chomsavanh was now being deported to Laos, Nguyen said.

Chomsavanh and the four other immigrants he was deported to Eswatini with were convicted of serious crimes in the U.S., but had served their sentences by the time they were sent to the Matsapha Correctional Complex near Eswatini’s administrative capital, Mbabane.

“Years after he finished serving his sentence in the United States, the Trump administration flew him to the small southern African kingdom and handed him over to a maximum-security prison, where he was held for more than a year without ever being charged with a crime,” Nguyen said.

He said in separate messages to The Associated Press that Chomsavanh had left Eswatini and landed in Johannesburg en route to Laos.

An Eswatini government spokesperson didn’t immediately acknowledge Chomsavanh’s release.

Chomsavanh was born in a refugee camp in Thailand after his parents fled Laos, and his family moved to the United States when he was 7, his lawyer said.

Chomsavanh is one of around 500 immigrants who have been deported from the United States to African countries that aren’t their home nations since the third-country program began last year, according to rights group Human Rights First, which has been monitoring the deportations.

Around a dozen African countries have accepted third-country deportees from the U.S., some in exchange for millions of dollars in payments. Eswatini, which is Africa’s last absolute monarchy and is ruled by a king, was paid $5.1 million by the Trump administration to take deportees, according to the agreement between the countries. Eswatini has received around 30 deportees so far.

The program, which results in immigrants being held in countries they have no ties with and where they haven’t been charged with any crime, has been fiercely criticized by rights groups and lawyers. It has been the subject of legal challenges in the U.S. and in some of the countries where immigrants have been sent.

The Trump administration has defended the policy as a way to quickly remove immigrants who have final deportation orders from the U.S. when their home countries might not immediately take them back.

Last month, a U.S. appeals court upheld a judge’s ruling to halt the program, because it didn’t give immigrants facing removal from the U.S. time to challenge their deportation to a third country because they fear persecution or torture there.

The U.S. Supreme Court ruled last week to temporarily allow U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration to continue swiftly removing immigrants to third countries, though it will hear arguments in the case in December.

The program has largely been carried out in secrecy, with little transparency over how many immigrants have been deported to third countries, and where and in what conditions they are being held.

text:
AUSTIN (KXAN) — A video circulating on social media has raised concerns over the detention of a woman by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents in Austin.

Mayor Pro Tem Chito Vela posted the video on X on Thursday. It was initially posted on Facebook by Leonardo Pelaez, where it has nearly 300,000 views as of Sunday.

Vela wrote in the caption of the X post, “ICE arrested the mom of a 9-year-old at a school bus stop in Austin, leaving him alone and crying. The video has profanity and is heartbreaking to watch, but it shows the fear/pain of what happened. This is evil. This is wrong. And it has to stop.”

Vela’s office told KXAN on Friday that it had “heard from community members and neighbors that the child went to school after the incident. While we don’t have more information on the mother’s detainment, we know the child is ok and with family.”

KXAN also reached out to ICE for more information about the arrest.

A spokesperson shared a statement that said ICE had encountered the woman, whom the agency referred to as an “illegal alien,” on Oct. 1 during a vehicle stop.

“After learning she was the sole caregiver for minor children who may have been left without supervision, ICE released her approximately 10 minutes later. No children were present during the stop, and ICE has not confirmed that the child heard crying in a circulating video is related to [the woman].”

The statement from ICE continued, saying the agency “encourages all illegal aliens to take control of their departure with the CBP Home App,” and that the US is offering people $3,000 and a free flight to self-deport.

“We encourage every person here illegally to take advantage of this offer and reserve the chance to come back to the U.S. the right legal way to live the American dream,” the statement continued. “If not, you will be arrested and deported without a chance to return.”

title: Nearly 1,500 Myanmar nationals repatriated from Malaysia as UN warns of risks - NY1

text:
YANGON, Myanmar (AP) — Nearly 1,500 Myanmar nationals who were sent back from Malaysia arrived in the country’s largest city on Sunday, despite warnings from the United Nations refugee agency and rights groups that conditions for return remain unsafe.

Myanmar has been in turmoil since the military seized power from the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi on Feb. 1, 2021, triggering widespread opposition and plunging large parts of the country into conflict.

The returnees, including 86 women, have been convicted of staying illegally and other immigration violations in Malaysia, according to reports from Myanmar state media. They were transported from Malaysia aboard two navy warships and a hospital ship last Tuesday. They arrived in southern Yangon early Sunday, Nay Lin Tun, a regional government minister, said.

The returnees are among 5,000 Myanmar nationals who will be repatriated in stages from Malaysia, where 10,388 others were being held at immigration detention centers, according to Malaysia’s Home Ministry.

The U.N. high commissioner for refugees and rights groups have criticized the repatriation, saying the security and humanitarian situation in parts of Myanmar remains volatile and returnees could face persecution and forced military conscription in an active war zone.

“Under international law, the Government of Malaysia is obligated to uphold the principle of non-refoulement and prevent the return of individuals to situations where they face a real risk of persecution, torture, or other serious human rights violations,” Kelley E. Currie, the U.N. special rapporteur on the situation of human rights in Myanmar, said in a statement on Thursday. “In my assessment, the risk of refoulement in the present circumstances is substantial.”

It was unclear if any of the returnees included minority Muslim Rohingya, who are facing persecution in Myanmar and have been denied citizenship.

Myanmar Foreign Ministry official Han Win Aung told The Associated Press that the repatriation involved “genuine citizens.”

Malaysia is home to about 215,600 refugees and asylum seekers registered with the UNHCR, including about 126,000 Rohingya who make up one of Southeast Asia’s largest refugee communities. Despite hosting them, Malaysia is not a party to the U.N. Refugee Convention and treats refugees as undocumented migrants.

Min Aung Hlaing, the leader of Myanmar’s military-backed government who was sworn in as president in April, is expected to visit Malaysia this month to discuss the refugee and migrant issues.

The Supreme Court justices return to the bench Monday for their new term, and their docket is already filling up with new confrontations on President Trump’s immigration agenda, among other major cases.

The term begins at a moment when the court’s public approval stands near record lows and in the shadow of a fraught relationship between Trump and the justices, namely the conservatives he appointed to the bench who’ve at times ruled against him.

“They voted against me too often,” Trump told Time magazine in an interview last week, referencing Justices Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett. “I gave them the position of a lifetime, and they vote against me often. They vote for me, too.”

It’s that mixed record that has fueled questions about how Trump’s agenda will fare this term at the Supreme Court, as lower-court judges repeatedly block the president’s policies, prompting the disputes to continually reach the justices in a barrage.

In just the past week, the justices cranked up their docket by adding two major appeals brought by the administration concerning the president’s immigration agenda.

The court will review whether officials are giving enough due process before deporting migrants to third countries where they have no ties. They’ll also rule on the legality of Trump’s mandatory detention policy, which has fueled a tsunami of litigation in the lower courts. Decisions in both cases are expected by summer.

“Because of the vast number of illegal immigrants — particularly during the Biden administration, but for many years up until now — that just creates an incredible backlog of issues and concerns,” said Carrie Severino, president of the Judicial Crisis Network and a former law clerk to Justice Clarence Thomas, “particularly as this president is trying to actually enforce the immigration laws.

“So, immigration is definitely an issue.”

It leaves groups that’ve prolifically fought the president in court, like the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU), gearing up for another major year at the Supreme Court.

“Last term, OT25, was one of the ACLU’s busiest ever,” Cecilia Wang, the group’s national legal director, told reporters during a briefing call last week. “This term may top that.”

Left-leaning groups have remained optimistic in their chances before the conservative-majority court after last term produced a mixed outcome for the president.

The court delivered Trump major wins on executive control over independent agencies and immigration but also struck down his signature tariff policy, thwarted his efforts to restrict birthright citizenship and blocked him from immediately firing Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook.

Trump’s foes have also found relief in the justices’ recent emergency decisions that kept the president’s mail-in voting plan blocked ahead of the midterms.

It’s some of those decisions that have left the president reeling. Trump, in one recent social media post, called his nominees “merely a shell of their original selves.”

In an interview with CBS News set to air Sunday, Justice Samuel Alito brushed off any notion the justices have a political agenda and pointed out the bipartisan nature of court criticism.

“He has his own way of saying things,” Alito said of Trump. “But the criticism of the court, I mean, I want to be even-handed on this. The criticism of the court by President Biden and justices by President Biden and his administration was very harsh. And President Trump has been very harsh.”

The public attacks didn’t stop the president from inviting Kavanaugh and Barrett to join him at the recent state dinner hosted for Chinese President Xi Jinping, however.

It’s not just Trump being critical. The Supreme Court’s public approval stands near record lows. A record-high 43 percent of Americans believe the court is too conservative, according to a Gallup poll conducted in early September. Just over one-third of those surveyed said it was “just about right” ideologically and 17 percent said it was too liberal.

Beyond the upcoming cases that directly implicate Trump’s agenda, some touch on political issues about which Trump’s base cares deeply.

The justices will hear challenges to an Arizona law that requires documentary proof of citizenship when registering to vote, a policy Republicans want implemented nationwide for federal elections. They’ll also take up several religious liberty disputes and examine the constitutionality of state bans on semi-automatic weapons, specifically AR-15s.

“We have a more exciting docket than we often do at this point,” said Severino.

“At the beginning of the Supreme Court term, some terms you would look at the list of the cases they’ve accepted already, and say, ‘Oh, it’s going to be kind of a snoozer,’” she added.

ACLU is asking the Supreme Court to add more cases to its plate. Among its pending requests is one that seeks to declare as unconstitutional Texas’s law requiring public school classrooms to post the Ten Commandments. The justices are set to consider taking up the case at a closed-door meeting after Texas responds in writing this fall.

“Our fundamental civil rights and civil liberties are under unprecedented attacks from all quarters,” Wang told reporters. “And many of those fights are poised to potentially make it up to the Supreme Court this term.”

On Monday, the term is set to begin with a bang as the justices consider a blockbuster case involving the fossil fuel industry. The Supreme Court will decide if cities and groups can use state law to force companies to pay potentially billions in damages over accusations they contributed to climate change and misled the public.

The case took an unanticipated turn last week when the court announced Alito’s last-minute recusal. Alito had faced pressure to exit the case due to perceived conflicts of interest related to his stock holdings in the oil and gas sector, but he told Bloomberg that his recusal was “prudent,” not required.

It’s a big week for Alito for unrelated reasons. On Tuesday, he’s set to release his first authored book since joining the bench, titled, “So Ordered: An Originalist’s View of the Constitution, the Court, and Our Country.”

His CBS News interview is at the beginning of a rare media tour to promote it.

“It’s part of the job that you’re going displease people by making decisions on controversial matters, because one side or the other is going to really dislike you,” Alito told the outlet.

text:
When the Supreme Court kicks off a new, nine-month term on Monday, one key player will be noticeably absent: President Donald Trump.

After months of near-constant confrontation with the White House, the nine justices will retake their seats behind the court’s mahogany bench without a docket full of Trump-driven, separation-of-powers blockbusters that defined the last term — from tariffs to birthright citizenship to the firing of once-independent government officials.

The respite is unlikely to last.

In the coming weeks, the justices will decide whether to wade into Trump’s messy defamation brawl with magazine columnist E. Jean Carroll, his mass cancellation of federal research grants, whether the Department of Government Efficiency must provide records detailing its slashing of federal agencies last year, and the administration’s ban on transgender Americans serving in the military.

Those and other cases could be added to a term that already includes an important Second Amendment challenge to bans on AR-15 rifles, the most significant case dealing with climate change to reach the justices in nearly two decades, and a fight over whether religious preschools receiving taxpayer money may decline to enroll the children of same-sex couples.

So far this next term, the court has granted 28 cases, less than half of what the justices will likely decide by June.

“There’s a very good chance that the 35 or so that the court is likely to grant in the remainder of the year will be the ones that are really the highlights,” Masha Hansford, an attorney at Davis Polk & Wardwell and a former assistant to the solicitor general, said at a recent event organized by the National Constitution Center.

One area where the court is already delving into Trump’s policies this term is immigration. The court has announced in recent days that it will hear arguments over the president’s mandatory detention policy and his push to deport migrants to countries other than their homeland. While important, neither of those cases has drawn the same level of attention as last year’s birthright citizenship case.

Dance with Trump

After Trump and his allies launched a rhetorical war against lower courts in early 2025, the president and the Supreme Court seemed to slide into a détente by the middle of the year — a delicate dance in which Trump has abided by the losses handed to him by the high court even as he has occasionally lashed out against the justices who supported them.

The court overwhelmingly sided with Trump on its emergency docket — the fast-track cases that are usually decided without argument. And it also backed the president in major regular cases that were argued during the last term and resulted in full opinions. One of those included the blockbuster decision allowing him to fire the leaders of agencies like the Federal Trade Commission. But the court was also willing to push back against Trump in some of those cases, such as by rejecting his emergency global tariffs and his push to undo birthright citizenship as it had been understood for more than a century.

Still, Trump has not shied away from railing against the 6-3 conservative court this past summer, including the three justices — Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett — whom he named to the bench during his first term. Trump told Time Magazine last week that he regretted nominated them.

“I gave them ​the position of a lifetime,” the president lamented, “and they vote against me often.”

The justices themselves have largely demurred when asked about Trump’s unusually personal attacks on the court. Justice Samuel Alito, a conservative who spoke to CBS as he prepares to publish a new book this week, said there has been a “great change in what presidents have said about the court when they are unhappy about our decisions.”

But, Alito said, that “very harsh” criticism has been “bipartisan.”

Pressed on Trump’s harsher statements, Alito said, “he has his own way of saying things.”

Girding for an election

Before the court decides any of the regular — or merits — cases it has granted, there’s a chance it will have to deal with a flood of litigation tied to next month’s midterm election. Whether that is a deluge or a trickle may be in voters’ hands.

Derek Muller, a law professor and election law expert at Notre Dame, said he believes the likelihood of post-election litigation will be low “because there probably won’t be enough decisively close cases where litigation would really matter.” But, he said, “if it does happen, it could significantly transform the upcoming Supreme Court term.”

The court has already juggled a series of redistricting disputes spun off from the president’s push for a mid-decade redrawing of House district boundaries. And last month it shut down Trump’s controversial proposal to give the US Postal Service a role in screening — and potentially rejecting — mail ballots sent to voters across the country.

Also waiting in the wings are several important non-Trump merits cases that could define the 2026-2027 term. It seems almost inevitable that the court will review state laws requiring the Ten Commandments to be posted in public school classrooms. Moreover, a legal battle raging between prediction sites like Kalshi and Polymarket and state governments has already reached the high court and could make its way to an oral argument sometime next year.

Banning AR-15 rifles

The court’s conservative majority has been steadily expanding gun rights under the Second Amendment for years. It have a huge opportunity to do so again this term.

In December, the court will hear arguments in cases challenging bans on AR-15 rifles enacted in Connecticut and Cook County, Illinois. Gun rights groups say the semi-automatic rifles are widely owned by Americans and are permitted in the vast majority of states. Gun control advocates counter that the weapons have been frequently used in mass shootings and should not receive Second Amendment protection because they are more “dangerous” and “unusual” than other types of guns.

The case draws heavily on a landmark 2008 decision from the Supreme Court, District of Columbia v. Heller, which stood for the prospect that arms “in common use” are protected under the Second Amendment.

“I think we know how this case is going to come out,” Deepak Gupta, a veteran appellate attorney, said at a recent event hosted by the Georgetown Law Center, suggesting that the court would likely strike down the AR-15 bans. “We know the outcome, but we don’t know how it’s going to be decided.”

Suing Exxon for climate change

On the very first day of the term, the justices will confront a long-running dispute about whether cities and states may sue fossil fuel companies for billions of dollars in damages caused by climate change. The appeal before the court deals with one such suit from Boulder, Colorado, but the decision will almost certainly play into dozens of other pending cases filed by cities and states attempting to hold oil companies accountable.

ExxonMobil and Suncor, the two companies that brought the case to the high court, argue that climate pollution is inherently a federal issue, in part because emissions waft across state lines. That understanding of federal control, they say, should effectively supersede state law. But Boulder says that there’s nothing in the Constitution or in federal law that backs up ExxonMobil’s position, and that the Supreme Court should let the lawsuit proceed.

Particularly notable is Alito’s decision to recuse himself from the case because of stock he owns in fossil fuel companies such as ConocoPhillips and Phillips 66. That opens the possibility of a 4-4 split, a rare outcome that would uphold the decision by Colorado’s Supreme Court that allowed Boulder’s lawsuit to proceed without setting a precedent.

Immigration emerges as a theme

One important Trump-related case that has reached the docket deals with the administration’s policy of imposing mandatory detention without bond hearings for people who entered the country illegally and who are targeted for deportation. Though the cases are lower profile than birthright citizenship, the court’s decision in the detention case could have enormous consequences for the president’s push to round up migrants living in the United States.

Trump broke with decades of past practice – including that of his first administration – and reinterpreted an immigration law Congress enacted in the 1990s to find that people in the country illegally should be subject to mandatory detention without bond hearings. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has recorded a massive increase in the number of migrants held in detention, from just under 38,000 at the end of the Biden administration to more than 65,000 this past summer.

The detention case is one of several dealing with immigration this term. Late last month, the court granted another important immigration case dealing with the Trump administration’s policy of removing certain people to countries other than their homeland – despite human rights concerns raised about some of those countries.

Religious schools v. LGBTQ rights

The Supreme Court in recent years has repeatedly sided with religious schools seeking public funding. Now it will answer a question it has largely avoided in those earlier cases: How to handle a religious school that declines to work with LGBTQ families.

The case comes out of Colorado, which enacted a ballot provision in 2020 that provides state funding for a universal preschool program. While the program allows religious preschools to take part, it also includes a nondiscrimination provision that requires each school receiving public money to provide eligible children an equal opportunity to enroll, regardless of race, religious affiliation, sexual orientation, gender identity and other factors.

Two Catholic parishes in Colorado that operate preschools sued over the policy and brought the case to the Supreme Court in November. They argue that honoring that anti-discrimination provision in the program would require them to violate their faith.

“The tea leaves are pretty good for the challengers generally,” Roman Martinez, a Latham & Watkins partner who regularly appears before the Supreme Court, said at the Georgetown event.

“What’s driving the court is a commitment to a type of pluralism,” he said. “The court, I think, is very concerned about religious groups sort of having equal access and being treated equally as a matter of practice, not just as a matter of formalism.”

text:
THANLYIN, Myanmar - Nearly 1,500 Myanmar migrants sent back from Malaysia arrived in their war-torn home country on Sunday, a Myanmar naval official said, returned under an opaque repatriation scheme.

Three ships carrying Myanmar migrants had all docked at the Myanmar navy base in Thanlyin just before 7.30am, according to the naval official, who asked for anonymity.

Hundreds of families were gathered at dawn to collect their relatives outside the base, where cars, taxis and buses were parked in ranks preparing to take them away, AFP journalists saw.

Kyaw Myint, 55, told AFP he was there to collect three grandchildren who had been in Malaysian detention for one and a half years, and who he has not seen in six years.

"Since they arrived in prison we lost contact with them," he said.

Now Kyaw Myint is worried about them being conscripted -- "not only by the military but also by ethnic armed groups", he added.

There are also concerns members of the persecuted Rohingya are among the returned group, after Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim announced the repatriations against a backdrop of anti-Rohingya sentiment, but this has not been confirmed.

The three Myanmar navy ships left Malaysia on Tuesday carrying 1,476 migrants, according to the Myanmar government -- the first of 5,000 that Anwar says Myanmar agreed to take back.

But the United Nations (UN) warns conditions in Myanmar, which has been consumed by civil war since a 2021 military coup, mean safe homecomings cannot be guaranteed as required under international law.

"We have no idea how his life will be back in Myanmar," said the 25-year-old sister of one migrant, who told his family he expected to be sent aboard the ships.

"Our main concern is his arrival won't be safe," she told AFP from Malaysia, requesting anonymity for security reasons after losing contact with her brother before the vessels set sail.

The arrivals were due to include 27 children and 79 women, Malaysian media said, the remaining 1,370 adult men.

Rohingya make up the majority of Myanmar refugees and asylum seekers in Malaysia, but Kuala Lumpur has not responded to an AFP query about the number onboard.

- Free and informed -

Anwar announced the repatriations in July, just days after the detention of more than 100 Rohingya asylum seekers in Kuala Lumpur amid rising xenophobia against refugees, particularly the Rohingyas in Malaysia.

News of the returns sparked widespread concern, as members of the ethnic group fled Myanmar en masse following a military crackdown starting in 2017, which rights experts say amounted to genocide.

Malaysia insists all returnees agreed to voluntary repatriation from detention centres, where Myanmar says they had completed sentences for immigration offences.

But monitor organisations such as Fortify Rights report dire conditions in the facilities.

The UN refugee agency said this past week its staff were not allowed to meet returnees to confirm whether migrants' decisions "were genuinely free and informed".

Myanmar state television has broadcast footage of the migrants on the journey home, being led in aerobics classes on a ship deck and wearing T-shirts saying: "Happy voyage back to motherland".

- Second group to follow -

Malaysia is already moving ahead with plans to return a second group of more than 3,500 migrants.

Migrants have "imposed a significant financial burden on the nation, triggered serious social crises, and created tangible security threats for the Malaysian people", the home ministry has said.

Myanmar leader Min Aung Hlaing, the coup leader who was installed as civilian president this April, is expected to soon visit Malaysia to discuss the scheme.

Myanmar last month pledged returns will be "safe and dignified".

But Yap Lay Sheng, a senior human rights specialist with Fortify Rights, told AFP: "There's no telling how the regime would treat returnees."

Myanmar is also riven by violence, with 50 killed late last month in a military airstrike on a marketplace in western Rakine state.

The civil war has so far killed more than 100,000 people, according to monitor ACLED.

"This is no time to return anyone forcibly to a country plagued by egregious human rights violations and abuses," UN rights chief Volker Turk said Tuesday.

text:
Election Day 2026 is less than a month away, and control of Congress is on the line, with a huge number of Illinois members of Congress leaving.

U.S. Sens. Dick Durbin and Reps. Danny Davis and Jan Schakowsky (D-Illinois) are among those retiring.

For 27 years, Schakowsky has represented Illinois' 9th District — which stretches from Chicago's north lakefront into the north and northwest suburbs and then northwest all the way to McHenry County. Evanston Mayor Daniel Biss is running to succeed her on the Democratic side, with Arlington Heights pastor John Elleson facing him on the Republican side.

The candidates have staked out dramatically differing positions on many issues, including immigration. Biss called for fighting for immigrants and refugees, and accused the U.S. Department of Homeland Security under President Trump of "terrorizing" them.

"Illinois 9 is a district for immigrants and refugees, has been for a very long time — people from literally all over the world — in a moment where Donald Trump is weaponizing ICE and CBP to attack our communities, abduct our neighbors, terrorize people," said Biss, "and so they want someone who's going to go not only fight for comprehensive immigration reform, but fight back against these grotesque and outrageous and illegal violent excesses."

But Elleson said the law must be respected.

"We have illegals in our church every Sunday, and they'll never come in. We'll never allow police to come in our church, but government's different. Government has to do their job. And you know, if I get a speeding ticket when I go there [and say]: 'I'm a pastor! Let me go!' you can't do that," he said. "So I believe that we have to have secure borders. I really do."

Elleson also said he supported Israel amid the war in Gaza — though not unconditionally.

"We've got to support Israel. Come on. We got to support Israel. I just think that, you know, we have a pact. They've been through a lot," he said. "Now, if they do something wrong, we don't got to rubber-stamp everything they do. But no, I think you've got to support them. They're in a tough region."

But Biss said the relationship between Israel and the U.S. needs to change.

"The U.S. has traditionally treated Israel kind of unlike any other country, right? Israel is a wealthy, developed economy that gets the type of military aid that no other country like it gets," he said. "That should be phased out."

On the war with Iran, Biss said the Trump administration should never have gotten involved.

"The Trump administration made a catastrophic mistake. They were basically blurry in their thinking, right?" he said. "They had this completely absurd, naïve idea that did not make sense to people who knew the situation that: 'Hey, we're just going to go in. It's going to be easy. We're going to effectuate regime change.' That was never going to work."

Elleson spoke in support of the U.S. efforts in Iran, and said President Trump should have stuck to a program.

"I don't like this back-and-forth talk, 'Oh, we're going to blow 'em up,' one day, and then this. I get lost there," he said. "If we could strike a deal, let's strike a deal."

Meanwhile, U.S. Rep. Robin Kelly (D-Illinois) is leaving her seat after a failed run in the Democratic primary to replace Sen. Durbin. Kelly's 2nd Congressional District stretches from the high-rises of Chicago's Hyde Park neighborhood through the rest of the South Side and south suburbs, and downstate all the way to the farms of Danville.

Cook County Commissioner Donna Miller (D-6th) is running for the seat on the Democratic side, while Kankakee County truck driver Mike Noack is running on the Republican side. The candidates agreed that the average American is struggling in the face of high prices and costs, with Miller focusing on health care.

"One of the first things is to put the Affordable Care Act back in place. All of the cuts — the $880 billion worth of cuts that this administration put forth — are affecting everyday people. We have to put those back," she said. "But I also believe in the conversation around preventative care, so we have to have expansive issues that come into the affordability for health care."

Noack agreed that there is a need to "get a hold of the health care system, while also noting consumer prices.

"We need to get a hold of the economy in ways that make a different. So like gasoline prices, they're killing us. We've got to try to get them to bring down the prices, somehow," he said. "I mean, they don't need to make record profits every year. I mean, that's down on the back of the people."

Miller said she has also spent a lot of time in rural communities listening to farmers.

"What I hear mostly from them is that they are concerned about the legacy of their farms. They're concerned about being able to do business in this country and outside of this country," she said. "I want to work on the Farm Bill when I get to Congress. That's something that has not also been focused on in many years."

Noack added that the "defunding of schools has to stop."

"I don't necessarily think that private schools are the answer. I mean, it's an answer for a lot of people, and private schools are good," he said. "But we still need to focus on the public schools too."

Miller also called for stronger guardrails on artificial intelligence. Noack called for building more hydroelectric dams.

Loss of veteran Illinois congresspeople will have an effect, experts say

As to the overall loss of members of the Illinois congressional delegation with all their power, experience and seniority, former CBS Chicago political reporter Derrick Blakley said it will have an effect on what the Illinois delegation can get done.

"Well, it means it's going to be harder to bring home the bacon, because seniority is crucial, especially in the House. You talk about career politicians, but career politicians in Congress are the people who have the clout to get things done, make decisions — funding for things like transportation, social programs — very important to the city," Blakley said. "So we lose that, and that is a loss."

Former Illinois Republican Party Chairman Pat Brady said the challenges the Illinois delegation will face with the loss of its veteran members will not necessarily be so dramatic as to mean a loss of highway projects or train line expansions. But he noted that the veteran members sit on committees with a lot of power.

"Jan Schaokwsky was on Energy and Commerce forever. That's where everything goes through; Ways and Means, all these major committees. So we'll have less of a voice," he said. "I don't know how much impact it's going to have. We still have a very good congressional delegation — we have Mike Quigley, Nikki Budinskki, and some others that kind of fill in the void. But it's a big loss."

title: ICE frees SF lawmaker's aide on bond. But the deportation fight isn't over - SF Standard
description: Ho-Yin Mo, a former KTSF anchor who works in Assemblymember Catherine Stefani’s SF office, was released after more than two weeks in ICE custody.
text:
By Jennifer WadsworthSenior News Editor

Published Oct. 3, 2026at12:35pm

Published Oct. 3, 2026at12:35pm

A San Francisco lawmaker’s aide arrested by ICE at the Las Vegas airport last month has been released from detention, though he still faces deportation to Hong Kong.

Ho-Yin Mo, a field rep for Assemblymember Catherine Stefani, was released Friday after an immigration judge granted his release on bond. Mo had been in custody since Sept. 17, when he was caught up in an enforcement operation during a layover at Harry Reid International Airport.

“Mo’s release confirms what we knew all along: He is a lawful public servant and a cherished part of our Bay Area family, and he should never have been detained,” Stefani said in announcing the news on Saturday.

ADVERTISEMENT

Getting Mo out of ICE custody became a “singular focus” for Stefani, a spokesperson for her office told The Standard. She canceled plans to join the California Legislative Italian American Caucus delegation to Italy so she could work on securing Mo’s release.

When she found out a couple days ago that he was getting released on bond, she traveled to Las Vegas to greet him when he walked out of the detention facility.

Mo thanked Stefani, his lawyer, and his supporters, saying he’s eager to get back to work for San Franciscans. On Saturday, he was en route to the city by car, since flying is out of the question.

His release doesn’t end the case. His attorney said the Trump administration has swept people into deportation proceedings “even while they were lawfully pursuing their immigration status.”

The Department of Homeland Security has said Mo entered the U.S. legally on a temporary basis in 2020 but overstayed. “Work authorization or a pending application do not confer legal status in the United States,” a DHS spokesperson told The Standard last month.

The arrest drew national attention and prompted an outpouring of local support. Mayor Daniel Lurie, who has made a point of dodging confrontations with the Trump White House, urged federal officials to release Mo.

Related

After his arrest, Mo was sent to an immigration jail in Pahrump, Nevada, according to detention records. His case comes amid a rise in airport immigration arrests under the Trump administration, including people detained on allegations of overstayed visas despite pending asylum applications, federal work permits, and no criminal records.

Mo has worked in Stefani’s 19th Assembly District office since January 2025, helping constituents access disability benefits, health coverage, childcare, and food stamps. He’s a point-person for residents who primarily speak Cantonese and Mandarin, and regularly provides interpretation services for Stefani and her staff, who work with one of the nation’s largest Chinese-speaking electorates.

Before joining Stefani’s office, Mo worked as an anchor and reporter at KTSF, a Bay Area Chinese-language TV station. He also worked as a field representative for Mayor London Breed during her re-election campaign in 2024.

Supporters for Mo have set up a crowdfunding campaign (opens in new tab) to help cover his legal costs. Because Mo is a state employee, he can accept gifts of no more than $630 from any one source, a spokesperson for Stefani’s office explained. So, even if wealthy supporters are willing to cover his legal costs, Mo must rely on many small donations rather than a single large backer.

As of Saturday, the GoFundMe effort had raised more than $27,000 from more than 180 donations.

It has taken the Trump Administration less than two years to make violent encounters with federal immigration agents a regular fact of American life. On a single day late last month, a citizen and a noncitizen—one in Illinois, the other in Texas—became the most recent examples of this new reality. That morning, in Evanston, a Black man walking to a pharmacy was left injured and bleeding by the side of a road after a group of ICE officers, mistaking him for an immigrant “fugitive,” threw him to the ground and tried to handcuff him. Once the agents realized that he was a U.S. citizen, they said that they offered him “assistance,” then drove off. A few hours later, in Austin, an ICE officer shot a Venezuelan delivery driver in the back as he tried to flee in his car. He was detained, and partial paralysis had set in before doctors removed the bullet, several days later. Last Tuesday, the Department of Justice announced that it was charging the man with assaulting the officer who shot him.

Almost as alarming as the incidents themselves has been the government’s refusal to acknowledge a pattern of abuse that is clearly metastasizing at the Department of Homeland Security. Since Donald Trump took office last year, agents from D.H.S. have shot at some two dozen people in the United States, killing six of them. The deaths of Renee Good and Alex Pretti during Operation Metro Surge, in Minnesota last January, were a turning point in the public’s awareness of the problem, but their deaths were not the first. Ten months earlier, in South Padre Island, Texas, Ruben Ray Martinez, a twenty-three-year-old U.S. citizen, was shot and killed by an ICE officer—something that the government didn’t disclose for nearly a year, until American Oversight, a nonprofit group, obtained the incident report. In one week this past July, ICE agents killed Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a Mexican national who had lived in this country for thirty-five years, raising a family and running a building company, and Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, a twenty-five-year-old Colombian with a wife and toddler. These incidents were documented as officer shootings. But how, for instance, should news outlets categorize the death, on July 14th, of a Mexican man visiting family in Florida, on a tourist visa, who was hit by a tractor-trailer as he ran from immigration agents?

Not only has no ICE officer been federally charged in these deaths, but the agency has made a habit of casting blame on the people it has appeared to victimize, turning impunity into another form of aggression. The most common claim is that immigrants attempting to escape arrest are “assaulting” officers and, in particular, that motorists are “weaponizing” their vehicles. In many cases, video evidence seems to contradict such accounts; in others, officers weren’t wearing their body cameras. The Times found that the Administration had filed assault charges against more than five hundred and fifty people and that, in about half of the roughly four hundred cases that have been resolved, “juries acquitted defendants, judges threw out charges, or prosecutors withdrew them.”

Because the federal government has largely forsworn—and, indeed, actively blocked—independent investigations of its agents, states have tried to bring their own cases. In August, prosecutors in Minnesota were seeking the extradition of Christian Castro, an ICE agent being held in Texas, who was wanted for shooting a Venezuelan national in the leg during Operation Metro Surge. When Greg Abbott, the Texas governor, refused Minnesota’s request, Castro was released. The Justice Department then charged Castro with making “false statements”—he claimed that he’d been attacked with a broom and a snow shovel before firing—a considerably lesser charge than the ones he could have faced. An Assistant U.S. Attorney in Minnesota, Matthew Evans, told the victim’s lawyers that he’d “objected in the strongest possible terms,” but that the decision had been made in Washington. Evans was fired and is now being investigated for allegedly leaking information about the case.

This all comes at a time when ICE arrests have reached a record high—nearly fifty-one thousand in August alone—with agents conducting operations nationwide at hospitals, at airports, and outside schools. Past calls by Democratic lawmakers for D.H.S. agents to end the practice of wearing masks in public were ignored, and this summer the department announced that it would be purchasing for its personnel twenty million dollars’ worth of gloves that deliver powerful electric shocks. Flush with cash from Congress, D.H.S. is planning to hire five thousand more ICE officers by the end of the year. Recently, it signed seven billion dollars in construction contracts to build more detention centers. Meanwhile, in all but one of the existing two hundred and thirty-nine immigration jails across the country, the A.P. reported, ICE has stopped listing in its online database, known as the detainee locator, the whereabouts of people in custody who have final deportation orders. If people’s names don’t show up in the locator, their family members and lawyers won’t immediately be able to find them. In July, sixteen thousand people arrested by ICE, or about a third of those entering detention that month, had final deportation orders.

text:
HOUSTON — As the sun set on a late-September evening, a voice rose over the din of traffic at the roadside memorial for Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, the 52-year-old husband and father fatally shot here by immigration authorities three months ago.

Sitting on barbershop steps, Berta Lopez, a nearby resident, alternately sang, recited prayers and cried for a man she never met.

“It was unjust — he was killed unjustly! The family is deeply hurt, his wife, his children. They are like family to us. And why don’t they show the people who did the killing? Why don’t they show them? Why don’t they release the names of the people who killed Lorenzo? Why don’t they expose them?” she said in Spanish.

In tears, Lopez said that after more than a year of intensive operations by Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Salgado Araujo’s killing was a clarifying moment. The government, she said, saw those who weren’t U.S. citizens as less than nothing. She was tired of it.

“Just because we’re Hispanic, shouldn’t we hold our heads high? No, God doesn’t want us hanging our heads in shame. He wants all of us, his children, to hold our heads up high,” Lopez said. “God doesn’t care about papers.”

Lopez’s hurt and anger was reflected in NBC News interviews with more than three dozen Houston-area Latinos, elected officials, activists and political strategists. They reveal a distraught community whose members feel degraded by the messages they hear out of Washington, D.C., during President Donald Trump’s second term. They said they have been terrorized by the constant stories of those detained, many wrongly, and left to languish. They were aghast that the government was sending immigrants to countries they had never heard of.

Many said Salgado Araujo’s shooting death crystallized their feelings of powerlessness. Most Latinos were better versed in the details of the incident than in the names and backgrounds of those running for some of the highest-profile offices in their state.

Their refrains were in the same vein: That could have been my dad, my brother, my uncle, my son — or me.

Pushing back

Lorenzo Salgado Araujo woke before dawn on a hot Houston morning on July 7, as he did most days. He had lived in the U.S. for decades without legal status but was in the process of getting a work permit. He had no criminal record.

He picked up workers in his white van and was driving to a jobsite when he was pursued by immigration agents in unmarked vehicles. An officer shot him, according to authorities, after they say he used his vehicle to ram them. It’s a story contradicted by witnesses in the van, but it’s one immigration authorities have told before in explaining how a traffic pursuit turned deadly.

This time, though, the family wasn’t having it. Salgado Araujo’s eldest son stood before cameras and delivered an emotional testimonial to his father that went viral.

“He was a hardworking family man who never wanted his name to be known by anyone outside of his family,” Ronaldo Salgado said at a news conference days after his father’s shooting, as his brother held up a photo of their father.

Ronaldo Salgado stressed that the story of his dad ramming government vehicles could not be true. Their father had always taught his kids that if law enforcement attempted to pull them over, they were to pull off the road, hand over their license and registration and act respectfully.

In the end, authorities admitted Salgado Araujo was not the intended target of the operation.

In an interview with NBC News, Ronaldo Salgado said as immigration arrests became more prevalent in 2025, they talked to their father about the procedure if he had an encounter, including calling his family, and that they’d contact their attorneys.

“Just remember, don’t sign anything. Call us,” Ronaldo Salgado said he told his father.

Sitting at Las Perras Cafe in Houston, where a makeshift altar to his father sits in the corner, Ronaldo Salgado recited the names of those who had been killed by immigration officers, including Renee Good, Alex Pretti and Ruben Ray Martinez, saying the country is not now safe because of their deaths.

“These are lives that are lost, and they need to be investigated, just like any other life lost. It needs to be investigated with the full cooperation of the agents involved and the agencies involved,” the son said.

“All of this isn’t making us any safer. How is going after my dad going to work making the city safer?” Ronaldo Salgado said. “Criminals don’t wake up at 5 in the morning to pick up their crew and go to do a day of backbreaking labor. You don’t.”

In an unusual move, federal officials made public an FBI search warrant to get inside Salgado Araujo’s van after his death. Then, federal officials released a stinging detail: The bureau sought entry to look at baggies with crystals that they said resembled meth.

When he heard that, Ronaldo Salgado said he couldn’t help but break into a little smile: “Ohhh, they messed up.”

He knew what it was. And it would only make things worse for federal authorities. It was a homemade electrolyte mixture, mainly of salt, that his father later mixed into Gatorade for himself and workers to combat the triple-digit Houston summer heat outside.

The U.S. attorney’s office later confirmed that the mix was in fact not methamphetamine, surprising few who knew Salgado Araujo.

Ronaldo Salgado felt it was an effort to sully his father’s reputation and dampen public outrage.

The implication just added to community anger, viewed as a thinly veiled attempt at smearing the man immigration authorities killed.

“It really shook the community,” said Jasmine Khadem González, an immigrant rights organizer with the Houston Democratic Socialists of America. “A lot of us who are Latino, we have somebody in our family: If it’s not our father then it’s our uncle who has a very similar job. … To see somebody like that be targeted for just being on his way to work or for the color of his skin or for the kind of truck that he’s driving — because it’s associated with Latino men — to see somebody like that be targeted for doing a very everyday thing. For just existing.”

In the NBC News/Telemundo poll, 31% of Latino voters say they or someone close to them started carrying identification over concerns about ICE enforcement, while 27% say they know someone who has been deported or detained by ICE in the last two years.

Amy Zachmeyer, the executive director of New Economy for Working Houston, a group that helped organize community vigils and demanded accountability and transparency in the probe, said the Salgado family’s high-profile pushback kept authorities in check.

“They’ve shown incredible strength to be able to really defend their father,” she said.

Zachmeyer grew emotional as she spoke about the sons. “They never let a narrative set in that he was anything but a loving father, a Houstonian, a Texan, a hard worker.”

Anger reshapes local politics

Adrian Garcia, a Harris County commissioner, said Latinos are “feeling a lot of attack and disrespect.” Over the last year, he’s worked to reach out to those who don’t vote often. From his view, people now are willing to walk across broken glass to send a message to the Trump administration.

“The low-propensity voters that I’ve been speaking to absolutely have a great intensity to vote in this election, and they specifically speak to ICE enforcement. A lot of young kids: ‘I’m voting for my mom. I’m voting for my dad.’ I hear that a lot,” Garcia said.

More Latino registered voters than ever — 72% — rated their interest in the upcoming election as 10 out of 10 in the NBC News/Telemundo poll.

Garcia described the greater impact that fear of immigration enforcement has had across the Texas economy.

“This is not what our community deserves, and it is also what is impacting the things that we care about the most, the business, the economy. They’re hurting the industry,” he said. “They’re hurting those who work hard and play by the rules.”

Jareli Barrera, who works as a server at the popular Cielito Cafe in Houston, said she has never been so tuned into an election. Today, she said she’s helping others, including co-workers, to register to vote.

She cannot stand seeing the level of fear in her community, including among those who are citizens but fear being separated from family or an aggressive encounter.

“Republicans are probably going to lose. It’s not going to be the greatest thing for them at the end of the day,” Barrera said. “Most of these immigrants are the ones that are making the U.S. successful. They’re doing the hard work. … If everyone’s deported, who’s gonna do the hard labor? Who’s gonna construct? Who’s going to do all this cleaning that they don’t want to do.”

Since 2025, local activist groups have tried to work with the city of Houston to better protect Latinos as they watched intense enforcement operations in cities like Minneapolis, Los Angeles and Chicago upend life for residents and lead to encounters with immigration authorities that turned violent or deadly.

Jennefer Canales-Pelaez, a Houston-based senior policy attorney and strategist with the Immigrant Legal Resource Center, said Salgado Araujo’s death was a “culmination of years of Texas entrenching itself, entangling itself with ICE” and “illustrated to them the fear, the levels of persecution of justice that immigrant communities have been living with in Texas for a very long time.”

Before Salgado Araujo’s death, Canales-Pelaez was among those who worked to deter cooperation between Houston police and federal police agencies and pushed for greater transparency into immigration operations. Abbott, the three-term governor and a staunch Trump ally who is up for re-election in November, threatened to block $200 million in grants to Houston and other major cities if they didn’t change local rules that directed police forces not to hold individuals they encounter for longer time periods to assist ICE. The cities, including Houston, reworded their ordinances.

Houston Mayor John Whitmire, a centrist Democrat, told The New York Times last October that he kept his head down as other city and state leaders in the country grew combative with the White House over immigration operations. Whitmire said his city had avoided “turmoil” that others faced.

Whitmire initially declared his hands were tied after the shooting; the Houston Police Department had no jurisdiction to conduct an independent investigation. After community uproar, the city changed course. Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare has now launched a probe, with the county government approving the $2.5 million request to fund it.

“It ignited this flame and really showed other people that aren’t necessarily living this experience or working in this line of work, ‘Oh, this got to us,’” Canales-Pelaez said. “When the mayor told us that we weren’t going to be another Minneapolis, we weren’t going to be a Los Angeles, well, now we are. Someone’s dead. That really has sparked this rage, this collective, righteous anger.”

text:
From the end of the U.S. mission in Iraq to a botched execution in Tennessee, here are stories that made headlines this past week. Or skip to the end to test your news savvy with a quiz.

Deportations to third countries can resume

The Supreme Court on Tuesday let President Donald Trump’s administration resume deporting migrants to countries other than their own without offering them the chance to show the harms they may face, at least for now.

The court granted the Justice Department’s emergency request to pause a lower judge’s ruling that the Department of Homeland Security’s policy to remove migrants to so-called third countries is unlawful. The justices also agreed to hear arguments in the dispute in December.

More than 25,000 migrants were deported to 29 countries under the policy implemented last year, according to a tally by human rights groups.

US troops leave Iraq as Iran war continues

BAGHDAD — U.S. forces ended their mission in Iraq on Wednesday, raising fears they will leave behind a security vacuum, further embolden Iranian-backed militias and give the Islamic State group an opening to regroup.

More than 200,000 Iraqi civilians were killed in chaos unleashed after U.S. forces toppled dictator Saddam Hussein in 2003, and 4,500 American troops died in the biggest U.S. war of the century so far.

Tehran views the pullout as a victory for its allied armed groups and a step toward its aim of driving U.S. forces out of the region. As the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran entered its eighth month, Iran said it received a U.S. response to its latest proposal to resurrect the collapsed ceasefire.

Renee Good’s family files federal lawsuits

The family of Renee Good, on Thursday announced the filing of federal civil rights lawsuits. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent Jonathan Ross shot and killed Good, 37, a U.S. citizen, on Jan. 7 during protests of deportation sweeps in Minneapolis. Her family sued the Trump administration, saying there had been “no accountability” for her killing.

In other news

Bills blocked: The Senate blocked legislation Wednesday requiring state utility regulators to consider whether large electricity users, including data centers, should bear the incremental costs of power infrastructure built to serve them, and a bill that would impose new controls on Congress members’ stock trades. Democrats said the bills didn’t go far enough.

Economy: U.S. gross domestic product increased at a 2.2% annualized rate, revised up from the previously estimated 1.5% pace, the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Economic Analysis said Wednesday in its third estimate of second-quarter GDP.

Reflecting Pool: A judge Thursday permanently dismissed the Trump administration’s criminal case against Olympic canoeist David Hearn, who was charged with vandalizing the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool. Evidence suggests the damage was caused by flawed installation.

USPS: The U.S. Postal Service said Thursday it will take extraordinary measures to ensure the delivery of ballots for next month’s congressional elections, including extending hours at some retail branches, expedited handling, extra deliveries and special pickups of ballots.

Powell probe: The Federal Reserve’s Inspector General said Wednesday it found no grounds for a criminal referral or administrative misconduct tied to cost overruns in a central bank renovation project that drew scorn from President Donald Trump and an investigation of former Fed chief Jerome Powell.

Big number

$20 million: Funds Democrats say the government transferred from the Department of Homeland Security to air TV ads of President Donald Trump, including one that resembles one of his 2024 campaign ads. The Federal Communications Commission chair said Wednesday the ads aren’t improper.

Quote of the week

“I will not be silenced by the continued threats of prosecution from the president or others,” former special counsel Jack Smith said Tuesday as he appeared voluntarily for his second public hearing before Congress on his investigations of President Donald Trump.

text:
HOUSTON, Oct 4 — A one-year-old toddler stumbles around an immigration court in Louisiana, crying. He throws a toy that nearly hits a prosecutor.

The judge instructs the baby and his mother, age 17, to apply for asylum. But the teenager can barely focus on what he is saying.

Roxana Avila-Cimpeanu, deputy director of a group that provides legal support for unaccompanied minors, described this scene, which she witnessed in August.

“This child is being expected to file her own application, also figure out how to file things for her one-year-old baby, while living through the distress of being a detained young mother,” Avila-Cimpeanu told AFP.

President Donald Trump’s administration has choked off funding for organisations that have years of experience assisting unaccompanied minors, bringing in substitutes that are under-equipped and unqualified, advocates say.

“We are gravely concerned that ORR would entrust a vulnerable population with firms so plainly unqualified for the task,” Democratic lawmakers said in a letter to the Deportment of Health and Human Services this week.

ORR is the Office of Refugee Resettlement, an agency traditionally tasked with the care of unaccompanied minor migrants.

The category describes children who arrive in the United States without an adult, or whose parents were detained by immigration agents and are in shelters or government custody.

Attack on children

Since he returned to the White House for his second term in January 2025, President Donald Trump has a mounted an aggressive and sometimes violent operation to deport undocumented immigrants from the United States.

Last year the administration tried to cut off funding that ORR used to support a national network of organisations that have for years provided legal services to unaccompanied migrant minors.

Following a lawsuit, the measure was blocked by a federal judge who ordered that the services, which were mandated by a 2008 law, be maintained.

Months later, the government stopped making payments, and in July 2026, it allowed a contract with the Acacia Centre for Justice — which managed a network of about 100 organisations — to expire.

Avila-Cimpeanu told AFP that in late 2025 that the government made funding contingent on the release of confidential information about some 20,000 children represented by the network — “and we did not do so.”

The government then announced plans to hand the cases over to the Burke Law Group, run by a former Trump administration official, but that firm withdrew its bid.

It then planned to deploy Our Rescue, an organisation founded by a controversial anti-trafficking activist and led by a former investigator for Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

The contract was put on hold following questions raised in Congress, amid a review of federal funds allocated for this purpose.

“Children’s legal protections should never be the currency Of political patronage,” Democratic lawmakers said in their letter.

Avila-Cimpeanu says the administration is trying to complicate the defense of minors “in order to get to their goal of deporting as many children as quickly as possible.”

“I have been doing this work for 10 years, and this is the worst time that I’ve ever seen with regard to the government’s concerted attack on children,” she said.

Babies in court

She said it is common for unaccompanied minors to appear in immigration courts. That is why a lawyer who understands the issue—and even speaks the child’s language if it is not English — is necessary.

Avila-Cimpeanu recalled a case in 2018 when her organisation was in court on behalf of a baby just months old.

“We had to say: this baby denies the allegations. This baby would like voluntary departure.

“It’s ridiculous that children have to go through this process as if they were adults, but it is part of the proceeding.”

This week, CNN reported that 25 migrant children, several without a lawyer, had a hearing in a Texas court.

In a statement to AFP, ORR said that in August it provided funding through the end of the year for the US Committee for Refugees and Immigrants (USCRI) to appear at immigration hearings.

“USCRI is appearing at 100 percent of the hearings and has expanded to provide legal orientation, legal consultations and direct representation,” it said.

Bilal Askaryar, a spokesman for Acacia, explained that USCRI is a small organization with about 50 attorneys, compared to the 800 in Acacia’s network.

“This isn’t about a contract for us. This isn’t about a dispute between an organization and the government. This is about 20,000 children who came to the United States seeking safety,” he said. — AFP

text:
YANGON, Myanmar (AP) — Nearly 1,500 Myanmar nationals who were sent back from Malaysia arrived in the country’s largest city on Sunday, despite warnings from the United Nations refugee agency and rights groups that conditions for return remain unsafe.

Myanmar has been in turmoil since the military seized power from the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi on Feb. 1, 2021, triggering widespread opposition and plunging large parts of the country into conflict.

The returnees, including 86 women, have been convicted of staying illegally and other immigration violations in Malaysia, according to reports from Myanmar state media. They were transported from Malaysia aboard two navy warships and a hospital ship last Tuesday. They arrived in southern Yangon early Sunday, Nay Lin Tun, a regional government minister, said.

The returnees are among 5,000 Myanmar nationals who will be repatriated in stages from Malaysia, where 10,388 others were being held at immigration detention centers, according to Malaysia’s Home Ministry.

The U.N. high commissioner for refugees and rights groups have criticized the repatriation, saying the security and humanitarian situation in parts of Myanmar remains volatile and returnees could face persecution and forced military conscription in an active war zone.

“Under international law, the Government of Malaysia is obligated to uphold the principle of non-refoulement and prevent the return of individuals to situations where they face a real risk of persecution, torture, or other serious human rights violations,” Kelley E. Currie, the U.N. special rapporteur on the situation of human rights in Myanmar, said in a statement on Thursday. “In my assessment, the risk of refoulement in the present circumstances is substantial.”

It was unclear if any of the returnees included minority Muslim Rohingya, who are facing persecution in Myanmar and have been denied citizenship.

Myanmar Foreign Ministry official Han Win Aung told The Associated Press that the repatriation involved “genuine citizens.”

Malaysia is home to about 215,600 refugees and asylum seekers registered with the UNHCR, including about 126,000 Rohingya who make up one of Southeast Asia’s largest refugee communities. Despite hosting them, Malaysia is not a party to the U.N. Refugee Convention and treats refugees as undocumented migrants.

Min Aung Hlaing, the leader of Myanmar’s military-backed government who was sworn in as president in April, is expected to visit Malaysia this month to discuss the refugee and migrant issues.
