text:
Welcome to the 2026 voter guide for Michigan's Aug. 4 primary election. The voter guide ‒ separate from the Detroit Free Press' news coverage and the Detroit Free Press Editorial Board's endorsements ‒ offers candidates the chance to communicate with voters in their own words. We remove entries that include false or unverifiable statements, personal attacks on other candidates or foul language, but responses are otherwise unedited.

El-Sayed's GOP opponent, Mike Rogers, did not return the Free Press Voter Guide questionnaire. Use this link to visit our Voter Guide.

Dr. Abdul El-Sayed

Candidate for U.S. Senate, Democrat

Age: 41

What is your current occupation? Please share any other work experience relevant to the role you are seeking.

I am a former public health official, having led both Detroit and Wayne County’s Health Departments, where we eliminated lead from public schools, secured free glasses for kids, and spearheaded a program to eliminate up to $700 million in medical debt for 300,000

Do you have previous political experience? If yes, please describe.

Though I have never held elected office, I have been appointed to serve in two public servant roles: the City of Detroit’s Health Director, and Wayne County’s Director of Health, Human, and Veterans services. I also ran for governor in 2018.

What should be the United States’ top foreign policy priority over the next six years, and where do you believe American military power has been overused or underused?

I believe in international law, and that we should be the first among equals to enforce it. But for too long, we have been among the first to break it. We are funding weapons for genocidal regimes abroad while our schools, hospitals and roads at home have been left to decay. We should make it our top priority to orient the United States’s foreign policy around peace, ending the illegal and immoral war in Iran, strictly enforcing the Leahy Laws, and ensuring that military assistance we provide is aligned with international law, rather than making exceptions for countries committing human rights atrocities. Our diplomacy should be rooted in seeking peace and open collaboration by reestablishing USAID and reentering institutions of global cooperation, such as the World Health Organization, in pursuit of cementing our nation as a leader among equals for shared rights.

What changes, if any, would you make to federal immigration law, border security and asylum policy? Please identify one proposal you would support even if it would anger your own party.

Our current immigration system treats any and all immigrants seeking a better life in our country as threats, rather than with dignity and respect. I believe in a safe, secure southern border and respect for immigration law—as well as a clear pathway to citizenship. The most consequential symptom of our misalignment on immigration is ICE, which has become a paramilitary force and set above the law. ICE has violently terrorized our communities and split families apart. I have been calling for the abolition of ICE since 2018 because I recognized the danger, and Trump’s weaponization of it has only cemented that belief. It should be replaced with an alternative enforcement mechanism that treats folks with the same respect afforded to everyone in America. We should also restructure CBP to focus on keeping our border secure rather than demonizing folks on the street, while investing in the legal infrastructure we need for a pathway to citizenship.

Michigan’s economy depends on autos, manufacturing, trade and union labor. What federal policy would you pursue to protect Michigan jobs while keeping the state competitive in a changing global economy?

I believe NAFTA and USMCA have been a disaster for working people, flattening industry at home and offshoring jobs that should have stayed in Michigan. We must renegotiate our trade deals to center labor. I support targeted tariffs deployed in a steady, thoughtful, and transparent way to incubate legacy and emerging manufacturing industries here at home. None of this is possible without thriving unions that empower workers to fight for what they need to live healthy and meaningful lives. As Senator, I will be proud to co-sponsor the PRO Act, a critical step to protect workers from retaliation, allow gig workers to unionize, and give real teeth to labor law enforcement. Finally, we must rethink the financial incentives that leave CEOs more interested in the next quarter’s stock price than the long term health of their companies. That means putting union representatives on boards, banning stock buybacks, and locking up executive stocks for 10 years after they leave their companies.

What should Congress do to lower costs for Michigan families, particularly on housing, health care, groceries, energy and child care? Please name the first bill you would sponsor or co-sponsor.

We must ban corporations from buying off politicians through PAC donations that leave them rigging the system against us. As prices go up, we should empower Michiganders, rather than giving more leeway to corporations to pick our pockets. One of our biggest assets in this fight is the Federal Trade Commission, which we should bolster to prevent companies from consolidating and colluding to raise prices. I believe in universal childcare and a massive increase in housing investments to reduce the price of rental and homeownership. Finally, healthcare is one of the fastest growing costs in Americans’ lives, which is why Medicare for All is a central part of my campaign, and I will be proud to make it the first bill I co-sponsor in Congress. Medicare for All is the only way to truly fix our broken healthcare system. Eliminating extreme out-of-pocket costs and guaranteeing coverage would pull millions of Americans out of the trap of medical debt, which we should eliminate entirely.

How would you approach federal spending and the national debt? Identify one major area of federal spending you would reduce, reform or protect from cuts.

Responsible fiscal policy is not about slashing programs with no regard for their function – we’ve seen how Elon’s DOGE has played out, and it’s completely disrupted our government’s ability to provide for Michiganders. We need to tax billionaires their wealth to create trillions in new revenue for critical programs. We need to curb our over-inflated military budget that is being spent to make war that only makes us less safe and raises our energy prices. I oppose any and all cuts to Medicare, Medicaid, Social Security, and other programs that folks need to get by, and believe we need more investment in programs that support Americans in their daily lives, such as childcare, paid leave, and Medicare for All.

What role should the federal government play in abortion, contraception and reproductive health care after the fall of Roe v. Wade? Should Congress set a national standard, and if so, what should it be?

Healthcare choices belong to a patient and their doctor and true reproductive choice must be accessible to all. I will cosponsor the Women's Health Protection Act to codify Roe v. Wade into federal law and will oppose any attempts to enact a national abortion ban. I am committed to repealing the discriminatory Hyde Amendment that blocks federal Medicaid funding for abortion services. I’ll vigorously defend funding for Planned Parenthood and other vital reproductive health centers, while opposing the direction of funds to deceptive anti-abortion "crisis pregnancy centers." Additionally, I will defend the right to family planning by cosponsoring the Right to Contraception Act. I will protect access to abortion medications like mifepristone by assuring that science, and only science, sets the standard by which we decide what medications are safe. As a champion for Medicare for All, I will work to guarantee that comprehensive reproductive healthcare is fully covered for every American.

The Senate has become a place where nominees, budgets and major legislation often stall because of partisan warfare. What Senate rule, norm or practice would you change to make the chamber function better, and what would you preserve?

We need to eliminate the Senate filibuster. It has only functioned as a roadblock to progress, causing intense partisan gridlock rather than facilitating compromise. It allows politicians afraid to take tough votes to hide from their constituents. But we cannot talk about reform without highlighting the influence of corporate money in our politics. You can count on your hand the number of Senators who have never taken corporate PAC money, and I’ll be proud to join that list when I make it to the senate. We need to pass legislation that prohibits members of congress from accepting corporate PAC money and bars them from trading individual stock. Without ridding the congress of dark money and corporate interests, it will not truly represent the people.

Health care costs continue to strain families, employers and government budgets. Do you believe Congress should pursue incremental reforms, such as lowering prescription drug prices and expanding subsidies, or sweeping changes, such as a public option or Medicare for All? What model would you support, and how would you pay for it?

As a doctor and former public health official, one of the first pieces of legislation I will sponsor in the US Senate is a bill to enact Medicare for All and eliminate medical debt nationwide. I spent my career fighting to fix our healthcare system and even wrote the book "Medicare for All: A Citizen’s Guide" to help folks understand how we can achieve a healthcare system that works for everyone. Beyond introducing legislation, I will use this office as a platform to change the conversation about healthcare in America and continue to galvanize a movement to elect leaders across the country who support Medicare for All. We already pay massive amounts of money for healthcare, but we pay it into corporate insurers rather than into a truly universal system. Medicare for All would reduce our overall costs while providing truly universal, durable coverage with no out-of-pocket costs or coverage drops.

Presidents of both parties have increasingly used executive orders to bypass Congress, and President Donald Trump has tested the limits of executive power through emergency declarations, aggressive agency action and attempts to pressure independent institutions. What specific limits should Congress place on presidential power, and where would you be willing to challenge Trump (or a president from your own party)?

Congress holds numerous checks over the executive branch that Congress has either weakly enforced or not utilized at all. My role as a U.S. Senator will be to throw sand in the gears of the Trump administration whenever possible to ensure that authoritarianism cannot creep further into our government. I will lead efforts to repeal the Authorization for Use of Military Force, which has allowed Trump to lead us into wars of aggression and raise prices on everyday goods, and wield my nomination powers to block the appointment of any nominee who swears blanket loyalty to the Trump administration. I also believe we must reform the presidential pardon and appoint oversight boards over critical organizations like the CDC to protect them from political games.

A measure to call a state Constitutional Convention is on this year's ballot. Do you plan to vote in favor of a con-con?

No

text:
Miami-Dade Democrats have endorsed Eliott Rodriguez for Florida’s 27th Congressional District in his race against Republican incumbent María Elvira Salazar. After a distinguished career reporting the news in South Florida, he is running for Congress with a platform centered on lowering the cost of living, protecting Social Security and Medicare, pursuing comprehensive immigration reform and bringing greater independence and accountability to Washington. His campaign has made South Florida’s affordability crisis a central issue.

Rodriguez has also earned the endorsement of the Miami Herald Editorial Board.

A History of Telling South Florida’s Story

For generations of Miami residents, Eliott Rodriguez has been a familiar face.

The son of Cuban immigrants, Rodriguez moved to Miami with his family when he was 12. He attended Shenandoah Junior High, studied at Miami Dade College and graduated from the University of Miami.

His journalism career began in newspapers before moving into television. Over the years, he reported for the Miami News and Miami Herald and worked at WTVJ, WPLG and CBS News Miami.

Rodriguez covered many of the stories that shaped modern South Florida, from Hurricane Andrew and the Mariel boatlift to the Surfside condominium collapse. His international reporting took him throughout Latin America, including assignments in Cuba, Panama, Nicaragua and Venezuela.

During his career, he received three Emmy Awards, four Edward R. Murrow Awards and the Silver Circle Award from the National Academy of Television Arts and Sciences.

His campaign for Congress is rooted in many of the same issues he spent his career covering: the rising cost of living in South Florida, immigration and government accountability.

A Focus on Affordability and Miami Families

Rodriguez has made affordability a centerpiece of his campaign.

His proposals include expanding workforce housing and incentives for first-time homebuyers, encouraging housing construction near transit and employment centers, pursuing a federal backstop to help stabilize Florida’s homeowners insurance market, and strengthening protections against price fixing and hidden fees.

On healthcare and retirement security, Rodriguez says he will defend Medicare, Medicaid, Social Security and Affordable Care Act coverage. He supports allowing Americans between ages 55 and 64 to voluntarily buy into Medicare and additional efforts to lower prescription drug costs.

On immigration, Rodriguez supports secure borders and faster immigration and asylum processing while also calling for humane treatment and comprehensive reform. His platform includes protections for Dreamers, Venezuelans and Haitians and fair processing for eligible Cubans with unresolved immigration cases.

He has also called for stronger congressional ethics rules, restrictions on stock trading by members of Congress and greater oversight of presidential power.

Voting Against Investments That Helped Miami-Dade

Salazar’s record also includes votes against major Biden-era legislation that ultimately brought substantial federal investment to Miami-Dade.

In 2021, she voted against the American Rescue Plan. Miami-Dade later received approximately $527.7 million from the law to maintain government services and respond to the economic effects of the pandemic.

She also voted against the bipartisan infrastructure law, which passed the House with support from Democrats and 13 Republicans and later funded transportation and infrastructure projects throughout South Florida.

Perhaps the clearest example came with the 2023 federal spending package. Salazar helped secure $4.17 million for Miami-Dade stormwater improvements and police technology, but then voted against the final legislation containing that funding. The package ultimately provided more than $20 million for Miami-Dade resilience projects.

These votes raise a straightforward question about whether District 27 should be represented by someone who will consistently support the investments South Florida families and communities depend on.

Immigration and Accountability

Immigration is another major dividing line in the race.

Rodriguez has criticized Salazar for supporting Republican immigration policies and funding while later distancing herself from the Trump administration’s enforcement approach.

In September, Salazar released a campaign advertisement saying some of Trump’s immigration enforcement efforts had gone “too far.” Rodriguez responded that mass deportation had long been part of Trump’s stated agenda and argued that Salazar was trying to distance herself from policies she had previously supported.

For Rodriguez, the issue is not simply rhetoric. His campaign argues that Miami deserves representation willing to stand up for immigrant families consistently, not only when political pressure grows.

The Choice in District 27

Both candidates come from Cuban-American families, built prominent careers in South Florida television and have deep connections to Miami-Dade.

But they offer voters very different approaches to Congress.

Salazar has represented the district since 2021 and has repeatedly supported major pieces of the Republican legislative agenda, including votes against federal investments that later delivered hundreds of millions of dollars to Miami-Dade.

Rodriguez is asking voters to send him to Washington for the first time. His campaign is focused on affordability, housing, healthcare, Social Security and Medicare, immigration reform and greater accountability in government.

After a career spent asking questions and reporting on the decisions that shaped South Florida, Rodriguez is now asking voters to give him the opportunity to help make those decisions in Congress.

The Miami-Dade Democratic Party has endorsed Eliott Rodriguez for Congress in Florida’s 27th District.

text:
With a month until the midterm elections, President Trump is hitting the campaign trail in an effort to ramp up voter turnout across traditionally red states, as rising costs and a deeply unpopular Iran war leave the GOP scrambling to protect its majority in Congress.

Trump’s October campaign blitz will feature stops in Oklahoma, Alabama, Ohio, Texas and Nebraska — Republican-friendly states that he comfortably won in 2024. The stops are part of the party’s strategy to replicate Trump’s 2024 success and voter turnout as the party grapples with Trump’s souring approval ratings ahead of November.

Several toss-up races have moved towards Democrats, indicating potential success for the party in November. The nonpartisan election handicapper Cook Political Report last week shifted the Senate races in Kansas and South Carolina towards Democrats, while 10 GOP House seats are now looking more likely to flip.

Vice President Vance is also hitting the campaign trail, with plans to head to Alaska for a midterm rally amid the red state’s highly competitive Senate race.

The campaign push comes as Republicans contend with voter concerns over the economy and the ongoing war with Iran, which has caused energy prices to surge and has become a point of tension for some GOP candidates.

Senate nominee Rep. Ashley Hinson (R-Iowa) publicly broke from Trump over the conflict, saying Iowans “shouldn’t have to foot the bill at the pump or the checkout line for the war in Iran.”

Trump, meanwhile, has increasingly tied the end of the war and economic relief to the election. While he has floated a prediction that the conflict will end after the November elections, he told reporters at a campaign rally in Oklahoma that he thinks it’s possible the war could cost him the midterm elections.

The Supreme Court is also taking center stage as the justices prepare to begin a new term Monday, with major cases involving immigration, gun rights, voting and religious freedom on the docket.

Justice Samuel Alito will make a rare Sunday show appearance this weekend on “Fox News Sunday” alongside Attorney General Todd Blanche.

Immigration is poised to remain a major issue before the justices, with prominent challenges to the Trump administration’s policies among the cases the court has agreed to hear, including the legality of Trump’s mandatory detention policy.

In a major expansion of the government’s immigration powers, the administration argues it can lawfully detain individuals without bond if they are found to have entered the country unlawfully, even if they have lived on U.S. soil for years.

The Trump administration also made a major push on artificial intelligence this week, with the president signing an executive order alongside leading tech executives focused on the development of AI and renaming it “superintelligence.”

As part of a series of other AI initiatives, the administration launched America.gov, an AI-powered portal intended to streamline access to federal services.

Executives from technology giants, including Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and xAI founder Elon Musk, all made a voluntary pledge outlining commitments surrounding the development of the advanced technology. Trump described the agreement as “morally binding.”

Elsewhere, a high-profile sexual assault investigation at Cornell University and Tennessee’s botched attempt to execute convicted murderer Christa Pike have dominated headlines.

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul (D) appointed state Attorney General Letitia James as a special prosecutor to investigate allegations that a 20-year-old Cornell student, labeled Jane Doe, was drugged and gang raped by seven men at a fraternity house in 2024.

The case has drawn renewed national attention following a civil lawsuit and questions surrounding the initial investigation, which concluded without criminal charges. Thomas Guiffra, an attorney representing the Cornell Jane Doe, will appear on CNN’s “State of the Union” this Sunday.

Meanwhile, Tennessee officials are facing scrutiny following two failed lethal injection attempts that have left death row inmate Pike is currently on life support and in critical condition.

Pike was convicted of first-degree murder in 1996 after admitting to murdering her 19-year-old classmate Colleen Slemmer with her then-boyfriend Tadaryl Shipp.

The botched execution attempts prompted Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee (R) to halt the state’s remaining executions for the year and order an independent investigation.

description:

David Brouillette of Manchester was identified by several people who know him, including an ex-wife, as the agent who shot Durán Guerrero.

text:
It’s been almost three months since Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero‘s death, and his family is still not used to the quiet.

Martha Karolina Rojas Alvarez, his widow, said he used to come home from a day of work — mornings at PetSmart, afternoons and evenings driving for DoorDash — and talk about his day, then ask about hers. He doted on their young daughter, reserving Monday afternoons for time with her.

“He didn’t like to be alone,” she said. “He always liked to be with us, to go out, to eat, visiting the lake … or simply staying at home and watching movies.”

On July 13, a Monday morning, Durán Guerrero was shot and killed by a federal immigration agent in Biddeford.

His death, and others by agents for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, have spurred protests and backlash across the country. Democratic members of Congress have held two forums since Durán Guerrero’s death, and his family is being represented by Gideon Asen, a law firm that has pursued high-profile lawsuits in Maine, including a recent complaint against several ICE agents accused of forcefully arresting a civil engineer in the country legally.

In an interview on Thursday, Durán Guerrero’s widow and his sister said they have been heartened by the support, and they want answers about what happened. They spoke in Spanish to the Portland Press Herald with their attorneys present, and a translator from Presente! Maine, a nonprofit that supports the state’s immigrant community.

“We would love to see above all a transparent investigation, that the people involved face consequences,” his sister, Daniela Durán Guerrero, said through translator Mae Hickey. “He was a good person, he was just working for his family.”

TAKING TIME FOR FAMILY

Durán Guerrero was the youngest of three siblings. He grew up in Bucaramanga, Colombia, hanging out with other kids in their neighborhood and riding his bike outside, his sister said. Daniela remembered helping him talk to their parents when he was scared of getting in trouble.

“Even though we were different, on separate paths, we were always together,” she said through an interpreter.

Durán Guerrero met Rojas Alvarez when they were teenagers. He lived in the same neighborhood and they would see each other every day, courting her and trying to catch her attention, she said. Years later, he was excited to learn she was pregnant and that they were starting a family. She said they came to the United States to work hard and give their daughter a better future.

Once here, Rojas Alvarez said, he worked long days but still took time for his family. His sister said he regularly helped bring her kids to school.

“He would put his work stuff on pause to help me do that,” she said.

He was the kind of uncle who spoiled her kids with video game gift cards and he liked getting everyone together.

“For me, it was really important, because me and him grew up together,” his sister said. “We were always together, so that’s why it was really important for me, for my kids to grow up together with their family, as well.”

‘TOOK A LITTLE PIECE OF EVERYONE’

The Office of the Maine Attorney General announced it was investigating the incident for deadly use of force and for any criminal activity. The office said it had no public updates on Friday. The Department of Homeland Security’s Office of the Inspector General announced an investigation into the shooting, as well, saying it was routine for all shootings involving one of its officers.

DHS has declined to identify the agents involved in the Biddeford shooting. David Brouillette of Manchester was identified by several people who know him, including an ex-wife, as the agent who shot Durán Guerrero.

Brouillette has not responded to numerous requests for comment and a phone number for him was still out of service on Friday.

Attorneys Benjamin Gideon and Sean Murphy, who are representing Durán Guerrero’s family, have criticized the Trump administration following a report from CBS that the FBI is not conducting a review for civil rights violations, citing a Department of Justice official. The New York Times also reported in July on guidance ICE agents received that month, saying that the FBI would no longer be investigating claims of assault against them.

The DOJ and DHS did not respond to requests for comment.

Murphy, a former federal prosecutor, told members of Congress during a forum on Sept. 22 that this was unusual.

Durán Guerrero’s sister and his widow say they, too, are calling for accountability.

“Through this community support we’ve come to understand it shouldn’t have happened this way, it should never have happened,” Rojas Alvarez said.

And while they wait for answers, they also want the world to know that Durán Guerrero was a good person who “took a little piece of everyone with him” when he was killed.

They said they honor him in their homes, where they keep small pictures of him near images of saints and a candle.

And, they said, by sharing his story.

text:
Transcript

SCOTT SIMON, HOST:

This week, the U.S. Supreme Court agreed to take up President Trump's mandatory immigration detention policy. And that is the focus of this week's immigration briefing.

(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)

SIMON: A weekly look at the Trump administration's immigration crackdown. This week, we're looking at Cuban Americans in Miami and their reaction to the president's aggressive enforcement operations in southern Florida. NPR immigration reporter Sergio Martínez-Beltrán joins us now. Sergio, thanks so much for being with us.

SERGIO MARTÍNEZ-BELTRÁN, BYLINE: Good to be with you, Scott.

SIMON: This week, the Supreme Court agreed to look at the legality of the administration's policy that denies bond hearings for detained immigrants in the U.S. What do we know about this policy?

MARTÍNEZ-BELTRÁN: This policy is part of President Trump's efforts to deport as many immigrants as possible. And at the core of this case the Supreme Court will take up is whether immigrants in the interior of the U.S. have a right to a bond hearing to decide whether they must stay in detention while they fight their deportation. Now, the Trump administration has said immigrants should face mandatory, indefinite detention without hearings while they challenge their removal.

The justices will only decide this term on whether this policy violates current federal law. They're not taking up the broader legal question of whether Trump's policy violates constitutional due process protections. So far, though, the appeal courts have been split on this question, although most have ruled this mandatory detention violates due process and federal law because they're holding people without a bond hearing.

SIMON: And how are the administration's actions different from what past presidents have done?

MARTÍNEZ-BELTRÁN: So other presidents have interpreted the law to apply only to those immigrants who have just crossed the border. Those folks were the ones to face mandatory detention. But for the Trump administration, it applies to immigrants who have been in the interior of the U.S. for years, some for many decades. You know, these folks have built families and businesses in the U.S. And the vast majority have no criminal record. So yeah, I mean, it's very different to what we've seen with other administrations.

SIMON: And how many people are in immigration detention right now?

MARTÍNEZ-BELTRÁN: Well, the last batch of government data was released in July. And it shows that there were about 66,000 immigrants in detention. Nearly 71% of detainees have no criminal convictions. But we know August was a very active month, so that number of detention might be higher. The Department of Homeland Security says ICE agents arrested nearly 51,000 immigrants in August. That's a monthly record high, Scott. The Trump administration says, overall, it has deported over 600,000 immigrants so far.

SIMON: Thousands of those deported are Cubans. This is a group of the population that historically has supported Republicans and many of President Trump's policies. You were in Miami recently, reporting on Cubans there. What did you find?

MARTÍNEZ-BELTRÁN: Well, there's a lot of discontent and frustration among Cubans and Cuban Americans in south Florida. A big part of it is because the Trump administration has said that many Cubans who arrived in the U.S. during the Biden administration do not qualify to get a permanent residency through the Cuban Adjustment Act. That's a Cold War-era law that protected Cubans fleeing communism. Now, that change is currently being challenged in court.

But in the meantime, Cubans have been deported to third countries like Mexico, where the administration has sent nearly 6,000 Cubans. And many others have been sent to African countries, including Aristides Fernandez Garcia. He was deported to the Central African Republic. He told NPR he's gotten sick there. He's still in detention. And he feels he has lost precious time.

ARISTIDES FERNANDEZ GARCIA: (Speaking Spanish).

MARTÍNEZ-BELTRÁN: Time with family, time with older people, those who have less time left, he says, that's something you can't recover. Not even with millions of dollars.

For now, the U.S. Supreme Court has allowed the Trump administration to continue with the third-country deportations, but the court has agreed to take up this issue as well this term.

SIMON: Now, Sergio, what have been some of the political consequences of these policies with Cubans and other Latino groups in south Florida?

MARTÍNEZ-BELTRÁN: Well, so far, it doesn't look great for Trump and his party. You know, I talk to many Cubans and Cuban Americans who say they feel disappointed. They are scared. They are angry at Trump's policies. You know, many of the Cubans felt that Trump's crackdown was not going to reach them, in part because Cubans have been historically shielded from shifting immigration policies. But that's not the case anymore. That's what Michael Bustamante told me. He teaches Cuban American history at the University of Miami.

MICHAEL BUSTAMANTE: People who have been here for 30, 40 years are often elderly or often vulnerable. They're being deported to Mexico - to southern Mexico - with not really having a path to immigration status in Mexico either. They're sort of stateless, effectively, as a result of this.

MARTÍNEZ-BELTRÁN: And now we're seeing more Republican elected officials denounce or push back against Trump on this issue. Congresswoman Maria Elvira Salazar - who represents south Florida and has been a staunch Trump supporter - she released an ad recently, telling Trump that Hispanics who helped get him elected in 2024 now feel betrayed, and that his immigration policies have gone too far. She's in a tight reelection race. But this discontent goes way beyond Florida, Scott.

In West Virginia, Republican Senator Jim Justice said recently, the Trump administration should take a step back, acknowledge it's doing something wrong and adjust its immigration enforcement approach. And all of this is happening, of course, as we're just a month away from the midterm elections.

SIMON: NPR's Sergio Martínez-Beltrán with this week's immigration briefing. Sergio, thanks so much.

MARTÍNEZ-BELTRÁN: You're welcome.

(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)

text:
In a new lawsuit the Council on American-Islamic Relations and CAIR-Florida are asking for emergency relief

October 3, 2026 8:00 am

ACLU of Florida

Media Contact

125 Broad Street

18th Floor

New York, NY 10004

TALLAHASSEE — On Friday, the Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR) and CAIR-Florida told a federal court that their civil rights work in Florida is in imminent danger after Gov. Ron DeSantis and other Cabinet officials baselessly voted to designate them as “domestic terrorist organizations” under an unconstitutional new state law. They asked the court for emergency relief to block the designation from going into effect. The filing comes in a new lawsuit the groups filed after the Florida Cabinet’s vote.

“For decades, we and CAIR-Florida have pursued a shared mission, rooted in faith, to help people understand Islam, protect civil rights, promote justice, and empower the millions of American Muslims across the country,” said CAIR. “Gov. DeSantis and other officials in his cabinet have spent months targeting us for our beliefs and civil rights work for months. If this unjustifiable designation is allowed to go into effect, our speech will be silenced, our advocacy will be halted, and our doors will be shut in Florida. This harms not only CAIR and CAIR-Florida, but all Floridians who believe in a vibrant constitutional democracy where people of all religious traditions can thrive.”

Under HB 1471, five Florida executive officials have the power to designate and debilitate U.S. groups—including nonprofits engaged in First Amendment-protected advocacy—without filing charges, initiating judicial proceedings, proving their case beyond a reasonable doubt, submitting the case to a jury, or complying with any of the other constitutional requirements of the criminal legal system. As the lawsuit explains, “The new regime transforms Florida’s Governor, Chief of Domestic Security, and Cabinet into judge, jury, and nonprofit executioner.”

Once designated, an elaborate set of prohibitions makes it a serious crime for the targeted American organization to do virtually anything in the state, and for others to work for or otherwise actively associate with it. The consequences of violating these prohibitions are severe, including up to life imprisonment. As a result of designation, an organization’s lawful, constitutionally protected speech and association are immediately rendered illegal and impossible—simply because a handful of state oﬃcials say so.

“We’re asking for urgent judicial intervention to prevent CAIR and CAIR-Florida from becoming the first casualties of Florida’s unconstitutional and draconian new law,” said Hina Shamsi, director of ACLU’s National Security Project. “The Constitution does not allow officials to punish U.S. organizations and deny them due process because of disagreement with their views, yet Florida’s Governor and Cabinet did so anyway. It’s hard to overstate the stakes here, not only for our clients, but also for other nonprofits and corporations that Florida officials may decide they dislike and want to target in the future.”

CAIR and CAIR-Florida initially challenged their designation under the new Florida law in a suit filed on July 1, the day the law went into effect, and Gov. DeSantis said he and other Cabinet officials would move quickly to designate CAIR. On October 1, the court dismissed their initial case, finding that the nonprofits did not have standing in July because their fears of harm were speculative. Hours later, counsel for CAIR and CAIR-Florida filed a new complaint, explaining that Gov. DeSantis and other Cabinet members had followed through on their threats and voted to designate CAIR and CAIR-Florida on September 29, 2026.

The complaint makes clear that this designation violates the non-profits’ First Amendment rights, as well as their right to due process and right to counsel. Targeted organizations receive no meaningful notice and have no meaningful opportunity to defend themselves before the designation and harsh penalties take effect. Florida’s law is also preempted by federal law.

“Without evidence, fair notice, or any opportunity to respond, Florida officials have arbitrarily and unjustly branded CAIR and CAIR-Florida with the scarlet letter of a 'DTO' designation, effectively rendering them pariahs.” said Scott McCoy, deputy legal director, Southern Poverty Law Center. “This designation is a political act that violates the First Amendment and due process rights of two nonprofit organizations that have served Floridians for more than 25 years. If state officials can do this to CAIR and CAIR-Florida with impunity, they can do it to any organization whose message they dislike.”

The designation, which effectively criminalizes the existence of any labeled organization, is set to go into effect on November 5. If it does, the impact on CAIR and CAIR-Florida would be immediate and devastating. In their October 2 motion for emergency relief, the nonprofits are asking that the court order Florida officials to rescind their designation of CAIR and CAIR-Florida and prevent it from going into effect. In the alternative, they are asking the court to prevent Florida state prosecutors from enforcing the law’s harsh penalties against the nonprofits and third parties connected with them.

The impact on the Floridian communities CAIR and CAIR-Florida serve would also be immense. CAIR-Florida provides a range of pro bono legal services to Florida residents, including those who suﬀer government and workplace discrimination in violation of their civil rights, as well as those navigating the immigration system. They help register people to vote, dispel and counter false stereotypes, prejudices, and disinformation, of Muslims, and advocate for human rights. For example, CAIR and CAIR-Florida supported the campaign to bring back Mohammed Ibrahim—a 16-year-old U.S. citizen from Florida—who was unjustly detained by Israel in February 2025 for almost ten months.

“No state government should hold the power to unilaterally extinguish domestic advocacy organizations because of their First Amendment-protected activity," said Daniel Tilley, legal director, ACLU of Florida. “Our democracy depends on freedom of speech and association and is fueled by those who advocate for their communities. For decades, CAIR and CAIR-Florida have sought to support a vibrant constitutional democracy where people of all religious traditions can thrive. This baseless designation will substantially harm the thousands of American Muslims who rely on CAIR’s advocacy — and we refuse to let it stand.”

CAIR and CAIR-Florida have done nothing to deserve this devastating designation. As the complaint explains, the state has never indicted, much less convicted, either CAIR or CAIR-Florida under any criminal law—and certainly not a criminal law involving the serious charge of terrorism. title: Adelanto ICE medical staff repeatedly failed detainee who died, internal report says
description:
Medical staff at the Adelanto ICE Processing Center repeatedly failed 39-year-old Ismael Ayala-Uribe before he died in custody, according to a mortality review by investigators with ICE’s Health Services Corp.
She has researched conditions inside ICE detention centers for about eight years.

“A medical staff member informed the officer all medical staff were preoccupied with other emergencies, and medical staff were waiting on a custody officer who could bring Mr. Ayala-Uribe to the medical clinic,” states the report.
text:
Medical staff at the Adelanto ICE Processing Center repeatedly failed 39-year-old Ismael Ayala-Uribe before he died in custody, according to a mortality review by investigators with ICE’s Health Services Corp.

The former DACA recipient died from complications related to a pelvic abscess while in ICE custody on September 22, 2025, a coroner’s report states, after being detained for nearly a month inside the Adelanto detention center, federal authorities said.

At least 27 detained people died after medical care failings while in U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention nationwide, according to dozens of ICE death reports briefly published by the agency last week.

This publication reviewed copies of the records obtained by Project Salt Box, an independent publication that focuses on ICE’s detention system, before the ICE website removed them.

Ayala-Uribe’s death was “very preventable,” said Dr. Katherine Peeler, an assistant pediatrics professor at Harvard Medical School and medical advisor with Physicians for Human Rights who reviewed the mortality report. She has researched conditions inside ICE detention centers for about eight years.

The report on Ayala-Uribe’s death comes as the Adelanto ICE Processing Center faces ongoing scrutiny over alleged inhumane conditions, including claims of inadequate medical care.

At least five people have died after being detained at Adelanto in the second Trump administration, four of which were connected to substandard medical care, according to the California Attorney General’s office 2026 report on ICE detention centers in the state.

In a request for comment on the findings about Ayala-Uribe’s death, an unnamed Department of Homeland Security spokesperson said that detained people receive comprehensive medical care from the moment a person enters ICE custody.

“This is the best healthcare that many aliens have received in their entire lives,” the spokesperson said.

ICE’s mortality review committee found that the care the Adelanto ICE facility provided to Ayala-Uribe “deviated beyond safe limits of practice.”

Here’s how the Adelanto ICE facility failed Ayala-Uribe, according to the mortality review:

Medical staff did not thoroughly evaluate him or complete wellness checks

Nurses did not adequately tell the on-call provider about his medical status

Medical staff did not effectively transfer care from one staff member to another

Medical staff did not consistently respond to Ayala-Uribe’s complaints in a timely manner

Ayala-Uribe did not receive all of his medications

Medical staff did not adequately document all of his care in a timely fashion or note all discussions related to his care

Adelanto’s lack of staffing hindered their ability to provide their patients medical care in a timely manner, the report states.

Jesus Arias, the lawyer representing Ayala-Uribe’s family, said the findings aren’t surprising. He’s also representing two other families whose loved ones died after being detained at Adelanto.

“They don’t care about the people that have symptoms or conditions that could be easily resolved until it’s way too late. … If you’re sick in Adelanto, you’re at risk of dying,” he said.

“This was not supposed to happen to Ismael,” he said.

Ismael Ayala-Uribe, 39, grew up in Westminster after being brought over from Mexico when he was four-years-old. He was detained by federal immigration agents on Aug. 17, 2025 during a raid at an Orange County car wash, and taken to the Adelanto ICE Processing Center on August 22, 2025, federal authorities said.

His mother visited him every week at the Adelanto facility and saw her son’s health decline, she said previously.

Ayala-Uribe was healthy when he was initially detained, his family has said, but he developed a cough that turned into fevers.

On September 17, 2025, Ayala-Uribe submitted a request for health services for a painful buttock abscess, the report states. A nurse documented the receipt two days later.

A day after he submitted the request, however, Ayala-Uribe suffered a medical emergency related to the abscess.

No medical care provider examined him, records show.

He had been given a variety of pain medications and laxatives, “but nothing to actually address what was going on,” Dr. Peeler said. “No examination to say, ‘Well, this is an abscess that should be actually addressed surgically or we should add antibiotics.’ None of that occurred.”

Two days later, on the morning of September 20, 2025, facility staff asked medical personnel to provide a wellness check on Ayala-Uribe due to his “ill appearance,” but medical staff did not respond to the request, records show.

Later that night, facility staff again requested that medics evaluate Ayala-Uribe. “A medical staff member informed the officer all medical staff were preoccupied with other emergencies, and medical staff were waiting on a custody officer who could bring Mr. Ayala-Uribe to the medical clinic,” states the report.

On the following day, Ayala-Uribe was transferred to a hospital after a nurse documented his severe pain related to the lump on his buttock. He was shaky and had vomited. He was admitted to the hospital for a list of reasons, including sepsis — a life-threatening response to an infection.

Ayala-Uribe died the following day at the hospital.

Jose, Ayala-Uribe’s younger brother, welcomed the report.

“It’s helping show what’s going on in there, in Adelanto, any detention center,” Jose said in an interview.

The report on Ayala-Uribe was part of a trove of dozens of internal in-custody death reviews dating back to 2019 that ICE published on Friday, September 25. ICE had removed the documents from their site by the following Monday morning, said Michael Wriston, a cofounder of the Project Salt Box.

But not before the publication archived all 33 mortality reports.

“Across the board with these reports, what we noticed was just a complete lack of medical regard for people in ICE’s care. That failure to provide medication on time, failure to get people to a clinic that was capable of caring for their needs in a timely manner directly contributed to people’s deaths,” Wriston said.

ICE and DHS did not respond to emails asking why the dozens of death reports were taken down.

text:
California Gov. Gavin Newsom signed a bill earlier this week that would impose a 25% tax on private detention centers, a policy that would apply to all the facilities that partner with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in the Golden State.

"If we can’t kick out private facilities, we’ll go after their profits," Newsom said in a press release.

The move, which Newsom hailed as a way to push back against President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown and what he sees as the practice of privatizing federal enforcement, is raising concerns among immigration experts who believe the increased tax could force the government to explore alternative sites less suited to housing detainees.

It also poses questions about what would happen if all eight of ICE's detention centers chose to suspend operations in California.

CITIZENS BANK CUTS TIES WITH ICE PRISON CONTRACTORS AFTER MONTHS OF ACTIVIST PRESSURE

That’s the view of Hans von Spakovsky, senior legal fellow and an immigration expert with Advancing American Freedom, a conservative-leaning think tank.

"It's very clear that there's only one purpose to this California gigantic tax increase, and that is to make sure that the federal government cannot find any private property owners, any private contractors in California that are willing to lease space to the federal government," Spakovsky said in an interview with Fox News Digital.

"The alternative for the federal government is to look at all the different federal properties that the government actually owns out there, over which neither Newsom nor anybody else in California can impose any kind of tax, and see if any of those federal facilities can be converted to being a detention facility."

Spakovsky explained that could mean repurposing warehouses or office space.

The newly minted law, AB 1633, is among 20 bills that Newsom signed Tuesday. In its current form, the 25% tax applies to the gross income of any private detention center and applies to federal, state and local contract recipients.

Revenue from the bill will go to a Due Process for All Fund, designated for immigration-related services, according to the bill’s language. Now that AB 1633 has been signed into law, it will go into effect July 1, 2028.

Newsom also signed a handful of other restrictions.

ICE EYES $20M PURCHASE OF ELECTRIC SHOCK GLOVES AS HOCHUL WARNS OF LEGAL CONSEQUENCES

"We’re also banning the Orwellian practice of using shock gloves in enforcement activity as well as further protecting access to our court system," Newsom said.

"We may not be able to dictate federal immigration policy, but we can make clear that activities taking place in California will be subject to California law."

Despite Newsom’s framing, Spakovsky believes the governor will affect federal immigration law enforcement by limiting the overall space it has to operate.

He pointed to reporting from Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) that details its detention needs. He explained that the government relies on private contractors, at least partially, to avoid the costs of building their own facilities.

"If you look at that report, currently ICE has about enough detention space for about 66,000 aliens. OK, that's the full size of the federal government's detention capacity," Spakovsky said.

If an entire state’s private detention contractors decided the tax is too high, ICE’s overall capacity could shrink.

California is home to eight ICE detention centers, according to reporting from the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). All of them are privately operated.

The GEO Group, a corrections company, owns five facilities. Imperial Valley Gateway Center LLC, a local detention company, owns one more. Two more were purchased by DHS in July but are run by CoreCivic, a prison company, and have contracts through 2027 and 2029.

Although the bill won’t go into effect until 2028, in Trump’s last year of his second term, Spakovsky believes the government might begin evaluating where else it can find partnerships to meet its detention needs sooner rather than later.

ICE MAKES NATIONWIDE ARRESTS OF ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS, MURDERERS, PEDOPHILES IN HOLIDAY BLITZ

"Look, if I was the federal government and I couldn't find enough federal properties in California to do this, I would then go into neighboring friendlier states that I could quickly transport aliens I've detained, and I would lease and rent facilities there.

"I'd go to Arizona. I'd potentially go to Nevada. I'd go to other states where they might be eager for federal government money and the increased employment from private contractors hiring people to work on these facilities."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The office of Gavin Newsom did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Fox News Digital.

text:
Layoffs at a statewide immigrant rights nonprofit raise questions about how the group will continue to run an ICE reporting hotline and other services that assist people facing deportation.

The Washington Immigrant Solidarity Network, or WAISN, terminated more than half of its staff in September, with most of the 18 cuts happening this week. A recently formed WAISN union claims supporters of the union were terminated in retaliation.

A spokesperson from WAISN’s leadership said the group has struggled to raise funds over the past year, a growing financial crisis that the organization had flagged in public messages earlier this year.

“The far-right has made the roadmap for this clear: intimidation and threats from the current administration have led funders who once saw themselves as allies to our movement to reassess political risk and pull back funding, leaving organizations like ours in incredibly challenging financial straits,” a WAISN spokesperson wrote in an emailed statement.

“Institutional philanthropy is not the only place where funding has shrunk. Immigrant and refugee-serving organizations and communities are also not receiving the same level of support from city, county, and state governments, which are facing immense pressure from the federal administration.”

The network operates as a statewide resource for immigrant and other community groups to reach out to when confronted with immigration enforcement issues. That includes documenting potential constitutional rights violations during an arrest on the street, accompanying immigrants to their immigration hearings, and other financial resources as a result of lost work, or family members.

“We will be operating under limited capacity, but the core resources supporting Washington’s immigrant communities will remain,” a WAISN statement said.

The eliminated positions include administrative staff, rapid-response coordinators, and hotline operators.

The group is temporarily shortening its hotline operating hours to 7 a.m. to 2 p.m. but said it will remain open Monday to Friday, with interpretation available in 300 languages. WAISN said they’ll also continue to help people in detention pay bond and also respond to accompaniment requests, among other ongoing services.

The staff and funding cuts come at a time when immigration arrests across Washington and the country are facing new highs, with more calls coming into the hotline. Former employees report receiving a thousand calls a week.

Over the past year, tensions had also escalated within the organization, and parts of the community it served, according to Marsha Enriquez, WAISN’s former finance and operations coordinator.

“ The hotline shared multiple times that they were understaffed, that they were burnt out, that they did not have the mental capacity to take on every single call,” Enriquez said.

“The workload was increasing. We were trying to find solutions and, and suggestions for how to repair this distrust with the community and to try to listen to the community concerns.”

Enriquez said part of the distrust stemmed from community requests the organization couldn’t provide, like food assistance. There was also a call for WAISN to be more actively present in the community, she said.

WAISN has regularly provided workshops and resources for volunteer immigrant advocate groups, with much of the training happening online.

Amid the increase in work, Enriquez said leadership was pursuing priorities that were not reflected in the needs workers heard through the hotline. Workers wanted more scaled down and grassroots community-facing events, legal clinics, and more hotline workers.

Everyone knew they were in financial troubles, and were trying to find ways to adjust, Enriquez said. But executive staff, including Brenda Rodriguez and Catalina Velasquez, hadn’t taken pay cuts, Enriquez pointed out, and they kept three assistants working for them.

“We have a five-person team for the executive team, but we [had] three operators in the hotline for the whole state of Washington.”

After four employees were laid off in early September, the workers decided to unionize.

“ We needed a voice at the table,” said Enriquez, who was also the union's co-chair. “ We tried to follow the proper protocols. We asked for voluntary recognition. We shared our working conditions on our Instagram page in hopes of letting the community know what we were experiencing internally at WAISN, and why things needed to change, and why a union was so important.”

Enriquez said WAISN refused to recognize the union, and instead all the workers who backed the effort have been let go. As of Wednesday 18 of the 32 staffers at WAISN are no longer at the nonprofit. A majority of them are unrecognized union workers or management who supported the effort.

Meanwhile, the terminated unionizing employees are fundraising as they decide what to do next. Other immigrant response groups are still trying to figure out how they’ll move forward as immigration arrests continue.

text:
Over 30 organizations submit emergency UN request after ICE removes individuals with final removal orders from its Online Detainee Locator System

September 30, 2026, Washington, DC – Earlier today, a group of over 30 organizations petitioned the United Nations Working Group on Enforced or Involuntary Disappearances (WGEID) to intervene after U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) removed thousands of detained immigrants with final orders from its Online Detainee Locator System (ODLS) on September 15, limiting their access to legal counsel, the court system, and due process.

ODLS is an online system used to track the locations of individuals in ICE custody. Originally created in 2010, it has become an especially crucial tool for attorneys, families, and community members amid the Trump administration’s extraordinary efforts to arrest, detain, and deport noncitizens – often without notice or due process, and pursuant to third-country agreements.

Detained immigrants are regularly transferred among hundreds of detention sites nationwide. Without ODLS, family members have no way to locate their detained loved ones, and attorneys cannot pursue legal avenues of relief for their clients, including motions to reopen, appeals, habeas petitions, or stays of deportation.

“The new ODLS policy is aimed at forcibly disappearing and secretly detaining noncitizens with final orders of removal,” said the signatories. “By subjecting noncitizens to this policy, the United States has placed these individuals beyond the reach of legal protections, and rendered them particularly vulnerable to unlawful detention and deportation.”

ICE made no public announcement or warning prior to this new policy change, leaving attorneys and family members to scramble for information after their clients and loved ones’ locations were removed from the system on September 15.

In one case cited in the petition, attorneys at the Robert & Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center were unable to locate their clients – a breastfeeding mother and her 7-year-old daughter – after their abrupt removal from ODLS, temporarily obstructing the clients’ access to counsel and leaving family members terrified about their possible deportation. Other participating organizations highlighted similar client stories, including an LGBTQ+ asylum seeker from Ghana whose legal team at Human Rights First has been unable to pursue lawful avenues for relief because they cannot confirm his location.

One client quoted in the report described the terror he felt when his mother, an elderly asylum seeker with a disability, disappeared from the ICE locator: "We speak on the phone at least three times every day. Several days ago, I became extremely frightened when, because of a technical problem, phone service at the detention facility was suddenly cut off. She did not call me the entire day, and by that evening I checked the ICE detainee locator webpage and discovered that she had disappeared from it. I almost had a heart attack because she had always been listed there, and then she suddenly vanished. At that moment, the darkest thoughts imaginable went through my mind as to what my mother could be going through.”

The participating organizations called upon the UN WGEID to issue a formal declaration stating that the new ODLS policy is a form of enforced disappearance; recommend an immediate end to the policy; and conduct an urgent on-site trip to the United States to investigate.

"At the Center for Constitutional Rights, we have two clients who have been 'disappeared' from the ICE online locator," said Senior Staff Attorney CJ Sandley. "Thankfully we know where they are currently, but they could be whisked away in the dark of night to another detention or a third-country, and we would not know where they are for hours or days. This is, of course, a strategic move on ICE's part: to further isolate people from their communities and lawyers in moments of high need. We are asking the U.N. Working Group to call this what it is: unlawful disappearances."

The UN WGEID was created in 1980 to investigate enforced disappearances, which are formally defined as “the arrest, detention, abduction or any other form of deprivation of liberty by agents of the State” followed by “a refusal to acknowledge the deprivation of liberty or by concealment of the fate or whereabouts of the disappeared person.” The UN Human Rights Committee has previously determined that such disappearances violate the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, which the United States ratified in the early 1990s.

The full list of signatories includes Abolitionist Law Center, Human Rights Program; Acacia Center for Justice; ACLU of Louisiana; American Gateways; Americans for Immigrant Justice; Amnesty International; CAIR-Chicago (The Chicago office of the Council on American-Islamic Relations); Cameroon Advocacy Network; Center for Constitutional Rights; Chicago United Families Coalition; Estrella del Paso; Florence Immigrant & Refugee Rights Project; Haitian Bridge Alliance; Human Rights First; Immigrant Children Advocates' Relief Effort (ICARE); Immigrant Defenders Law Center (ImmDef); Immigrant Legal Resource Center; Law Offices of Stephen C. Zollman; Lawyers for Good Government; LSN Legal LLC; Mountain State Justice; New Jersey Consortium for Immigrant Children; Prisoners' Legal Services of New York; Public Counsel; RAICES; Refugees International; Robert & Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center; Sur Legal Collaborative; The Immigration Project Inc.; VECINA; Witness at the Border; and Young Center for Immigrant Children's Rights
